steps.title: Naïve Bayes score
steps.text: Each class scores s_c = P(c)·P(x₁∣c)·P(x₂∣c). The probabilities given are already for the observed values (x₁=1, x₂=0), so use them directly. Remember that P(T) = 1 − P(S).

steps.title: Score for S
steps.text: Multiply P(S) = 0.4 by the two probabilities given under S, 0.8 and 0.25.

check.retry: Include the prior 0.4 as well as both feature probabilities.

steps.title: Score for T
steps.text: T's prior is the complement of S's. Multiply it by 0.2 and 0.5.

check.prompt: What is s_T?
check.retry: P(T) = 1 − 0.4. Multiply it by T's two probabilities.

steps.title: Normalise across both classes
steps.text: P(S∣x) is s_S divided by (s_S + s_T). Give it as a fraction or decimal, and say which class MAP picks. Show both scores and the normalisation, since each is worth 2 marks.

solution: Priors: P(S) = 0.4, P(T) = 0.6. The given probabilities already refer to the observed values x = (1, 0).
Answer: P(S∣x) = 4/7 ≈ 0.571, so MAP chooses S.

steps.title: Bayes' rule for two classes
steps.text: With two exhaustive classes, P(1∣E) = P(E∣1)P(1) / [P(E∣1)P(1) + P(E∣2)P(2)]. Compute the score likelihood × prior for each class first, then normalise.

steps.title: Weighted score for each class
steps.text: Multiply each class's likelihood by its prior: class 1 uses 0.8 and 0.3, class 2 uses 0.2 and 0.7.

check.prompt: What is the score of class 2, P(E∣2)·P(2)?
check.retry: Use the likelihood of E under class 2 (0.2) and class 2's prior (0.7).

steps.title: Evidence total
steps.text: The two scores add up to P(E), the normaliser.

check.prompt: What is P(E) = s₁ + s₂?
check.retry: Add the two prior-weighted likelihoods from the previous step.

steps.title: Normalise and choose
steps.text: Divide class 1's score by P(E) to get P(1∣E), as a fraction and a decimal. Then name the class with the larger posterior, which is the MAP class. Show both scores, since each criterion is worth 2 marks.

solution: Answer: P(class 1∣E) = 12/19 ≈ 0.632, so the MAP (more probable) class is class 1.

steps.title: The inequality to test
steps.text: The triangle inequality says the direct distance from 0 to 2 must be at most the distance 0→1 plus 1→2. Compute both sides using squared Euclidean distance d²(a,b) = (a − b)².

steps.title: Direct squared distance
steps.text: Compute d²(0,2).

check.retry: Square the coordinate difference 2 − 0.

steps.title: Sum of the two hops
steps.text: Compute d²(0,1) + d²(1,2).

check.why: Each hop has squared distance 1² = 1, so the sum is 2.
check.retry: Each hop moves one unit; square each and add.

steps.title: State the violated comparison
steps.text: Write both computed values, then state which side is larger and why that contradicts d(0,2) ≤ d(0,1) + d(1,2). Two marks for the distances, two for the comparison.

solution: Triangle inequality requires d(0,2) ≤ d(0,1) + d(1,2).
Squared Euclidean: d²(0,2) = (2 − 0)² = 4.
Since 4 > 2, the triangle inequality is violated, so squared Euclidean distance is not a metric.

steps.title: Three linkages from one table
steps.text: All three linkages use the same cross-cluster distances |a − b| with a ∈ {1,3} and b ∈ {7,10}. Single takes the minimum, complete the maximum, and average the mean over all |A||B| pairs.

check.prompt: What is the sum of the four cross-pair distances?

steps.title: Apply each aggregation
steps.text: Take the minimum, the maximum and the sum divided by the number of pairs.

check.prompt: What is the average-linkage distance?
check.retry: Divide the sum by the 4 pairs, not by 2.

steps.title: Write the three values
steps.text: List the four cross distances, then state the single, complete and average linkage values, naming which aggregation each uses.

solution: Single linkage = minimum = 4.
Complete linkage = maximum = 9.

steps.title: Assign, then average
steps.text: In 1D with two centers, the assignment boundary is the midpoint between them: points below it go to the lower center. Each center then moves to the mean of its assigned points.

steps.title: First assignment
steps.text: With centers 0 and 9, find the midpoint boundary and split 0, 2, 5, 9.

check.prompt: What is the boundary between centers 0 and 9?
check.why: (0 + 9)/2 = 4.5, so 0 and 2 go to center 0 and 5 and 9 go to center 9.
check.retry: Average the two centers.

steps.title: Update the centers
steps.text: Average each cluster.

check.prompt: What is the new center of {5, 9}?
check.why: (5 + 9)/2 = 7; the other center is (0 + 2)/2 = 1.
check.retry: Add 5 and 9 and divide by 2.

steps.title: Reassign with the new centers
steps.text: Find the new boundary between 1 and 7 and check whether any point crosses it.

check.prompt: What is the new boundary between centers 1 and 7?
check.why: (1 + 7)/2 = 4; 0 and 2 are below it, 5 and 9 above.
check.retry: Average the two updated centers.

steps.worked: Boundary 4: 0, 2 still go to center 1 and 5, 9 still go to center 7.

steps.title: Report the round and the check
steps.text: Write the first clusters and the updated centers, then compare each point with the new boundary and state whether any assignment changed (and so whether K-means has converged).

solution: Initial centers 0 and 9 give boundary 4.5, so clusters are {0, 2} and {5, 9}.
Updated centers: (0 + 2)/2 = 1 and (5 + 9)/2 = 7.
New boundary (1 + 7)/2 = 4; 0 and 2 lie below it and 5 and 9 above it.
No assignment changes, so the algorithm has reached a fixed point with centers 1 and 7.

steps.title: Shape and parameter formulas
steps.text: Apply O=⌊(I+2P−F)/S⌋+1 to height and width separately, because the input is not square. The depth equals the number of filters. Parameters = K(F_h·F_w·C_in + 1).

steps.title: Output height
steps.text: Use I=12, P=1, F=3, S=2. Work out (12+2−3)/2, then take the floor before adding 1.

check.prompt: What is the output height?
check.retry: Take the floor of 5.5 first, then add 1.

steps.title: Output width
steps.text: Repeat the calculation with I=10 and the same P, F and S.

check.prompt: What is the output width?
check.retry: Work out (10 + 2 − 3)/2, take the floor, then add 1.

steps.title: Parameters
steps.text: Each filter is 3×3×3 and has one bias. There are four filters.

check.prompt: How many trainable parameters does the layer have?
check.why: Each filter has 3·3·3 + 1 = 28 parameters, and 4·28 = 112.
check.retry: Remember that each filter spans all 3 channels and has its own bias.

steps.title: Report shape and count
steps.text: Write the output as height × width × depth, with the depth equal to the 4 filters, using the height and width you found. Then give the parameter count, showing the weights and biases. Neither the output size nor the stride changes the parameter count.

solution: Depth is the number of filters, 4, so the output is 6×5×4.
Parameters: 4(3·3·3 + 1) = 4·28 = 112 (108 weights and 4 biases).

steps.title: Cross-correlation means no flip
steps.text: In the CNN convention, put filter [[1,−1],[0,1]] directly on top of patch [[3,2],[1,4]], multiply the entries in matching positions, add the products, then add the bias once.

check.prompt: Which patch entry is multiplied by the filter's top-right weight −1?
check.why: Without a flip, top-right lines up with top-right: the patch value 2.
check.retry: Cross-correlation keeps the filter's orientation. Find the patch's top-right entry.

steps.title: Aligned products and their sum
steps.text: Work out 3·1, 2·(−1), 1·0 and 4·1, then add the four products. Leave the bias for the next step.

check.prompt: What is the sum of the four aligned products?
check.retry: The products are 3, −2, 0 and 4. Add them.

steps.title: Add the bias and report
steps.text: Add the single bias −1 to the dot product from the previous step. No activation is applied. Show the aligned products, their sum and the bias step, then state the raw output.

solution: Align the filter with the patch without flipping it: (3,1), (2,−1), (1,0), (4,1).
Products: 3, −2, 0 and 4. Their sum is 5.
Add the bias once: 5 + (−1) = 4.
Raw output before activation: 4.

steps.title: Spatial size and depth
steps.text: Use O=⌊(16−2)/2⌋+1 on each spatial axis. Max pooling works on each channel separately, so the 8 channels stay as they are.

check.prompt: What is the pooled height? (The width works out the same.)
check.why: ⌊14/2⌋ + 1 = 8 on each axis.

steps.worked: ⌊(16 − 2)/2⌋ + 1 = 8 per axis, and the depth stays 8, so the output is 8×8×8.

steps.title: Parameters and what is lost
steps.text: Max pooling just keeps the largest of the four values in each window. Decide whether it learns anything, and what happens to the three values that are thrown away.

check.prompt: Which is a genuine information loss from 2×2 max pooling?
options: The exact position of the maximum inside each 2×2 window, and the other three values
check.why: Only the maximum survives. Where it was and how big the other values were is lost. Channels are kept, and there are no weights.
check.retry: Out of four numbers in a window, how many survive, and is their position recorded?

steps.worked: 0 trainable parameters. Each window keeps only its maximum, so the precise location within the window and the other three activations are lost.

steps.title: Write the three facts
steps.text: State the output shape (pooled spatial size × unchanged depth), the number of trainable parameters, and one specific kind of lost information, such as position or the non-maximum values.

solution: Spatial size: ⌊(16 − 2)/2⌋ + 1 = 8 on each axis. Pooling works per channel, so the depth stays 8. The output is 8×8×8.
Max pooling has no trainable weights or biases, so it has 0 parameters.
Information lost: only the maximum of each 2×2 window is kept, so its exact position inside the window and the other three activations are thrown away.

steps.title: Lookup vs reasoning
steps.text: Compare the systems by their input and their decision process. A lookup returns a stored record that matches a key. A reasoning system builds or compares alternatives against an objective and can change its choice when conditions change.

steps.title: The barcode scanner
steps.text: Describe the scanner's input and what it does with it.

check.prompt: How does the barcode scanner decide what to return?
options: It retrieves the record whose key matches the barcode
It compares candidate products against an objective
It learns a new product from each scan
check.why: Input: the barcode. Decision: exact key match against a stored table; nothing is weighed.
check.retry: Does the scanner weigh any alternatives, or just find a match?

steps.worked: Input: the barcode. Process: a key-to-record lookup. Output: the stored product record. No alternatives are compared.

steps.title: The journey planner
steps.text: Describe the planner's input and why a road closure changes its output.

check.prompt: When a road closes, the planner returns a different itinerary because…
options: it re-evaluates route alternatives with the closed road removed
its stored itinerary record is overwritten by an administrator
it imitates what a human driver would say
check.why: The closure changes the set of feasible routes, so re-optimising gives a new best route.
check.retry: What changes in the planner's search space when a road closes?

steps.worked: Input: the map, origin, destination and current road status. Process: search over route alternatives and pick the best by time/distance. A closure removes edges, so the search returns a new best itinerary.

steps.title: Write your answer
steps.text: Write two short parts: (1) the scanner's input and lookup mechanism; (2) the planner's inputs, how it compares routes against an objective, and how the closure changes the result. Each part is worth 2 marks.

solution: Barcode scanner: its input is the barcode. It performs a lookup, returning the stored product record whose key matches; no alternatives are weighed.

Journey planner: its inputs are the road map, origin, destination and current road conditions. It searches over alternative routes and selects the one that best meets its objective (e.g. shortest time).
When a road closes, those routes become infeasible, so the planner re-runs its search and returns the new best itinerary. Its decision adapts to conditions; the lookup's does not.

steps.title: Back up from the leaves
steps.text: Each MIN node takes the minimum of its leaves; then the MAX root takes the maximum of those MIN values. A big single leaf (like 9) is not available to MAX if MIN can avoid it.

steps.title: Left MIN node
steps.text: Back up the left MIN node with leaves [9,1].

check.prompt: What value does the left MIN node back up?
check.why: min(9,1)=1; MIN avoids the 9.
check.retry: MIN picks the smaller leaf.

steps.title: Right MIN node
steps.text: Back up the right MIN node with leaves [5,6].

check.prompt: What value does the right MIN node back up?
check.retry: Take the smaller of 5 and 6.

steps.title: MAX decides
steps.text: Write both MIN values, then let MAX take the larger. State which branch MAX picks and the value it guarantees under optimal play.

solution: Left MIN node: min(9,1) = 1.
Right MIN node: min(5,6) = 5.
MAX root: max(1,5) = 5, from the right branch.
Answer: MAX chooses the second (right) branch and guarantees a value of 5.

steps.title: Cutoff rule
steps.text: Search left to right, depth first. A MIN child lowers β; once β ≤ α (α inherited from the MAX root) the MIN node's remaining leaves are skipped.

steps.title: Left MIN node and α
steps.text: Evaluate the left MIN node [8,5] fully, then pass its value up to the root as α.

check.prompt: What is the root's α after the left branch?
check.why: min(8,5)=5, so MAX can guarantee at least 5.
check.retry: The left MIN node returns the smaller of 8 and 5.

steps.title: First leaf of the right node
steps.text: The right MIN node starts with α=5, β=+∞ and reads its first leaf 3.

check.prompt: After reading 3, what happens at the right MIN node?
options: β=3 ≤ α=5, so 7 and 9 are skipped
β=3, but 7 and 9 must still be read
check.why: The node is worth at most 3 < 5, so MAX would never pick it; its other leaves cannot matter.
check.retry: A MIN leaf updates β, then compare β with α.

steps.worked: β = 3 ≤ α = 5, cutoff: leaves 7 and 9 are not examined. Right node is worth ≤ 3.

steps.title: Write the trace
steps.text: State α after the left branch, β after the first right leaf, name the pruned leaves, and give the root value with the chosen branch (pruning does not change it).

solution: Left MIN node: min(8,5) = 5, so root α = 5.
Right MIN node: first leaf 3 sets β = 3; now α = 5 ≥ β = 3, so cut off.
Leaves 7 and 9 are pruned; the right node is worth at most 3.
Root value = max(5, ≤3) = 5 via the left branch, the same as full minimax.

steps.title: Measure the gap
steps.text: Compare training error 3% with validation error 22%. A large gap together with low training error points to variance rather than bias.

check.prompt: What is the validation-minus-training gap in percentage points?
check.why: 22 − 3 = 19 points. That is a large gap, while training error is already low.
check.retry: Subtract the training error from the validation error.

steps.worked: Gap = 22 − 3 = 19 points, with training error only 3%.

steps.title: Read the more-data result
steps.text: Validation error fell from 22% to 13% when more data was added. Decide which error source responds like this.

check.prompt: Validation error dropping sharply with more data is evidence of…
options: high variance (overfitting), since more data reduces sensitivity to the sample
high bias, since more data increases capacity
irreducible noise, which more data removes
check.why: Extra data mostly reduces variance. Bias depends on model capacity, and noise cannot be reduced at all.
check.retry: Which part of the error depends on which particular sample was drawn?

steps.worked: Validation error fell by 9 points (22 → 13) with more data. That is consistent with variance or overfitting, not high bias.

steps.title: Choose an intervention and a check
steps.text: Pick something that reduces variance and say how you would confirm it works without touching the test set.

check.prompt: Which plan fits the evidence?
options: Collect more representative data, use valid augmentation or stronger regularisation, and compare validation error
Use a much larger model and judge it on training error
Tune regularisation strength on the test set
check.why: It targets variance and checks the result on held-out validation data.
check.retry: The problem is variance. Which plan reduces it and checks on the right split?

steps.worked: Add representative data, use label-preserving augmentation or increase weight decay or dropout, then confirm that validation error drops and the gap narrows.

steps.title: Write evidence then action
steps.text: Part 1 (2 marks): explain what the 3%/22% gap and the fall to 13% with more data show. Part 2 (2 marks): give a variance-reducing intervention and say you will confirm it on validation data.

solution: Training error is low (3%) but validation error is 22%, a 19-point gap. That pattern means high variance, or overfitting.
More data brought validation error down to 13%, a 9-point improvement. That backs up the diagnosis, since extra data mainly reduces variance.
Intervention: add more representative data, use label-preserving augmentation, or strengthen regularisation (weight decay or dropout).
Check: compare validation error and the train–validation gap before and after the change, and keep the test set for the final report.

steps.title: What memorisation means
steps.text: A deep network trained on only 100 examples has far more capacity than it needs, so it can fit each example perfectly, noise included. Good remedies either add variety to the data or limit what the model can rely on.

steps.title: Remedy on the data side
steps.text: Pick a remedy that makes the training inputs more varied without changing their labels.

check.prompt: How does label-preserving augmentation reduce memorisation?
options: It shows the model varied versions of each example, so it must learn features that hold across them
It removes hard examples from the training set
It adds the test set to training
check.why: Variations such as small shifts, crops or flips that keep the class mean the model cannot memorise one exact input.
check.retry: What changes about the inputs the model sees on each pass?

steps.worked: Augmentation (small crops, flips, colour jitter that keep the label) gives many variants of each of the 100 examples, so the model has to learn invariant features.

steps.title: Remedy on the model side
steps.text: Pick a second, different remedy that limits the model, and state its mechanism.

check.prompt: Which pairing of remedy and mechanism is correct?
options: Dropout: random masks stop units relying on fragile combinations of other units
Weight decay: makes weights larger so the fit is sharper
Dropout: removes training examples at random
check.why: Dropout randomly switches off units during training. Weight decay (L2) shrinks large weights. Neither removes data.
check.retry: Dropout masks units, not examples. Weight decay pulls weights towards zero.

steps.worked: Dropout resamples masks every update so units cannot co-adapt. Alternatively, weight decay penalises large weights, which gives a smoother function.

steps.title: Write two remedies and the check
steps.text: Give two distinct remedies, for example augmentation and dropout or weight decay. For each, say how it reduces memorisation. Finish by saying you tune their strength on validation data and watch the train–validation gap.

solution: Remedy 1: label-preserving augmentation (small shifts, crops, flips, colour jitter). It turns each of the 100 examples into many varied inputs, so the network has to learn features that stay the same across them instead of memorising exact pixels.

Remedy 2: dropout or weight decay. Dropout randomly masks units during training so the network cannot rely on fragile combinations of units. Weight decay penalises large weights, which favours a smoother, simpler function.

Check: tune the augmentation and regularisation strength on a validation set and confirm that validation error falls and the train–validation gap shrinks. Too much regularisation can cause underfitting.

steps.title: Where the leak happens
steps.text: PCA learns a mean and principal directions from the data it is fitted on. Ask which samples that included when it was fitted before the folds were made.

check.prompt: Why is fitting PCA on all samples before k-fold cross-validation a problem?
options: Each validation fold's data helped choose the components the model is evaluated with
PCA cannot handle more than k samples
PCA uses the labels, so the folds are mislabelled
check.why: The held-out fold helped define the feature space, so the CV score is optimistic. This leaks even though PCA never sees the labels.
check.retry: Did the held-out samples help decide the projection the model is trained and scored with?

steps.worked: Fitting PCA on all samples uses each held-out fold's distribution to choose the mean and components. That leaks information, so CV accuracy is overstated.

steps.title: The correct workflow
steps.text: Every learned preprocessing step has to be re-fitted inside each fold, using only that fold's training part.

check.prompt: Inside one fold, what is the correct order?
options: Fit PCA on the training folds, transform both training and validation folds with it, train, then score on the validation fold
Fit PCA on the validation fold, then train on the training folds
Fit PCA once on all data, then shuffle the folds again
check.why: The validation fold is only transformed with components learned elsewhere, just as new data will be.
check.retry: Which data should PCA learn from in a fold, and which data does it only transform?

steps.worked: For each fold: fit PCA (and any scaler) on the training part only, transform the training and validation parts with it, fit the model, score on the validation part, then average over folds. A pipeline object does this automatically.

steps.title: Write problem and fix
steps.text: Part 1 (2 marks): name the leak, meaning held-out folds influence the PCA components, and its effect, an optimistic score. Part 2 (2 marks): describe fitting PCA inside each training fold and only transforming the validation fold.

solution: Problem: PCA fitted on all samples learns its mean and components partly from the samples that later act as validation folds. That leaks information about the held-out distribution into training, so cross-validation scores are too optimistic, even though PCA does not use labels.
Fix: in each of the k folds, fit PCA (and any scaling) only on that fold's training part.
Use that fitted PCA to transform both the training part and the held-out fold, train the model, and evaluate on the held-out fold. Average over folds, for example with a pipeline object.

steps.title: A* priority
steps.text: For every node on OPEN record g (cost from A), h (given) and f=g+h. Always expand the smallest f, and stop only when G is removed from OPEN.

steps.title: Expand A
steps.text: A generates B with g=3 and C with g=1. Add each h.

check.prompt: What is f(B) after expanding A?
check.why: g(B)=3 and h(B)=3, so f=6; C has f=1+4=5.
check.retry: f = g + h with g(B)=3 from the edge A→B.

steps.title: Expand C and update B
steps.text: C has the smallest f. Its edge C→B gives a new path to B. Compare its g with the stored g(B)=3.

check.prompt: What is B's new g via A→C→B?
check.why: 1+1=2 < 3, so B's g, f and predecessor are updated.
check.retry: Add g(C)=1 to the cost of C→B.

steps.worked: g(B)=2, f(B)=2+3=5, predecessor of B becomes C.

steps.title: Expand B and reach G
steps.text: B (f=5) is now the only node on OPEN. Expanding it generates G through B→G with cost 4.

check.prompt: After G is generated from B, may A* stop?
options: Yes, once G is removed from OPEN as the smallest-f node, which happens next
Yes, A* always stops the moment a goal is generated
No, A* must first expand every node in the graph
check.why: The goal test is applied when G is removed; here G is the only (and so smallest-f) entry, so it is removed next.
check.retry: A* tests for the goal when a node leaves OPEN.

steps.worked: G: g=6, f=6, predecessor B. G is then the smallest (only) entry on OPEN and is removed, ending the search.

steps.title: Report the result
steps.text: Write the f scores after expanding A, the update of B (new g, f and predecessor), then follow the predecessors back from G to give the route and its cost when G is removed from OPEN.

solution: Expand A: C has g=1, f=1+4=5; B has g=3, f=3+3=6.
Expand C (f=5): path A→C→B gives g(B)=1+1=2 < 3, so update B to g=2, f=5, predecessor C.
Expand B (f=5): generate G with g=2+4=6, f=6+0=6.
Remove G from OPEN at f=6; predecessors give G←B←C←A.
Answer: route A→C→B→G with cost 6.

steps.title: What must be shown
steps.text: With unit costs, consistency means h(n) ≤ 1 + h(n') for every legal move n→n', plus h(goal)=0. Manhattan h sums, over numbered tiles only, each tile's row and column distance from its goal square.

steps.title: What one move changes
steps.text: A legal 8-puzzle move slides one tile into the blank. Think about how many tiles change position and by how far.

check.prompt: During one legal move, which numbered tiles change position?
options: Exactly one tile, by one orthogonal square
Every tile in the moved tile's row
check.why: Only the tile next to the blank slides one square; the blank is not counted in h.
check.retry: The blank swaps with one neighbouring tile.

steps.worked: Exactly one numbered tile moves one square up, down, left or right; every other tile's Manhattan term is unchanged.

steps.title: Bound the drop in h
steps.text: A one-square move changes that tile's row or column distance by exactly 1 in some direction.

check.prompt: By at most how much can h decrease in one move?
check.why: The moved tile's term changes by ±1 and no other term changes, so h(n) − h(n') ≤ 1.
check.retry: Only one tile's distance changes, and it moves one square.

steps.title: Write the proof
steps.text: Write: (1) each action moves exactly one numbered tile one orthogonal step, so only its term changes, by 1; (2) hence h(n) ≤ 1 + h(n') on every arc, and at the goal every tile is home so h(goal)=0. Each part is worth 2 marks.

solution: Manhattan h(n) is the sum, over numbered tiles (blank excluded), of each tile's row plus column distance to its goal square.
Each unit-cost action slides exactly one numbered tile one orthogonal square into the blank; all other tiles keep their terms.
That tile's distance changes by exactly 1, so h can drop by at most 1: h(n) ≤ 1 + h(n') = c(n,n') + h(n') for every legal move.
At the goal every tile is in place, so h(goal)=0. Both conditions hold, so Manhattan distance is consistent.

steps.title: What greedy ranks by
steps.text: Greedy best-first picks the OPEN node with the smallest h(n). The g values are listed in the question, but greedy does not use them.

steps.title: Choose the next expansion
steps.text: Compare h(B)=1 with h(C)=5.

check.prompt: Which node does greedy best-first expand next?
check.why: Greedy uses h alone; comparing f=g+h is what A* would do.
check.retry: Use only the remaining estimates, not the costs already paid.

steps.worked: h(B)=1 < h(C)=5, so greedy expands B.

steps.title: Estimated totals
steps.text: To see what greedy overlooks, compute the estimated total g+h through B and through C.

check.prompt: What is g(B)+h(B)?
check.why: 9+1=10, while C gives 2+5=7.
check.retry: Add B's paid cost 9 to its estimate 1.

steps.worked: Through B: 9+1=10. Through C: 2+5=7. C looks cheaper overall, but greedy never sees that because it ignores g.

steps.title: Write the answer
steps.text: State (1) which node greedy expands and the h comparison that decides it, and (2) why ignoring the already-paid cost g can lead to a goal whose complete path is more expensive, using the totals 10 and 7 as an illustration. Each part is worth 2 marks.

solution: Greedy best-first ranks OPEN by h only: h(B)=1 < h(C)=5, so it expands B next.
It ignores the cost already paid: B has g=9, so a path through B costs at least 9, while C's estimated total is only 2+5=7 versus 9+1=10 for B.
Because greedy never adds g, it can reach and return a goal early along an expensive path, missing a cheaper complete path through C.
Answer: Greedy expands B (h=1); ignoring g means the first goal found can have a higher total path cost.

steps.title: Join then prune
steps.text: Apriori joins two frequent pairs that share the same first item (sorted order) to form a triple, then prunes the triple if any of its three 2-subsets is not frequent.

steps.title: Join step
steps.text: Group the sorted pairs AB, AC, BC, BD, CD by first item and join pairs within a group.

check.prompt: Which triples does the join produce?
options: ABC (from AB, AC) and BCD (from BC, BD)
check.why: Prefix A: AB+AC → ABC. Prefix B: BC+BD → BCD. Prefix C has only CD, so no join.
check.retry: Join only pairs whose first items match.

steps.title: Prune step
steps.text: For each joined triple, list its three 2-subsets and check each against the frequent pairs. Also note why triples such as ABD or ACD can never appear.

check.prompt: Why would ABD be pruned even if it were generated?
options: Its subset AD is not a frequent pair
Its subset BD is not frequent
check.why: AD is not in the frequent list, so by antimonotonicity ABD cannot be frequent.
check.retry: List ABD's 2-subsets and look for one missing from AB, AC, BC, BD, CD.

steps.worked: ABC: AB, AC, BC all frequent → keep. BCD: BC, BD, CD all frequent → keep. ABD and ACD contain AD → pruned.

steps.title: List the candidates
steps.text: List the triples that survive both join and prune, cite their 2-subsets as evidence, and explain the subset check using AD.

solution: Join pairs sharing a prefix: AB+AC → ABC; BC+BD → BCD.
Prune: ABC has subsets AB, AC, BC, all frequent, so it survives.
BCD has subsets BC, BD, CD, all frequent, so it survives.
Any triple containing A and D (ABD, ACD) would contain AD, which is not frequent, so antimonotonicity rules it out.
Answer: candidate triples ABC and BCD.

steps.title: Weighted prefix counts
steps.text: In a conditional pattern base, each prefix path counts as many times as its weight. An item's conditional count is the sum of the weights of the paths that contain it. Here (A,B) has weight 2 and (A) has weight 3.

steps.title: Conditional counts
steps.text: Add the weights of the paths containing A, then those containing B.

check.prompt: Conditional count of A in X's base?
check.why: A is in both paths: 2 + 3 = 5.
check.retry: A appears in (A,B) with weight 2 and in (A) with weight 3.

steps.title: Prune and build itemsets
steps.text: Remove items whose conditional count is below 3. Each surviving item joins X to form a frequent itemset with that count. {X} itself has count equal to all its occurrences.

check.prompt: Is B kept in X's conditional tree with minimum count 3?
options: Yes, because B is frequent globally
Yes, because it shares a path with A
check.why: Pruning uses conditional support; B co-occurs with X only twice.
check.retry: Compare B's conditional count with the minimum count.

steps.worked: B removed. {A,X} has count 5. {X} has count 5 (all five occurrences).

steps.title: List the itemsets
steps.text: Show the weighted sums for A and B, state which item is pruned, and list each frequent itemset containing X with its support count.

solution: Conditional count of A: it appears in (A,B)×2 and (A)×3, so 2 + 3 = 5.
Conditional count of B: it appears only in (A,B)×2, so 2 < 3 and B is removed.
{X} has count 5 (all five occurrences), which is ≥ 3.
Answer: {A,X} with count 5 and {X} with count 5.

steps.title: Two goals, two tasks
steps.text: The shop has two separate goals. Customer segments are groups of similar customers with no predefined labels. Products bought together are co-occurrences inside baskets. Match each goal to a task and to the data shape that task needs.

check.prompt: Finding customer segments without predefined segment labels is which task?
check.why: No labels exist, and the goal is to discover groups of similar customers.
check.retry: Are the segments known in advance, or must they be discovered?

steps.title: Represent customers for segmentation
steps.text: Clustering compares records with a distance or similarity, so each customer must be one record of comparable attributes.

check.prompt: Which representation suits clustering customers?
options: One feature vector per customer (e.g. spend, visit frequency, category shares)
One set of items per transaction
A single total sales figure for the whole shop
check.why: A fixed-length vector per customer lets a distance measure compare customers.
check.retry: What does a distance function need to compare two customers?

steps.worked: Customer i → vector (total spend, visits per month, share of spend per category, ...), scaled, then clustered (e.g. k-means).

steps.title: Represent baskets for co-purchases
steps.text: 'Often bought together' is a co-occurrence question over individual purchases.

check.prompt: Which representation and method find products bought together?
options: Each transaction as a set of items; mine frequent itemsets and association rules
Each customer as a feature vector; cluster the vectors
Each product as a labelled record; train a classifier
check.why: Support and confidence are counted over transactions represented as item sets.
check.retry: Over what unit do you count how often two products appear together?

steps.worked: Transaction t → {bread, milk, eggs}. Run Apriori or FP-growth for frequent itemsets, then derive rules X→Y by confidence/lift.

steps.title: Write both mappings
steps.text: Write two parts: (1) segmentation: representation per customer plus the clustering method; (2) co-purchases: representation per transaction plus association mining. Each part is worth 2 marks.

solution: Segments: represent each customer as a feature vector (e.g. spend, visit frequency, category mix), scale it, and apply clustering such as k-means to discover unlabelled groups.
Co-purchases: represent each transaction as a set of items and mine frequent itemsets and association rules (Apriori or FP-growth), judged by support, confidence and lift.
Answer: feature vectors per customer with clustering for segments; item sets per transaction with association rule mining for co-purchases.

steps.title: Rule measures
steps.text: With N = 20, n(A) = 8, n(B) = 10 and n(A∪B) = 6, write supp = n(A∪B)/N, conf = n(A∪B)/n(A), lift = conf/supp(B).

steps.title: Support and confidence
steps.text: Support divides the joint count by all baskets. Confidence divides the joint count by the antecedent's count.

check.prompt: Confidence of A→B (as a decimal)?
check.why: conf = 6/8 = 0.75: the denominator is the 8 baskets that contain A.
check.retry: Divide the joint count by n(A), not by N or n(B).

steps.title: Baseline and lift
steps.text: The baseline rate of B is n(B)/N. Divide the confidence by it.

check.prompt: What is supp(B), the overall rate of B?
check.why: 10 of 20 baskets contain B, so supp(B) = 0.5.
check.retry: Use n(B)/N.

steps.title: Report and interpret
steps.text: Report support, confidence and lift with their fractions. Interpret lift by comparing B's rate in A baskets with its rate overall, and do not claim A causes B.

solution: Support(A→B) = n(A∪B)/N = 6/20 = 0.30.
Confidence(A→B) = n(A∪B)/n(A) = 6/8 = 0.75.
Interpretation: B appears in 75% of A baskets versus 50% of all baskets, so B is 1.5 times as common when A is present. This is an association, not evidence that A causes B.

steps.title: Two metrics
steps.text: Manhattan: |Δx₁| + |Δx₂|. Euclidean: √(Δx₁² + Δx₂²). The query is the origin, so the differences are just the coordinates of each point.

steps.title: Manhattan distances
steps.text: Sum the absolute coordinates of (3,0) and of (2,2).

check.prompt: What is the Manhattan distance from (0,0) to (2,2)?
check.retry: Add the absolute differences in each coordinate.

steps.title: Euclidean distances
steps.text: Compute √(3² + 0²) and √(2² + 2²).

check.prompt: What is the Euclidean distance to (2,2) (decimal)?
check.retry: Square 2 and 2, add, then take the square root.

steps.title: Compare the rankings
steps.text: State both distance pairs and which point is nearer under each metric, then note that the choice of metric reverses the neighbour ranking.

solution: The metric changes which point is the nearest neighbour.

steps.title: Where the boundary goes
steps.text: With one point per class, the maximum-margin boundary is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them. Both points then become support vectors with scores −1 and +1.

check.prompt: Where is the boundary between (1,0) and (5,0)?
check.why: The perpendicular bisector of a horizontal segment from x₁=1 to x₁=5 is x₁ = 3.
check.retry: Find the midpoint of the two points; the boundary is perpendicular to the segment.

steps.title: Canonical w and b
steps.text: Take w = (w₁, 0). Require w₁·1 + b = −1 for the negative point and w₁·5 + b = +1 for the positive one, then solve.

check.prompt: What is w₁?
check.why: Subtracting gives 4w₁ = 2, so w₁ = 0.5 and b = −1 − 0.5 = −1.5.
check.retry: Subtract the two equations to eliminate b.

steps.title: Full margin
steps.text: The full width between the two support planes is 2/‖w‖.

check.prompt: What is 2/‖w‖ for w = (0.5, 0)?
check.why: ‖w‖ = 0.5, so 2/0.5 = 4, matching the gap between x₁ = 1 and x₁ = 5.
check.retry: Compute ‖w‖ first, then divide 2 by it.

steps.worked: Full width = 2/0.5 = 4, which equals the distance from (1,0) to (5,0).

steps.title: State the separator
steps.text: Give w and b, show they produce scores −1 and +1 at the two points, then state the boundary equation, that both points are support vectors, and the full width.

solution: Set w = (w₁, 0). Canonical equalities: w₁·1 + b = −1 and w₁·5 + b = +1, giving w₁ = 0.5, b = −1.5.
Check: (1,0) scores −1 and (5,0) scores +1, so both are support vectors.
Boundary: 0.5x₁ − 1.5 = 0, i.e. x₁ = 3.
Full margin = 2/‖w‖ = 2/0.5 = 4.

steps.title: Minimum slack
steps.text: From y_i f(x_i) ≥ 1 − ξ_i and ξ_i ≥ 0, the smallest allowed slack is ξ_i = max(0, 1 − y_i f(x_i)).

steps.title: Compute the slack
steps.text: Substitute y_i f(x_i) = −0.3.

check.prompt: What is the minimum slack?
check.retry: Subtracting a negative number adds it.

steps.title: Classification outcome
steps.text: The sign of y_i f(x_i) tells you whether the prediction agrees with the label.

check.prompt: With signed score −0.3 (ξ > 1), the point is…
options: a support vector exactly on its margin plane
check.why: A negative signed score means the predicted sign differs from the label.
check.retry: Is −0.3 positive or negative?

steps.worked: Signed score < 0 (equivalently ξ > 1), so the point is on the wrong side of the boundary.

steps.title: Role of C
steps.text: The objective is ½‖w‖² + C·Σξ_i (or Σξ_i²). Consider what multiplying a fixed ξ by a larger C does.

check.prompt: Raising C does what to the cost of a fixed slack?
options: Increases it, so the optimizer tolerates fewer violations
check.why: Cost = C·ξ grows with C; it pushes toward fewer or smaller violations but cannot guarantee separability.
check.retry: C multiplies the slack term.

steps.worked: Larger C makes each unit of slack more expensive, trading a narrower margin for fewer violations; it does not promise separability.

steps.title: Write the answer
steps.text: State the slack value with its calculation, say whether the point is correctly classified and why, then explain the effect of increasing C on violation cost and the margin trade-off, without claiming it makes the data separable.

solution: The signed score is negative (ξ > 1), so the point is misclassified.
In the objective ½‖w‖² + C·Σξ_i, raising C makes any fixed slack more costly, so the optimizer prefers fewer violations at the expense of a narrower margin; it does not guarantee separability.

steps.title: Deltas and updates
steps.text: Output (linear): δ_o = (t − o)·1. Hidden (ReLU): δ_h = ReLU'(net_h)·v·δ_o. Updates: Δv = η δ_o h and Δw = η δ_h x, both computed from the original weights.

steps.title: Forward pass
steps.text: net_h = w x = 0.5 × 2. Apply ReLU, then o = v h.

check.prompt: What is the output o?
check.why: net_h = 1, so h = 1, and o = 2 × 1 = 2.
check.retry: h = ReLU(0.5 × 2) and o = 2h.

steps.title: Output and hidden deltas
steps.text: δ_o = t − o. Then δ_h = 1 × v × δ_o, using the original v = 2 (ReLU' = 1 because net_h > 0).

check.prompt: What is δ_h?
check.retry: First find δ_o = t − o, then multiply by the old v and by ReLU'(1) = 1.

steps.title: Weight changes
steps.text: Δv = η δ_o h and Δw = η δ_h x. Note that w's input is x = 2.

check.prompt: What is Δw?
check.retry: Multiply η = 0.1, δ_h and w's input x = 2.

steps.title: Apply the updates
steps.text: Add each Δ to its original weight (w_new = w + Δw under the δ = −∂E/∂net convention). Report h, o, both deltas, and the new v and w.

solution: Forward: net_h = 0.5 × 2 = 1, h = ReLU(1) = 1, o = 2 × 1 = 2.
δ_h = ReLU'(1) × v × δ_o = 1 × 2 × (−1) = −2, using the original v.

steps.title: Pre-activation then ReLU
steps.text: For each x, compute net = 2x − 3, then h = ReLU(net) = max(0, net), then o = 3h + 0.5. Keep net and h in separate columns.

steps.title: x = 1
steps.text: Compute net = 2(1) − 3 and apply ReLU.

check.prompt: For x = 1, what is h?
check.why: net = −1 < 0, so ReLU gives h = 0.
check.retry: ReLU outputs max(0, net). Is net negative here?

steps.title: x = 2
steps.text: Compute net = 2(2) − 3, apply ReLU, then the output layer.

check.prompt: For x = 2, what is h?
check.why: net = 1 > 0, so h = 1.
check.retry: 2 × 2 − 3 = ? It is positive, so ReLU leaves it unchanged.

steps.title: Report both cases
steps.text: For each x, write net, h and o. Show that ReLU zeroes the negative pre-activation and that the output still adds the 0.5 offset. The hidden outputs and the outputs are worth 2 marks each.

solution: Answer: x=1 gives h=0, o=0.5; x=2 gives h=1, o=3.5.

steps.title: Why the gradient shrinks
steps.text: In a deep sigmoid network each layer contributes a factor σ'(net) ≤ 0.25 to the backpropagated gradient. A remedy must stop these small factors from compounding.

steps.title: Choose a remedy
steps.text: Choose a change that keeps the local derivative close to 1 along active paths.

check.prompt: Which remedy directly targets the repeated small sigmoid derivatives?
options: Replace sigmoid hidden units with ReLU, whose derivative is 1 when active
check.why: ReLU' = 1 for net > 0, so active paths do not shrink the gradient. A smaller learning rate shrinks steps further, and a larger batch only reduces noise.
check.retry: Which option changes the local derivative factor itself?

steps.worked: Use ReLU activations: for active units the derivative is 1, so the gradient is not repeatedly scaled down by ≤ 0.25.

steps.title: Name a drawback
steps.text: Think about what ReLU's derivative is for a negative pre-activation.

check.prompt: What is a realistic drawback of ReLU?
options: Units with negative pre-activation have zero gradient and can stop learning ('dying ReLU')
ReLU's derivative is also bounded by 0.25
ReLU makes the network linear overall
check.why: ReLU'(net) = 0 for net < 0, so inactive units pass no gradient. Leaky ReLU keeps a small slope there.
check.retry: What is max(0, net)'s slope when net < 0?

steps.worked: Inactive ReLU units (net < 0) have zero derivative and may never recover. Leaky ReLU retains a small negative-side gradient.

steps.title: Write remedy and drawback
steps.text: In two sentences: (1) the remedy and how it keeps gradient flowing through active units; (2) the zero-gradient limitation for inactive units, optionally with leaky ReLU as a fix. Each is worth 2 marks.

solution: Problem: backprop multiplies one σ' ≤ 0.25 factor per sigmoid layer, so gradients reaching early layers vanish.
Remedy: use ReLU hidden units. In the active regime (net > 0) ReLU' = 1, so the gradient is not repeatedly shrunk along active paths.
Drawback: for net < 0 ReLU' = 0, so inactive units receive no gradient and can 'die'. Leaky ReLU keeps a small negative-side slope to mitigate this.

steps.title: Eigenvectors of the covariance
steps.text: The principal directions are eigenvectors Su = λu. For a symmetric matrix [[a,b],[b,a]], try the vectors (1,1) and (1,−1).

check.retry: Each row sums to 3 + 1.

steps.title: Test (1,−1)
steps.text: Multiply the matrix by the orthogonal vector (1,−1) and compare eigenvalues.

check.retry: Compute 3·1 + 1·(−1) for the first entry.

steps.title: Normalize the leading direction
steps.text: Principal directions are unit vectors. Divide (1,1) by its length.

check.prompt: What is the length of (1,1)? (decimal)
check.retry: Square each entry, add, take the square root.

steps.title: State PC1 and its variance
steps.text: Show both eigenpairs to justify the ordering, then give the normalized leading eigenvector (up to sign) and its eigenvalue as the variance.

solution: S(1,1) = (4,4) = 4(1,1), so (1,1) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 4.
S(1,−1) = (2,−2) = 2(1,−1), so (1,−1) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 2.
Since 4 > 2, the first principal direction is along (1,1); normalized it is ±(1,1)/√2.
PC1 = ±(1,1)/√2 with variance 4.

steps.title: Score, reconstruction, error
steps.text: z = uᵀ(x − μ), x̂ = μ + uz, and squared error = ||x − x̂||². Center first.

steps.title: Center and score
steps.text: Compute x − μ = (4,5) − (1,0), then dot with u = (0,1).

check.prompt: What is the score z?
check.retry: Subtract the mean, then take the second coordinate (the dot with (0,1)).

check.prompt: What is the first coordinate of x̂?
check.retry: u has zero first entry, so only μ contributes to it.

steps.title: Squared error
steps.text: Report z and x̂, then form the error vector x − x̂ = (4,5) − x̂ and give its squared length.

solution: Centered point x − μ = (4,5) − (1,0) = (3,5).
Reconstruction x̂ = μ + uz = (1,0) + 5(0,1) = (1,5).
Error vector x − x̂ = (3,0); squared reconstruction error = 3² + 0² = 9.

steps.title: Two different objectives
steps.text: PCA picks the direction of largest variance (an eigenvector of the covariance). OLS of y on x has slope Cov(x,y)/Var(x). Independent x and y means Cov(x,y) = 0, so the covariance matrix is diag(1, 4).

steps.title: PCA direction
steps.text: For a diagonal covariance, the eigenvectors are the coordinate axes and the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries.

check.prompt: Which direction is PC1 for covariance diag(1, 4)?
check.why: The y-axis carries variance 4 > 1.
check.retry: Which axis has the larger variance?

steps.title: OLS slope
steps.text: Compute m = Cov(x,y)/Var(x).

check.prompt: What is the OLS slope?
check.why: Cov(x,y) = 0 for independent variables, so m = 0/1 = 0.
check.retry: What is the covariance of independent variables?

steps.worked: m = 0, so the fitted line is horizontal, direction (1,0).

steps.title: Compare
steps.text: State the PCA direction with its variance justification and the OLS direction with its covariance justification, then note that the two lines are perpendicular because the objectives differ.

solution: Independent x, y give covariance matrix diag(1, 4).
PCA: the largest eigenvalue is 4 along (0,1), so PC1 is the vertical direction.
OLS: m = Cov(x,y)/Var(x) = 0/1 = 0, so the regression line is horizontal (direction (1,0)).
The directions are perpendicular: PCA follows maximal variance, OLS follows how y covaries with x.

steps.title: OLS slope and intercept
steps.text: m = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) / Σ(x − x̄)², b = ȳ − m·x̄. Start with the means of x = 0, 1, 2 and y = 2, 3, 7.

steps.title: Means
steps.text: Compute x̄ and ȳ.

check.prompt: What is ȳ?
check.retry: Add the three y values and divide by 3.

steps.title: Centered sums and slope
steps.text: Deviations: x − x̄ = −1, 0, 1; y − ȳ = −2, −1, 3.

check.prompt: What is Sxy = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ)?
check.retry: Multiply each pair of deviations and add.

steps.title: Intercept
steps.text: Use b = ȳ − m·x̄.

check.prompt: What is b?
check.retry: Substitute ȳ = 4, m = 2.5, x̄ = 1.

steps.title: Predict at x = 3
steps.text: Report m and b with the centered sums, then substitute x = 3 into ŷ = mx + b and state the prediction.

steps.title: Follow the left branch
steps.text: Start at A and always try the leftmost untried child. A's first child is B, and B's only child is D.

check.prompt: After A, which two nodes are visited next, in order?
check.why: Depth-first with left-to-right order goes A→B and then into B's only child D before considering C.
check.retry: Does backtracking try a sibling before the current node's own children?

steps.worked: Visits so far: A, B, D. SL = [D, B, A].

steps.title: Back out of the dead end
steps.text: D is a dead end with no children. Decide how far the path retreats.

check.prompt: After D fails, which nodes leave the current path before the search continues?
options: D and B (B has no other children)
check.why: D is a dead end; B then has no untried children, so it is also a dead end. A still has C, so the retreat stops at A.
check.retry: Does B have any child left to try after D?

steps.worked: DE gains D then B; SL shrinks to [A]; A's untried child C is next.

steps.title: Try the alternative
steps.text: Visit C and apply the goal test.
steps.worked: C is the goal, so the search stops with SL = [C, A], i.e. path A→C.

steps.title: Report visits and path
steps.text: List every visited node in order (2 marks), then give the returned path and note that D and B were dead ends removed from it (2 marks).

solution: From A try B first, then B's only child D: visits A, B, D.
D is a dead end; B then has no untried children, so both go to DE and are removed from the path.
Resume at A's untried child C, which is the goal.
Answer: visit order A, B, D, C; returned path A→C (D and B are dead ends, not part of the path).

steps.title: Where children are inserted
steps.text: The next node is taken from the left of OPEN. BFS appends children at the right (queue); DFS inserts them at the left in left-to-right order (stack). After expanding A, both have OPEN = [B, C] and CLOSED = [A].

steps.title: BFS after expanding B
steps.text: Remove B from OPEN = [B, C], add it to CLOSED, and append its child D at the back.

check.prompt: BFS OPEN after expanding B is…
check.why: FIFO: D goes behind C, which is still waiting.
check.retry: In BFS, do new children go at the front or the back?

steps.title: DFS after expanding B
steps.text: Remove B from OPEN = [B, C], add it to CLOSED, and push its child D on the front.

check.prompt: Left-first DFS OPEN after expanding B is…
check.why: LIFO: D goes in front of C, so it is expanded next; C remains waiting.
check.retry: In DFS, which node should be expanded right after B?

steps.title: Write both states
steps.text: Give OPEN and CLOSED for BFS (2 marks) and for DFS (2 marks), with the next node at the left of OPEN.

solution: Expand A: both searches have OPEN = [B, C], CLOSED = [A].
BFS expands B and appends D at the back: OPEN = [C, D], CLOSED = [A, B].
DFS expands B and pushes D on the front: OPEN = [D, C], CLOSED = [A, B].
Answer: BFS OPEN = [C, D]; DFS OPEN = [D, C]; CLOSED = [A, B] in both.

steps.title: When each direction branches less
steps.text: Forward reasoning fires every rule whose premises match the facts, so many facts mean many branches. Backward reasoning only explores rules that conclude the target, so a single goal with few concluding rules gives a narrow search.

steps.title: Compare the branching here
steps.text: There are thousands of facts, one claim to prove, and only a few rules conclude that claim.

check.prompt: Which direction should you choose?
options: Backward (goal-driven): only a few rules can conclude the claim
Forward (data-driven): there are many facts to start from
Either: the branching is the same in both directions
check.why: Starting from thousands of facts fires many irrelevant rules; starting from the claim touches only the few relevant rules.
check.retry: From which end does the search have fewer starting branches?

steps.worked: Goal-driven: one target and few concluding rules give a small backward branching factor; thousands of facts would make forward search broad and mostly irrelevant.

steps.title: What to inspect first
steps.text: Say what backward reasoning looks at after picking the goal.

check.prompt: What do you inspect first?
options: The rules whose conclusion is the eligibility claim, then their premises
All facts, to see which rules they trigger
The rule with the most premises
check.why: Backward reasoning matches the goal against rule conclusions and turns their premises into subgoals checked against the facts.
check.retry: Which part of a rule is matched against the goal?

steps.worked: Find the rules that conclude the claim; their premises become subgoals, checked against the relevant facts or proved recursively.

steps.title: State choice and justification
steps.text: Name the direction (2 marks), then justify it with the branching argument and say that you inspect the concluding rules and their premises first (2 marks).

solution: Choose backward (goal-driven) reasoning.
Justification: there is a single target and only a few rules can conclude it, so backward branching is small; forward reasoning from thousands of facts would fire many irrelevant rules.
First inspect the rules whose conclusion is the eligibility claim, then treat their premises as subgoals and check the relevant facts.
Answer: Goal-driven search, working backward to the premises of the few rules that conclude the claim.

steps.title: Depth-limited passes
steps.text: With the root at depth 0, bound L allows nodes down to depth L. Each pass is a fresh left-first DFS from A. Here B, C are at depth 1 and D, E at depth 2.

steps.title: Pass with bound 1
steps.text: Visit nodes of depth ≤ 1 in left-first DFS order and decide how the pass ends.

check.prompt: How many nodes are visited in the bound-1 pass?
check.why: A (depth 0), then B and C (depth 1); D and E are beyond the bound.
check.retry: Count the root plus its children only.

steps.worked: Bound 1: A, B, C. No goal found and depth-2 nodes were cut off, so the pass reports cutoff and the bound increases.

steps.title: Pass with bound 2
steps.text: Restart at A and go to depth 2, left-first, stopping at the goal E.

check.prompt: In the bound-2 pass, which node is visited immediately after B?
check.why: Left-first DFS explores B's child D (depth 2 is allowed now) before moving to C.
check.retry: With bound 2, may DFS go into B's child?

steps.worked: Bound 2: A, B, D, C, E. E is the goal, so the pass succeeds with path A→C→E.

steps.title: Report both passes
steps.text: List the visits for bound 1 and bound 2 (2 marks), then say the second pass restarts from A and give the returned path (2 marks).

solution: Bound 1: depth-limited DFS from A visits A, B, C; depth-2 nodes are cut off and no goal is found.
Bound 2: restart from A and visit A, B, D, C, E (left children first).
E is the goal, so the search succeeds and returns path A→C→E.
Answer: Bound 1: A,B,C, cutoff. Bound 2: A,B,D,C,E, success with A→C→E.

steps.title: What the state must record
steps.text: Ask what decides whether 'enter locked room' is legal and what changes afterwards. The robot's location matters (is it next to the door?) and so does whether it holds the key.

check.prompt: Which state is minimal but sufficient for this problem?
check.why: Location decides adjacency and the goal; the key flag decides whether the locked door can be passed.
check.retry: Without a key flag, how would the operator know if the door may open?

steps.worked: State = (room, hasKey), where room is the robot's current room and hasKey ∈ {true, false}.

steps.title: Precondition of the operator
steps.text: Write the conditions that must hold before the robot may enter locked room L.

check.prompt: Enter(L) is legal from state (r, k) when…
options: r is adjacent to L and k = true
k = true, whatever room the robot is in
r is adjacent to L, whether or not it has the key
check.why: The robot must be next to the door and hold the key; both conditions are needed.
check.retry: Can the robot teleport, and can it open the door without the key?

steps.title: Successor update
steps.text: State what the operator changes: the room becomes L. Decide what happens to the key flag under the rules given (nothing says the key is consumed).
steps.worked: Effect: (r, true) → (L, true). The key flag is preserved unless the rules say using the key consumes it, in which case the successor is (L, false).

steps.title: Write state and operator
steps.text: Give the state tuple with the meaning of each component (2 marks), then the operator with its precondition and successor update (2 marks).

solution: State: (room, hasKey), where room is the robot's current room and hasKey is true if it holds the key.
Operator Enter(L) for the locked room L: precondition adjacent(room, L) ∧ hasKey = true.
Update: (room, true) → (L, true); the key status is preserved unless the rules say the key is consumed.
Answer: Use (room, hasKey); entering requires adjacency and hasKey = true, then changes room and keeps the key flag.

steps.title: Pick the right denominators
steps.text: Recall = TP/(TP+FN) uses actual positives. Precision = TP/(TP+FP) uses predicted positives. FPR = FP/(FP+TN) uses actual negatives.

check.prompt: Which counts form the FPR denominator?
check.why: FPR is the fraction of actual negatives wrongly flagged positive.
check.retry: FPR is measured within the population of real negatives.

steps.title: Recall and precision
steps.text: Actual positives = 20 + 5 = 25. Predicted positives = 20 + 10 = 30.

check.prompt: What is the precision (as a fraction or decimal)?
check.retry: Divide TP by everything predicted positive.

steps.title: False-positive rate
steps.text: Actual negatives = FP + TN = 10 + 65 = 75.

check.prompt: What is the FPR?
check.retry: Divide FP by the 75 actual negatives.

steps.title: Report all three
steps.text: Write each metric as formula, substituted counts and value: recall from actual positives, precision from predicted positives, FPR from actual negatives. Naming each denominator earns the method marks.

solution: Answer: recall 0.80, precision 2/3, FPR 2/15.

steps.title: Why averaging helps
steps.text: Averaging many trees reduces variance only to the extent their errors are not correlated. If every tree makes the same mistakes, averaging them changes nothing.

check.prompt: When does averaging B trees reduce variance the most?
options: When the trees' errors are weakly correlated
When each tree is as deep as possible regardless of correlation
check.why: Highly correlated errors do not cancel when averaged; independent-ish errors do.
check.retry: Would averaging ten copies of the same tree change its prediction?

steps.title: Bootstrap alone is not enough
steps.text: Suppose one feature is a very strong predictor. Think about which feature each bootstrap tree would choose at its root.

check.prompt: Without feature subsampling, what happens with a dominant predictor?
options: Most trees split on it near the root, so they look alike and their errors are correlated
Each bootstrap sample hides that feature from the tree
The trees become pure at the root and need no further splits
check.why: Bootstrap samples overlap heavily, so the same strong feature wins the top splits in almost every tree.
check.retry: Bootstrap changes the rows, not the columns. Which feature would the greedy split pick each time?

steps.worked: Bootstrap samples share most rows, so a dominant feature wins the root split in nearly every tree, giving similar trees with correlated errors.

steps.title: What random feature subsets add
steps.text: At each split, a forest considers only a random subset of features. Connect this to diversity and then to the variance of the averaged prediction.
steps.worked: Some splits cannot use the dominant feature, so trees explore other features and structures. Trees become more diverse, their errors less correlated, and averaging/voting reduces variance more.

steps.title: Write the explanation
steps.text: Write two linked points: (1) feature subsets force diversity in which features each tree splits on, so no single strong predictor dominates every tree; (2) this lowers the correlation between tree errors, which is what lets averaging reduce variance. Each point is worth 2 marks.

solution: Bootstrap samples overlap heavily, so if one predictor is strong, almost every tree would choose it for its top splits and the trees would look alike.
Random feature subsets at each split stop that predictor from dominating every split, so trees use different features and become more diverse.
Averaging reduces variance only when errors are not strongly correlated; decorrelated trees therefore give a larger variance reduction for the forest.

steps.title: Gini and weighting
steps.text: Gini G = 1 − Σ p_c². The split's impurity is Σ (|D_j|/|D|)·G(D_j), and the impurity reduction is G(parent) minus that weighted value.

steps.title: Parent and left child
steps.text: The parent [6+,6−] has p = 6/12 for each class. The left child [4+,0−] contains a single class.

check.prompt: What is the parent Gini?
check.retry: Square each class fraction (6/12), add them, and subtract from 1.

steps.worked: Parent: 1 − (0.25 + 0.25) = 0.5. Left [4+,0−] is pure, so its Gini is 0.

steps.title: Right child
steps.text: The right child [2+,6−] has 8 samples, so p₊ = 2/8 = 0.25 and p₋ = 6/8 = 0.75.

check.prompt: What is the right child's Gini?

steps.title: Weight the children
steps.text: The left child holds 4/12 of the samples and the right child 8/12. Multiply each child Gini by its weight and add.

check.prompt: What is the weighted split Gini?
check.retry: Only the right child contributes, with weight 8/12.

steps.title: Report the three values
steps.text: State the parent Gini, both child Gini values, the weighted split Gini, and finally the reduction = parent Gini − weighted split Gini. Show the weights 4/12 and 8/12 so the marker sees the weighting.

solution: Impurity reduction = 0.5 − 0.25 = 0.25.
Answer: parent Gini 0.5, split Gini 0.25, reduction 0.25.

steps.title: Subsets as in/out choices
steps.text: Each itemset over 5 distinct items is formed by deciding, for every item, whether it is in or out. Count all such choices, then remove any that is not a valid nonempty itemset.

steps.title: All subsets
steps.text: Multiply the number of choices per item across the 5 items.

check.prompt: How many subsets of 5 items are there, including the empty set?
check.why: 2 choices per item, 2⁵ = 32.
check.retry: Each item is either in or out: multiply 2 by itself 5 times.

steps.title: Exclude the empty set
steps.text: The question asks only for nonempty itemsets. Remove the single subset where every item is 'out' and submit the count.

solution: Each of the 5 items is either in or out of an itemset: 2⁵ = 32 subsets.
One of these is the empty set, which is not an itemset to count.
Answer: 32 − 1 = 31.

steps.title: Consistency on one arc
steps.text: Consistency on A→B requires h(A) ≤ c(A,B) + h(B). The right-hand side is the largest h(A) allowed on this arc.

steps.title: Compute the bound
steps.text: Substitute c(A,B)=2 and h(B)=6.

check.prompt: What is c(A,B) + h(B)?
check.retry: Add the arc cost to the heuristic at the arc's end node B.

steps.worked: Bound = 2 + 6 = 8, so a consistent h(A) could be at most 8.

steps.title: Find the excess
steps.text: Subtract the bound from the actual h(A)=10 and submit that difference as a number.

solution: Consistency requires h(A) ≤ c(A,B) + h(B) = 2 + 6 = 8.
h(A) = 10 exceeds the bound by 10 − 8 = 2, so h is inconsistent on this arc.
Answer: 2.

steps.title: Recompute f
steps.text: f=g+h. When a better route is found, keep the new smaller g; h depends only on the state and stays 6.

check.prompt: Which g should A* store for node A now?
check.why: A* keeps the best (smallest) known path cost, 11 < 14.
check.retry: The better route replaces the old one; don't add them.

steps.title: Add the terms
steps.text: Add the stored g to the unchanged h=6 and submit the resulting f as a number.

solution: The better route lowers g from 14 to 11; h(A)=6 is unchanged.
Answer: 17.

steps.title: Bayes' rule with H and not-H
steps.text: P(H∣E) = P(E∣H)P(H) / [P(E∣H)P(H) + P(E∣¬H)P(¬H)]. You need P(¬H) = 1 − 0.1.

steps.title: Prior-weighted terms
steps.text: Compute P(E∣H)P(H) = 0.7 × 0.1 and P(E∣¬H)P(¬H) = 0.2 × 0.9.

check.prompt: What is P(E∣¬H)·P(¬H)?
check.retry: Use the prior of not-H, 1 − 0.1 = 0.9, with the likelihood 0.2.

steps.worked: H term: 0.07. Not-H term: 0.18. Evidence P(E) = 0.07 + 0.18 = 0.25.

steps.title: Normalise
steps.text: Divide the H term by the evidence total P(E) and submit the posterior as a decimal proportion.

solution: Answer: 0.28.

steps.title: Bayes' rule in odds form
steps.text: Divide Bayes' rule for H by Bayes' rule for ¬H and the evidence term cancels: posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio. Each likelihood ratio is P(E∣H)/P(E∣¬H).

steps.title: Combining two observations
steps.text: The two observations are independent given each hypothesis. Decide how their likelihood ratios combine.

check.prompt: With conditional independence, the combined likelihood ratio of both observations is…
check.why: P(E₁,E₂∣H) = P(E₁∣H)P(E₂∣H), and the same holds under ¬H, so the ratios multiply.
check.retry: Write the joint likelihood under each hypothesis as a product, then take their ratio.

steps.title: Posterior odds
steps.text: Multiply the prior odds 1:4 (that is, 1/4) by the combined ratio.

check.prompt: What are the posterior odds H:¬H, as a single number?
check.retry: Prior odds 1:4 equal 0.25. Multiply by 6.

steps.title: Convert odds to probability
steps.text: Odds a:b correspond to probability a/(a+b), or equivalently odds/(1 + odds). Convert the posterior odds and submit P(H) as a decimal.

solution: Prior odds H:¬H = 1:4 = 0.25.
The observations are conditionally independent, so the likelihood ratios multiply: 3 × 2 = 6.
Posterior odds = 0.25 × 6 = 1.5 = 3:2.
Answer: 0.6.

steps.title: Nodes per level
steps.text: In a perfect binary tree each node has two children, so the number of nodes doubles from one depth to the next: depth k has 2^k nodes.

check.prompt: How many nodes are at depth 3?
check.retry: Double the count three times starting from the single root.

steps.title: Add the levels
steps.text: List the counts at depths 0, 1, 2 and 3 and add them.

check.prompt: How many nodes are at depths 0 to 2 together?
check.retry: Add the root, its two children and their four children.

steps.title: Total visits
steps.text: Since the search visits every node, add the depth-3 count to the depths 0–2 total and submit that number.

solution: Depth k of a perfect binary tree has 2^k nodes: 1, 2, 4, 8 for depths 0–3.
The search visits every node: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8.
Answer: 15.

steps.title: Error decomposition
steps.text: Expected squared error at x = Bias² + Variance + σ². Note that the bias is squared, so its sign does not matter.

steps.title: Square the bias
steps.text: Square the bias −0.4.

check.prompt: What is Bias²?
check.why: (−0.4)² = 0.16, which is positive.
check.retry: Multiply −0.4 by itself. The result cannot be negative.

steps.title: Add the three terms
steps.text: Add Bias², the variance 0.05 and the noise variance 0.09, then submit the total expected squared error.

solution: Expected squared error = Bias² + Variance + σ².

steps.title: Independence given what?
steps.text: Every factor in ∏P(x_j∣c) is conditioned on the class. So the features are assumed independent once the class label is fixed, not necessarily in the pooled population.

steps.title: Fill the blank
steps.text: Type the one-word adverb meaning 'given', as in '___ independent given the class'.

check.prompt: Do Naïve Bayes features have to be independent in the overall (pooled) data?
options: Yes, in the pooled data as well
check.why: Features can be correlated across the whole population (for example through the class) yet independent within each class.
check.retry: Look at which probabilities appear in the product: P(x_j∣c), not P(x_j).

solution: Naïve Bayes assumes P(x∣c) = ∏_j P(x_j∣c), so the features are independent given the class label.
They can still be dependent in the pooled population.
Answer: conditionally (conditional).

steps.title: Posterior vs likelihood decisions
steps.text: Two decision rules are compared. One maximises the likelihood P(E∣H) and is called ML. The other maximises the posterior P(H∣E). Its name is Latin for 'from the posterior'.

check.prompt: Which rule maximises P(E∣H) alone, ignoring the prior?
check.why: ML uses only the likelihood. The posterior-maximising rule includes the prior.
check.retry: Which quantity contains only P(E∣H), with no prior?

steps.title: Write the abbreviation
steps.text: The rule that maximises the posterior is 'maximum a posteriori'. Type its three-letter abbreviation (or the full phrase).

solution: Choosing argmax_H P(H∣E) ∝ P(E∣H)P(H) is the maximum a posteriori rule.
It agrees with maximum likelihood (ML) when the priors are uniform.
Answer: MAP.

steps.title: The fourth metric axiom
steps.text: The fourth axiom says a direct route is never longer than a detour through a third point: d(a,c) ≤ d(a,b) + d(b,c). It is named after the triangle formed by a, b and c.

check.prompt: Which relation does the fourth axiom state between d(a,c) and d(a,b) + d(b,c)?
check.why: It is an upper bound on the direct distance, not an equality.
check.retry: Is going through b ever shorter than going straight?

steps.title: Name the relation
steps.text: A statement of the form 'x ≤ y' is called an in… relation. Type the one-word name that completes 'triangle ___'.

solution: A metric satisfies nonnegativity, identity, symmetry and d(a,c) ≤ d(a,b) + d(b,c).
That last property is the triangle inequality.
Answer: inequality.

steps.title: Complete vs single linkage
steps.text: Single linkage uses d_min(A,B). Complete linkage requires all pairs to be close, so it is set by the pair that is least close.

check.prompt: For {0,2} and {6,7}, cross distances are 6, 7, 4, 5. What is the complete-linkage distance?
check.why: Correct: of the cross distances 6, 7, 4 and 5, complete linkage uses 7.
check.retry: Not the smallest (that is single linkage) and not the average.

steps.title: Name the aggregation
steps.text: Type the word for the aggregation you used to get 7 from {6, 7, 4, 5}.

solution: Complete linkage defines d(A,B) = max over a∈A, b∈B of d(a,b).
Answer: maximum (largest).

steps.title: Read the objective
steps.text: J = Σ_k Σ_{x_i ∈ C_k} ||x_i − μ_k||². Each term is the squared length of the gap between a point and its own cluster's centroid.

check.prompt: What does ||x_i − μ_k|| measure?
options: How far point x_i is from its cluster centroid
check.why: It is the Euclidean distance (error) of the point from its prototype.
check.retry: Which two objects appear inside the norm?

steps.title: Fill the blank
steps.text: The objective adds up the squared point-to-centroid quantities you just identified. Type the plural word for them (either the geometric word or the 'prediction gap' word is accepted).

solution: J = Σ_k Σ_{x∈C_k} ||x − μ_k||² sums the squared point-to-centroid distances within each cluster.
Answer: distances (equivalently, errors).

steps.title: Growing the border
steps.text: In O=⌊(I+2P−F)/S⌋+1, the term P counts extra rows and columns added around each side of the input. They are usually filled with zeros so the filter can sit centred on edge pixels.

check.prompt: With F=3 and S=1, which P keeps the output the same size as the input?
check.retry: Solve I + 2P − 3 + 1 = I for P.

steps.title: Name the border
steps.text: The P in the formula is the name for these added zeros. Type the single word that completes 'zero ___'.

solution: Adding P rows and columns of zeros around each side lets the filter cover edge pixels and controls the output size.
For example, P=1 keeps a 3×3, stride-1 convolution the same size as its input.
Answer: padding.

steps.title: Same detector everywhere
steps.text: A convolution layer slides one filter over every position and uses the same weights each time. That is why its parameter count does not depend on the image size.

check.prompt: Why does a convolution layer's parameter count stay the same when the image gets bigger?
options: The same filter weights are reused at every position
Larger images are always padded with zeros
Pooling removes the extra positions before learning
check.why: Reusing one set of weights everywhere keeps the count at K(F_hF_wC+1), whatever the height and width.
check.retry: Does each position get its own weights, or does it use the same ones?

steps.title: Name the property
steps.text: The weights are shared across every position. Type the one word that completes 'weight ___'.

solution: A convolution filter is applied at every spatial location with the same weights.
So all positions share one set of parameters, which keeps the count independent of image size.
Answer: sharing.

steps.title: What an output unit can see
steps.text: One unit in a deep layer depends only on a limited region of the original input. That region grows as more local layers are stacked.

check.prompt: Two stacked 3×3 convolutions with stride 1. How wide is the input region one output unit depends on?
check.why: Each 3×3 layer adds 2 to the region: 1 + 2 + 2 = 5, so 5×5.
check.retry: Start at 1 and add F − 1 = 2 for each layer.

steps.title: Name the region
steps.text: This region is the unit's receptive ___. Type the one missing word.

solution: The input region whose values can change a given output unit grows with each stacked local layer. For example, two 3×3 layers see a 5×5 region.
This region is called the receptive field.
Answer: field.

steps.title: Two families of AI
steps.text: The lecture contrasts AI that manipulates explicit rules and representations with AI that learns patterns from data. The blank asks for the name of the rule-based family.

steps.title: Name the family
steps.text: Systems that reason with explicit symbols (facts, rules, logic) are named after those symbols. Type that one-word name.

check.prompt: Which family learns patterns from data instead of following explicit rules?
check.why: Learned systems infer patterns from data; the other family uses explicit symbols and rules.
check.retry: Which family does not need hand-written rules?

solution: AI that manipulates explicit symbols and rules (e.g. a rule-based puzzle solver) is symbolic AI.
AI that infers patterns from data (e.g. a trained classifier) is learned or statistical AI.
Answer: symbolic.

steps.title: Cutting off the search
steps.text: When the depth limit is reached at a state that is not terminal, there is no true utility yet. A heuristic function estimates how good the position is for MAX instead.

check.prompt: Which states get a true utility U(n) rather than an estimate?
options: Every state at the depth limit
check.why: Only finished games have exact utilities; nonterminal cutoff states need estimates.
check.retry: When is the outcome of the game actually known?

steps.title: Fill the blank
steps.text: Type the one word for the heuristic score assigned to a nonterminal cutoff state (the function is often called an '___ function').

solution: Terminal states have exact utilities; at a nonterminal depth cutoff the game result is unknown.
A heuristic evaluation function estimates the position's value for MAX and is backed up like a utility.
Answer: evaluation.

steps.title: Which bound belongs to MIN
steps.text: Each player maintains one bound. MAX raises a lower bound as it finds better children; MIN lowers an upper bound as it finds smaller children.

check.prompt: Which bound is raised when a MAX node finds a larger child value?
check.why: α is MAX's guaranteed lower bound; the other bound belongs to MIN.
check.retry: MAX's bound is the lower bound.

steps.title: Fill the blank
steps.text: Type the name (or Greek letter) of MIN's upper bound, the one lowered when MIN finds a smaller child.

solution: α is MAX's lower bound; β is MIN's upper bound.
When a MIN node finds a smaller child value, MIN can hold MAX to less, so the upper bound tightens.
Answer: beta (β).

steps.title: The decomposition terms
steps.text: Expected squared error = Bias² + Var + σ². Bias measures how far the average prediction is from the truth. σ² is noise. The remaining term measures how much the fitted model changes from one training sample to another.

check.prompt: Which term would be zero if every training sample produced exactly the same fitted model?
check.why: If the fitted model never changes between samples, its spread is zero. Bias and noise can still be non-zero.
check.retry: Which term measures how much the fitted model spreads across training sets?

steps.title: Name the term
steps.text: Type the one-word name of the decomposition term that measures sensitivity to the training sample.

solution: In Bias² + Var + σ², the term that measures how much the fitted model changes across random training samples is the variance.
Answer: variance.

steps.title: Two common penalties
steps.text: L1 regularisation adds λΣ|w| and tends to push weights to exactly zero. The other common penalty adds λΣw², which shrinks large weights smoothly. It is named after the norm whose square it is.

check.prompt: Which penalty is more likely to produce exactly zero weights?
check.why: The |w| penalty has a sharp corner at zero, so weights get stuck there. The w² penalty only shrinks them.
check.retry: Which penalty keeps pushing just as hard on a small weight as on a large one?

steps.title: Name the squared penalty
steps.text: Type the name of the regularisation that penalises squared coefficients. Either the norm name or its regression name is accepted.

solution: L1 penalises λΣ|w| and encourages sparsity. The penalty λΣw² shrinks large weights smoothly.
The squared penalty is the (squared) L2 norm, also called ridge regularisation or weight decay.
Answer: L2 (ridge).

steps.title: Validation is used, the final split is not
steps.text: Once validation data has been used to pick hyperparameters or checkpoints, its score is slightly optimistic. An unbiased final estimate needs a split that played no part in any decision.

check.prompt: Why is the validation score not an unbiased final estimate?
options: It was used to make model choices
It is always smaller than the training set
check.why: Choosing the best setting on a split fits the choice to that split, so its score is optimistic.
check.retry: What did you use the validation set for during development?

steps.title: Name the split
steps.text: Type the one-word name of the split that is held back until every choice is fixed and used only for final reporting.

solution: The validation set is used for tuning, so its score is optimistic.
The final unbiased evaluation uses a separate held-out split that was never used for any decision.
Answer: test.

steps.title: Which part depends on the path
steps.text: f(n)=g(n)+h(n). h(n) depends only on the state n, so reaching n by another route leaves h unchanged. The other term depends on the route taken to n.

check.prompt: If a cheaper route to n is found, what also changes along with the improved term?
