check.why: A cheaper route lowers the route-dependent term, which lowers f, and the new parent replaces the old predecessor.
check.retry: h is fixed for a state; what does A* store per node besides h?

steps.title: Fill the blank
steps.text: Type the symbol (or its name) for the accumulated cost from the start to the state, the term that a better path lowers.

solution: h(n) depends only on the state, so it is unchanged by a new route.
The accumulated path cost from the start is route dependent; a better path lowers it, which lowers f and updates the predecessor.
Answer: g (g(n), the path cost).

steps.title: The per-arc inequality
steps.text: Rearrange h(n) ≤ c(n,n') + h(n') as h(n) − h(n') ≤ c(n,n'): across any arc, h may fall by no more than the arc cost.

check.prompt: Which property instead compares h(n) with the true cost-to-go h*(n)?
check.why: Admissibility is h(n) ≤ h*(n); the drop-per-arc rule is a different, stronger property.
check.retry: One property uses h*, the other uses an arc cost c.

steps.title: Fill the blank
steps.text: Type the name of the property defined by h(n) ≤ c(n,n') + h(n') on every arc.

solution: The condition h(n) ≤ c(n,n')+h(n') means h(n) − h(n') ≤ c(n,n'), limiting how far h drops across an arc.
That property is called consistency (a consistent heuristic); it implies admissibility.
Answer: consistency.

steps.title: Paid cost or forecast
steps.text: Greedy best-first orders OPEN by h(n) alone. Recall what h(n) measures: it is not the cost of the path already followed from the start.

check.prompt: Which cost does greedy best-first ignore?
options: The estimated cost from n to the goal
check.why: Greedy drops g and keeps only the heuristic forecast.
check.retry: Greedy uses exactly one of the two quantities.

steps.title: Fill the blank
steps.text: Type the one word describing the part of the path cost that h(n) estimates, the part still left between n and the goal.

solution: Greedy best-first ranks OPEN by h(n) and ignores g(n).
h(n) estimates the cost still left from n to a goal.
Answer: remaining (also accepted: future).

steps.title: Maximal vs closed
steps.text: Two compact summaries of frequent itemsets exist. Closed: no proper superset has the same support. The other: no proper superset is frequent at all, so it sits on the border of the frequent region.

steps.title: Name the property
steps.text: The blank describes a frequent itemset that cannot be extended without becoming infrequent. Type that one-word name.

check.prompt: 'No proper superset has equal support' defines which kind of frequent itemset?
check.why: That is the closed definition; the blank uses the 'no frequent superset' definition instead.
check.retry: Which definition talks about equal support rather than being frequent?

solution: A closed frequent itemset has no proper superset with the same support.
A frequent itemset with no frequent proper superset is on the border of the frequent itemsets.
Answer: maximal.

steps.title: Conditional mining in FP-growth
steps.text: For a suffix item, FP-growth follows its header links, collects each prefix path weighted by the suffix node's count, and builds a conditional FP-tree from that collection. The blank names the collection, not the tree built from it.

steps.title: Name the collection
steps.text: Complete the term 'conditional pattern ___' with one word for a collection of data that later mining builds on.

check.prompt: What is built from the weighted prefix paths after pruning infrequent items?
options: The header table of the full database
check.why: The weighted paths are pruned and inserted into a conditional FP-tree; the paths themselves are a different object.
check.retry: The header table belongs to the original tree. What gets built per suffix?

solution: For a suffix item, the weighted prefix paths that lead to its nodes are collected.
That collection is then pruned and turned into a conditional FP-tree.
Answer: base (conditional pattern base).

steps.title: The four core tasks
steps.text: The main mining tasks are classification (predict labels), clustering (find groups), association analysis (find co-occurrences) and one more that looks for records that do not fit the normal pattern, such as fraudulent transactions.

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: The blank names the task that flags rare, deviating records. Type the word that describes such a record (one word).

check.prompt: Which task finds groups of similar records, rather than isolated deviating ones?
check.why: Clustering finds groups; the blank asks for the task that flags points far from any normal group.
check.retry: Which task's output is a set of groups?

solution: Classification, clustering and association analysis look for typical structure.
Detecting rare records that deviate from the normal pattern (e.g. fraud) is a separate task.
Answer: anomaly (also called outlier) detection.

steps.title: Lift under independence
steps.text: lift = conf/supp(Y) = P(X∪Y)/(P(X)P(Y)). Independence means P(X∪Y) = P(X)·P(Y), i.e. P(Y|X) = P(Y).

steps.title: Substitute
steps.text: Replace the joint probability by the product of the marginals and simplify the ratio. Type the resulting number.

check.prompt: Under independence, conf(X→Y) equals…
check.why: P(Y|X) = P(Y) when X and Y are independent.
check.retry: Independence means knowing X does not change the probability of Y.

solution: Independence gives P(X∪Y) = P(X)P(Y), so conf = P(Y|X) = P(Y).
lift = conf/supp(Y) = P(Y)/P(Y).
Answer: 1.

steps.title: r = 1 in Minkowski
steps.text: With r = 1, d = Σ|x_j − z_j|. It is the distance travelled on a grid of streets, moving only along axes.

check.prompt: What is this distance between (1,2) and (4,6)?
check.retry: Add the absolute differences in each coordinate.

steps.title: Name the distance
steps.text: This metric is named after a city with a grid street layout (also called the L1 or city-block distance). Type its name.

solution: Summing absolute coordinate differences is the Minkowski distance with r = 1.
It is called the Manhattan (L1, city-block) distance.
Answer: Manhattan.

steps.title: Which points define the SVM
steps.text: A point with a nonzero dual weight must sit on a margin plane, y_i(w·x_i + b) = 1. These points alone determine the separator: removing any other point leaves the solution unchanged.

check.prompt: If you delete a training point far from the margin, the SVM solution…
check.why: Only the points on the margin planes hold up the solution.
check.retry: Does a point with y_i f(x_i) > 1 constrain the optimum?

steps.title: Name them
steps.text: These points 'hold up' the margin planes, which gives them their name. Type the one word that goes before 'vectors'.

solution: Points with y_i(w·x_i + b) = 1 lie on the canonical margin planes.
They alone determine the separator and are called support vectors.
Answer: support.

steps.title: Relaxing the constraint
steps.text: Soft-margin SVM relaxes y_i f(x_i) ≥ 1 to y_i f(x_i) ≥ 1 − ξ_i with ξ_i ≥ 0. ξ_i measures how much 'give' each point needs.

check.prompt: For a point satisfying the hard constraint y_i f(x_i) ≥ 1, the minimum ξ_i is…
check.why: max(0, 1 − y f(x)) = 0 when y f(x) ≥ 1.
check.retry: No violation means no extra allowance is needed.

steps.title: Name the variable
steps.text: The variable is named for the 'loose rope' it gives the constraint. Type that one word.

solution: ξ_i ≥ 0 relaxes the margin constraint to y_i f(x_i) ≥ 1 − ξ_i.
It is called a slack variable.
Answer: slack.

steps.title: Derivatives through compositions
steps.text: A network computes E(o(net(w))). To get ∂E/∂w, multiply the local derivatives: ∂E/∂o · ∂o/∂net · ∂net/∂w. This rule from calculus is named after linked pieces.

steps.title: Name the rule
steps.text: Type the one-word name of the calculus rule for differentiating composed functions.

check.prompt: Which rule would you use for d/dx of f(x)·g(x)? (This is not the one asked for.)
check.why: f·g uses the product rule. Backprop deals with compositions f(g(x)).
check.retry: f(x)·g(x) is a product, not a composition.

solution: Backprop computes ∂E/∂w by multiplying local derivatives along the composition: ∂E/∂o · ∂o/∂net · ∂net/∂w.
Answer: chain.

steps.title: Parts of the net input
steps.text: net_j = Σ_i w_ji o_i + b_j. The w_ji multiply inputs. The last term is added regardless of the inputs and shifts the decision threshold.

steps.title: Name the offset
steps.text: Type the one-word name of the learned constant b_j that is added to the weighted sum.

check.prompt: Which parameters are multiplied by the inputs o_i?
check.why: Weights scale inputs. The offset is added on its own.
check.retry: Look at which symbol sits next to o_i in the formula.

solution: net_j = Σ w_ji o_i + b_j: the weights scale the inputs, and b_j is a learned constant added on.
Answer: bias.

steps.title: Role of η
steps.text: θ_{t+1} = θ_t − η ∇E(θ_t). The gradient gives the direction, and η scales how far each step moves. It is a hyperparameter chosen before training.

steps.title: Name the hyperparameter
steps.text: Type the word that completes '___ rate' for η.

check.prompt: If η is made much too large, gradient descent tends to…
options: converge more slowly but more stably
check.why: Large steps jump past the minimum. Small η is slow but stable.
check.retry: η multiplies the step length. What happens if the steps are huge?

solution: In θ_{t+1} = θ_t − η∇E, η sets the step size.
Answer: learning (the learning rate).

steps.title: What λ₁ measures
steps.text: Su₁ = λ₁u₁ with ||u₁|| = 1 gives u₁ᵀSu₁ = λ₁: the variance of the data along the unit vector u₁.

check.prompt: u₁ is the eigenvector of S with the…
check.why: PCA sorts eigenvalues in descending order, so λ₁ is the largest.
check.retry: Which direction does PCA keep first?

steps.title: Fill the blank
steps.text: u₁ is called the first principal ___. Type the word (component, direction or axis are all accepted).

solution: For unit u₁ with Su₁ = λ₁u₁, the projected variance is u₁ᵀSu₁ = λ₁.
So the leading eigenvalue is the variance along the first principal component (direction/axis).
Answer: component.

steps.title: The two PCA mappings
steps.text: Encoding computes z = Uᵀ(x − μ) and subtracts the mean. The reverse mapping x̂ = μ + Uz adds it back.

check.prompt: In which step is the mean subtracted?
check.why: z = Uᵀ(x − μ) subtracts μ before projecting.
check.retry: Look inside the brackets of z = Uᵀ(x − μ).

steps.title: Name the reverse step
steps.text: Type the one-word name for the step x̂ = μ + Uz that rebuilds a point in the original coordinates.

solution: Encoding z = Uᵀ(x − μ) subtracts the mean.
Rebuilding the point, x̂ = μ + Uz, adds the mean back.
Answer: reconstruction.

steps.title: PCA's error direction
steps.text: PCA reconstructs each point by its projection onto the subspace. The leftover residual is at right angles to the subspace, unlike OLS residuals, which are vertical.

check.prompt: Which distances does OLS (y on x) square?
check.why: OLS residuals are y − ŷ at fixed x. PCA uses the other, shortest-distance kind.
check.retry: OLS keeps x fixed and compares y values.

steps.title: Name PCA's distance
steps.text: Type the one-word name for a distance measured at right angles to the subspace ('orthogonal' is also accepted).

solution: OLS squares vertical residuals; PCA squares the distance from each point to its orthogonal projection on the subspace.
These are the shortest, right-angle distances to the subspace.
Answer: perpendicular (orthogonal).

steps.title: Observed minus fitted
steps.text: For each observation, yᵢ − ŷᵢ is the signed vertical gap OLS squares and sums. It is positive when the point lies above the line.

check.prompt: Observed y = 6 and fitted ŷ = 4.5. What is y − ŷ?
check.why: 6 − 4.5 = 1.5; the point lies above the line.
check.retry: Subtract the fitted value from the observed value.

steps.title: Name the quantity
steps.text: Type the standard one-word name for y − ŷ in regression (the word 'error' is also accepted).

solution: The quantity eᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ is the signed gap between observation and fit.
OLS minimizes Σ eᵢ².
Answer: residual.

steps.title: The four backtracking lists
steps.text: The lecture's backtracking algorithm tracks CS (current state), SL (current solution path), NSL (new states not yet processed) and DE. A state goes into DE once it and all its descendants have failed.

check.prompt: Which list holds states that are generated but not yet examined?
check.why: NSL is the list of unprocessed states; SL is the current path and CS the state being examined.
check.retry: Which list name contains 'new'?

steps.title: Expand DE
steps.text: DE stores states proved to lead nowhere, so they are not tried again. Type the two-word term that the letters D and E stand for.

solution: CS = current state, SL = solution path, NSL = unprocessed states.
DE stores states whose descendants all failed, so they are never re-examined.
Answer: dead ends.

steps.title: Frontier order in BFS
steps.text: BFS removes the oldest generated node first and adds new children at the back, so a level is finished before the next begins. That is first-in, first-out (FIFO) order.

check.prompt: Which structure gives last-in, first-out order, as used by DFS?
check.why: A stack is LIFO; DFS uses it to follow the newest branch.
check.retry: Which structure returns the most recently added item first?

steps.title: Name the FIFO structure
steps.text: BFS needs the FIFO counterpart of the stack. Type the name of that data structure.

solution: BFS expands the oldest frontier node first and appends children at the back (FIFO).
DFS uses a LIFO stack; best-first search uses a priority queue.
Answer: queue (FIFO queue).

steps.title: Naming the two directions
steps.text: The two directions are named after their starting point. Goal-driven search starts from the goal; the other starts from what is already known.

check.prompt: Search that starts from a target hypothesis is called…
check.why: It is named after its starting point, the goal.
check.retry: Which name mentions the target?

steps.title: Fill the blank
steps.text: The method in the blank starts from facts (the known data). Type the word that completes '___-driven'.

solution: Goal-driven search starts from the goal; the opposite direction starts from the known facts.
Starting from facts and firing applicable rules is forward reasoning, named after the data it starts from.
Answer: data (data-driven).

steps.title: What each pass is
steps.text: Iterative deepening runs DFS with a cap on depth, then raises the cap and repeats. The name of each pass describes that cap on the depth.

check.prompt: Within one pass, what happens at a node exactly at the current bound?
options: Its children are queued for BFS
check.why: Nodes at the cap are treated as leaves; the cap only rises between passes.
check.retry: Does the bound change during a pass or between passes?

steps.title: Fill the blank
steps.text: Each pass is a depth-first search whose depth is capped. Type the word that completes 'depth-___ search'.

solution: Each pass is a DFS that does not expand nodes beyond the current depth bound.
Iterative deepening repeats this with bounds 0, 1, 2, ….
Answer: limited (depth-limited).

steps.title: The four parts of [N,A,S,GD]
steps.text: A state space is written [N,A,S,GD]. N is the set of nodes (states), S the initial states, GD the goal descriptions, and A the connections produced by operators between states.

check.prompt: Which component holds the initial states?
check.why: S is the start set; N is all nodes and GD describes goals.
check.retry: Which letter stands for 'start'?

steps.title: Name A
steps.text: With N, S and GD accounted for, A is the remaining graph component: the links that represent legal moves between nodes. Type that word.

solution: [N,A,S,GD]: N = nodes/states, S = initial states, GD = goal descriptions.
A holds the links between states, one per legal operator application.
Answer: arcs (edges).

steps.title: Rates over actual negatives
steps.text: Among actual negatives, each case is either a TN or an FP. TN/(TN+FP) is specificity; FP/(FP+TN) is the other rate, plotted on the ROC x-axis.

check.prompt: Which ROC axis uses FP/(FP+TN)?
check.why: ROC plots TPR (y) against FPR (x).
check.retry: ROC plots TPR against what?

steps.title: Fill the blank
steps.text: The rate is named after the kind of error in its numerator: a false ___. Type that one word.

solution: FP/(FP+TN) is the fraction of actual negatives predicted positive.
It is called the false positive rate (FPR = 1 − specificity).
Answer: positive.

steps.title: How a forest classifies
steps.text: Each tree in a random forest outputs a class label. The forest combines these by a majority (plurality) decision.

check.prompt: For regression, forests average tree outputs. For classification they instead…
options: take the most common class among the trees
check.why: Classification uses plurality voting over the trees' labels.
check.retry: Class labels cannot be averaged; how else do many trees agree?

steps.title: Fill the blank
steps.text: Each tree casts one of these for a class, and the class with the most wins. Type that one word (plural).

solution: Each tree predicts a class label for the input.
The forest outputs the class chosen by the most trees (plurality voting).
Answer: votes (tree predictions).

steps.title: Why normalize gain
steps.text: Raw information gain favours attributes with many values, such as an ID column. C4.5 divides the gain by the split information (the entropy of the child sizes) to penalize such splits.

check.prompt: Which kind of attribute does raw information gain unfairly favour?
options: Attributes with many distinct values, like an ID
check.why: A many-valued attribute can make every child pure, inflating gain without generalizing.
check.retry: Which split makes every child contain exactly one record?

steps.title: Name the quantity
steps.text: The quantity is gain divided by split information, i.e. one quantity expressed as a fraction of another. Type the word that completes 'gain ___'.

solution: Information gain is biased toward many-valued attributes.
C4.5 divides it by split information, the entropy of the child-size distribution.
Answer: gain ratio.

steps.title: Set up the Naïve Bayes score
steps.text: s_c = P(c)·P(X=1∣c)·P(Y=0∣c). The question gives P(Y=1∣c), but the observation is Y=0, so you need the complement 1 − P(Y=1∣c). P(D) = 1 − 0.25.

steps.title: Handle the negative feature
steps.text: Find the probability of the observed value Y=0 under each class.

check.prompt: What is P(Y=0∣C)?
check.retry: Y is binary, so P(Y=0∣C) = 1 − P(Y=1∣C).

steps.title: Score for C
steps.text: Multiply the prior 0.25 by P(X=1∣C) = 0.8 and P(Y=0∣C) = 0.4.

check.prompt: What is s_C?
check.retry: Use 0.4 for Y=0, not 0.6.

steps.title: Score for D
steps.text: Multiply P(D) = 0.75 by P(X=1∣D) = 0.2 and P(Y=0∣D) = 0.3.

check.prompt: What is s_D?

steps.title: Normalise
steps.text: Add the two scores to get the evidence. The posterior of C is s_C divided by that total.

check.prompt: What is the evidence total s_C + s_D?
check.retry: Add the scores from the two previous levels.

steps.title: The assumption and when it misleads
steps.text: Name the assumption that let you multiply P(X∣c) by P(Y∣c), and think about what happens when it fails.

check.prompt: When could this factorised model mislead?
options: When X and Y are strongly correlated within a class, so the product misstates the joint likelihood
When X and Y are correlated in the pooled data but independent within each class
Whenever the class priors are unequal
check.why: The model assumes X ⟂ Y given the class. Within-class correlation double-counts (or under-counts) evidence. Pooled correlation and unequal priors are handled correctly.
check.retry: The assumption is conditioned on the class. Which kind of dependence breaks it?

steps.worked: Assumption: X and Y are conditionally independent given the class. If they are correlated within a class (e.g. redundant features), the product misstates P(X,Y∣c) and the posterior can be overconfident or wrong.

steps.title: Write the three parts
steps.text: Present: (1) both scores, using the Y=0 complements and both priors; (2) the normalised posterior of C and the MAP class; (3) the conditional-independence assumption and a within-class correlation case where it misleads. Each part is worth 3 marks.

solution: Assumption: X and Y are conditionally independent given the class, so P(X,Y∣c) = P(X∣c)P(Y∣c).

It can mislead when the features are correlated within a class (e.g. redundant or causally linked features). The product then double-counts or distorts the joint likelihood, and the posterior can be miscalibrated or even pick the wrong class.
Answer: P(C∣X=1,Y=0) = 0.64 (MAP = C), under the conditional-independence assumption, which misleads when features are correlated within a class.

steps.title: K-means in 1D
steps.text: Each round: assign every point using the current centers (boundary at their midpoint, ties to the lower center), then replace each center with the mean of its cluster.

steps.title: Round 1 assignment
steps.text: Centers 0 and 3. Find the boundary and assign 0, 2, 3, 9, 10.

check.prompt: What is the round-1 boundary?
check.why: (0 + 3)/2 = 1.5, so only 0 is below it.
check.retry: Average centers 0 and 3.

steps.title: Round 1 update
steps.text: Average each cluster.

check.prompt: What is the new upper center (mean of 2, 3, 9, 10)?
check.retry: Sum the four points and divide by 4.

steps.title: Round 2 assignment and the tie
steps.text: Centers 0 and 6 give boundary 3. Point 3 is exactly on it.

check.prompt: Where does point 3 go in round 2?
options: To center 0 (tie goes to the lower center)
It stays where it was in round 1
check.why: |3 − 0| = |3 − 6| = 3, and the rule sends ties to the lower center.
check.retry: Compute its distance to both centers and apply the tie rule.

steps.title: Round 2 update
steps.text: Average the two new clusters.

check.prompt: What is the new lower center (mean of 0, 2, 3)? Give a decimal or fraction.
check.retry: There are three points in the lower cluster.

steps.title: Single-linkage merges
steps.text: Neighbouring gaps in sorted order are 0–2: 2, 2–3: 1, 3–9: 6, 9–10: 1. Single linkage always merges the clusters with the smallest gap between any members.

check.prompt: After merging {2,3} and {9,10} at height 1, which merge comes next?
check.why: The smallest remaining single-linkage distance is d(0, 2) = 2.
check.retry: Compare the closest member distances between each remaining pair of clusters.

steps.worked: Merges: {2,3} at 1, {9,10} at 1, {0,2,3} at 2. Stop at two groups: {0,2,3} and {9,10}.

steps.title: Write and compare
steps.text: Present (1) round-1 boundary, clusters and means; (2) round-2 boundary, the tie at 3, clusters and means; (3) the single-linkage merge order and the two final groups. Finish by comparing the K-means round-2 clusters with the single-linkage groups. Each part is worth 3 marks.

solution: Round 1: centers 0 and 3, boundary 1.5. Clusters {0} and {2, 3, 9, 10}; new means 0 and 24/4 = 6.
Round 2: centers 0 and 6, boundary 3. Point 3 is tied (distance 3 to both) and goes to the lower center. Clusters {0, 2, 3} and {9, 10}; new means 5/3 ≈ 1.667 and 9.5.
Single linkage: merge 2 and 3 at distance 1 and 9 and 10 at distance 1; then 0 joins {2, 3} at distance 2. Stopping at two groups gives {0, 2, 3} and {9, 10}.
Comparison: both methods give the same two groups, {0, 2, 3} and {9, 10}.

steps.title: Carry H×W×C through each layer
steps.text: For each layer, use O=⌊(I+2P−F)/S⌋+1 on height and width separately. The filters are 5×3, so height uses F=5 and width uses F=3. A convolution's depth is its filter count, and pooling keeps the depth. Parameters = K(F_h·F_w·C_in + 1), with C_in taken from the layer's own input.

steps.title: Conv1 output shape
steps.text: Input 32×28×3, filter height 5, filter width 3, S=1, P=0, 8 filters. Work out each axis.

check.prompt: What are Conv1's output height and width?
check.why: Height 32 − 5 + 1 = 28 and width 28 − 3 + 1 = 26.
check.retry: Use F=5 for height and F=3 for width. Do not swap them.

steps.title: Conv1 parameters
steps.text: Each of the 8 filters is 5×3×3 (it spans the 3 input channels) and has one bias.

check.prompt: How many parameters does Conv1 have?
check.retry: Work out 5·3·3 + 1, then multiply by 8.

steps.title: Pooling
steps.text: A 2×2 window with stride 2 and no padding, applied to 28×26×8. Pooling works per channel and learns nothing.

check.prompt: What is the pooled height and width?
check.retry: Apply ⌊(I − 2)/2⌋ + 1 to 28 and to 26.

steps.title: Conv2 output shape
steps.text: Input 14×13×8, twelve 3×3 filters, S=1, P=1. With F=3 and P=1, stride 1 keeps the spatial size the same.

check.prompt: What is Conv2's output height?

steps.worked: Height 14 + 2 − 3 + 1 = 14 and width 13 + 2 − 3 + 1 = 13, so Conv2 output is 14×13×12.

steps.title: Conv2 parameters
steps.text: Conv2's input depth is 8, the pooled channels, not the original 3. Each of the 12 filters is 3×3×8 and has one bias.

check.prompt: How many parameters does Conv2 have?
check.retry: Use C_in = 8: work out 3·3·8 + 1 = 73, then multiply by 12.

steps.title: List shapes and total
steps.text: List the three output shapes in order (Conv1, Pool, Conv2), each as H×W×C. Note that pooling has no parameters. Then add the two convolution counts to get the total number of learned parameters.

solution: Conv1: height 32 − 5 + 1 = 28, width 28 − 3 + 1 = 26, depth 8, so the output is 28×26×8.
Pool: ⌊(28 − 2)/2⌋ + 1 = 14 and ⌊(26 − 2)/2⌋ + 1 = 13, depth unchanged, so the output is 14×13×8. It has no trainable parameters.
Conv2: 14 + 2 − 3 + 1 = 14 and 13 + 2 − 3 + 1 = 13, depth 12, so the output is 14×13×12.
Total learned parameters: 368 + 0 + 876 = 1244.

steps.title: Retrieval vs decision making
steps.text: Part (a) asks what changed. Contrast a system that retrieves a stored answer with one that generates and evaluates candidate answers against constraints and an objective.

steps.title: (a) What has changed
steps.text: Describe how each version produces a room assignment.

check.prompt: What is the key change from legacy to replacement?
options: From retrieving a stored timetable to generating feasible assignments and optimising them
From a slow lookup to a faster lookup
From human-written rules to a chatbot interface
check.why: The replacement searches over assignments that satisfy constraints and scores them by walking distance.
check.retry: Does the replacement still just read a stored answer?

steps.worked: Legacy: a lookup returns the stored timetable. Replacement: generates assignments that satisfy capacity and timing rules, then evaluates them by travel cost.

steps.title: (b) Symbols for classes and rooms
steps.text: A symbolic representation needs objects with attributes and rules over them. List the attributes of a class and of a room that the constraints need.

check.prompt: Which attributes are needed to check the capacity and timing constraints?
options: Class size and time slot; room capacity and location
Lecturer's name and course code only
check.why: Capacity needs class size vs room capacity; clashes need time slots; walking distance needs room location.
check.retry: Which attributes appear in a capacity rule or a time-clash rule?

steps.worked: Class(id, size, timeslot, cohort); Room(id, capacity, location). Assign(class, room).

steps.title: (b) Feasibility constraints
steps.text: Write the rules as conditions on the symbols: one for capacity and one for double booking.
steps.worked: Capacity: Assign(c, r) ⇒ size(c) ≤ capacity(r). No clash: Assign(c1, r) ∧ Assign(c2, r) ∧ c1 ≠ c2 ⇒ timeslot(c1) ≠ timeslot(c2).

steps.title: (c) A rationality metric
steps.text: A rational system is judged against its objective. The stated objective is walking distance among feasible timetables, so the metric must be measurable and consistent with it.

check.prompt: Which metric fits the replacement's objective?
options: Total (or average) student walking distance over feasible timetables, with violations counted separately
How closely the timetable matches last year's
Whether staff say the timetable feels sensible
check.why: It measures the stated objective and keeps feasibility separate from cost.
check.retry: What did the replacement say it optimises?

steps.worked: Minimise total walking distance between consecutive classes of each cohort, among timetables with zero constraint violations; report violations separately.

steps.title: Write the three parts
steps.text: Structure the answer as (a) retrieval vs constraint-based decision, (b) the class/room symbols plus the capacity and clash rules, (c) the walking-distance metric with feasibility checked separately. Each part is worth 3 marks.

solution: (a) The legacy system retrieves a stored timetable record. The replacement generates candidate assignments that satisfy capacity and timing rules and evaluates them by travel cost, so it makes a decision rather than a lookup.

(b) Represent Class(id, size, timeslot, cohort) and Room(id, capacity, location), with Assign(class, room). Constraints: Assign(c, r) ⇒ size(c) ≤ capacity(r); two classes in the same room must have different timeslots.

(c) Measure total walking distance between consecutive classes for each cohort, compared only among feasible timetables. Count constraint violations separately so an infeasible timetable is never rated as good.

steps.title: Minimax and cutoffs
steps.text: First compute exact minimax values (MIN takes the smallest leaf, the MAX root the largest child). Then trace alpha–beta: each MIN child inherits the root's α, lowers β leaf by leaf, and stops when β ≤ α.

check.prompt: What is the minimax value of A?
check.retry: Take the smallest of 7, 5 and 6.

steps.title: Left-to-right: A then B
steps.text: A is read fully (7, 5, 6) and returns 5, so α=5. B's first leaf is 4.

check.prompt: Which leaves of B are skipped in the left-to-right run?
check.why: β=4 ≤ α=5 after the first leaf, so the rest of B is pruned.
check.retry: Compare B's first leaf with α=5.

steps.worked: α=5 after A. B: β=4 ≤ 5, cutoff; skip 10 and 9.

steps.title: Left-to-right: C
steps.text: C is read with α=5: track β over 8, 7, 9.

check.prompt: Does C cause any cutoff in the left-to-right run?
options: No, β stays at 8 then 7, both above 5, so all leaves are read
check.why: A cut needs β ≤ α = 5; β never falls that low in C.
check.retry: Check each β against α=5.

steps.worked: C reads 8, 7, 9, returns 7; α rises to 7. Root = 7 via C. Leaves visited: 3+1+3 = 7; skipped: 10, 9.

steps.title: Right-to-left: C then B
steps.text: Now every level is reversed: visit C first reading 9, 7, 8, then B reading 9, 10, 4.

check.prompt: What is α after C, and does B prune any leaf?
options: α=7; B prunes nothing because β only reaches ≤7 at its last leaf 4
α=7; B prunes 10 and 4 after seeing 9
check.why: C=min(9,7,8)=7. In B, β goes 9, 9, then 4; 9 > 7, so no cut happens until no leaves remain.
check.retry: C's value is its minimum, not its first leaf; then compare B's running β with α.

steps.worked: C returns 7 (all 3 leaves), α=7. B: β=9, then 9 (10 is larger), then 4 ≤ 7 at the last leaf; all 3 read, none skipped.

steps.title: Right-to-left: A
steps.text: A is visited last in reverse order: 6, 5, 7, with α=7.

check.prompt: Which leaf occurrences of A are omitted in the right-to-left run?
check.why: The first leaf 6 gives β=6 ≤ α=7, so the remaining 5 and 7 are pruned.
check.retry: A's first leaf in reverse order is 6; compare it with α=7.

steps.worked: A: β=6 ≤ 7, cutoff; skip 5 and 7. Leaves visited: 3+3+1 = 7. Root still 7 via C.

steps.title: Write both runs
steps.text: Give the three exact MIN values, the root value and chosen branch; then for each order list the α/β changes, each cutoff and the omitted leaves, and note how many terminal values each run visits. Point out that the root value and choice do not depend on the order.

solution: Exact values: A=min(7,5,6)=5, B=min(4,10,9)=4, C=min(8,7,9)=7. Root = max(5,4,7) = 7, so MAX chooses C.
Left-to-right: A reads 7,5,6 and returns 5, so α=5.
B reads 4: β=4 ≤ α=5, cutoff; 10 and 9 are omitted.
C reads 8,7,9 (β=8, 7, both > 5), returns 7; α=7. Root 7 via C; 7 leaves visited.
Right-to-left: C reads 9,7,8 and returns 7, so α=7.
B reads 9,10,4: β stays 9 until the last leaf 4, so no leaf is omitted; B returns 4.
A reads 6 first: β=6 ≤ α=7, cutoff; 5 and 7 are omitted. 7 leaves visited.
Answer: root value 7, choose C; left-to-right omits B's 10 and 9, right-to-left omits A's 5 and 7; both runs visit 7 terminal values.

steps.title: Select checkpoints on validation loss
steps.text: Early stopping keeps the epoch with the lowest validation loss, not the lowest training loss. Training loss nearly always keeps falling, so it cannot tell you when to stop.

steps.title: Find the best checkpoint
steps.text: Scan the validation losses 0.72, 0.45, 0.30, 0.33, 0.42 for the smallest value.

check.prompt: Which epoch has the lowest validation loss?
check.why: Validation loss is lowest at epoch 3 (0.30), then rises to 0.33 and 0.42.
check.retry: Ignore training loss. Find the minimum of the validation sequence.

steps.worked: The validation minimum is 0.30 at epoch 3.

steps.title: Measure the divergence
steps.text: Compare the train–validation gap at epoch 3 with the gap at epoch 5 to show what happens later.

check.prompt: What is the validation-minus-training gap at epoch 5?
check.retry: Subtract the epoch-5 training loss from the epoch-5 validation loss.

steps.worked: Gap at epoch 3: 0.30 − 0.23 = 0.07. Gap at epoch 5: 0.42 − 0.10 = 0.32. Training loss keeps falling while validation loss rises.

steps.title: Diagnose and propose a remedy
steps.text: Explain what training loss falling while validation loss rises means, and pick a matching remedy.

check.prompt: After epoch 3, the behaviour indicates…
options: overfitting, so use early stopping plus a penalty, dropout or label-preserving augmentation
underfitting, so train longer with a bigger model
a learning-rate bug, because training loss should rise too
check.why: Fitting the training data better while held-out loss gets worse means the model is learning patterns specific to the training sample.
check.retry: Which split keeps improving, and which one gets worse?

steps.worked: After epoch 3 the model fits sample-specific patterns, which is overfitting. Remedies: stop early at epoch 3, add weight decay or dropout, or use label-preserving augmentation.

steps.title: Evaluate a new regularisation setting properly
steps.text: Decide which data is used to compare regularisation settings and when the test set may be used.

check.prompt: Which protocol keeps the test set out of tuning?
options: Train each setting on training data, compare them by best validation loss, fix the choice, then evaluate once on the test set
Try each setting and keep the one with the lowest test loss
Merge validation and test data to get a larger tuning set
check.why: All comparisons use validation data. The test set is used once, after every choice is fixed.
check.retry: Comparing settings is a choice. Which split is meant for making choices?

steps.worked: Retrain with each candidate penalty, pick its best epoch by validation loss, compare settings on validation loss (or with k-fold CV), freeze the choice, then report a single test-set score.

steps.title: Write the three parts
steps.text: Part 1 (3 marks): state the chosen checkpoint and that you chose it by validation loss. Part 2 (3 marks): describe the widening gap after that epoch, name the cause and propose a remedy. Part 3 (3 marks): describe tuning on training and validation data, with the test set used only once at the end.

solution: Checkpoint: choose by validation loss. The minimum is 0.30 at epoch 3, so keep the epoch-3 weights.
Later behaviour: training loss keeps falling (0.23 → 0.14 → 0.10) while validation loss rises (0.30 → 0.33 → 0.42). The gap grows from 0.07 to 0.32, which is overfitting.
Remedy: use early stopping at the validation minimum and try a weight penalty, dropout or label-preserving augmentation.

Evaluating a new regularisation setting: train with it on the training data, pick its best epoch and compare it with other settings using validation loss (or cross-validation on the training data). Only once all choices are fixed, evaluate a single time on the untouched test set and report that score.

steps.title: Two priorities
steps.text: A* removes the OPEN node with the smallest f=g+h and updates g, f and the predecessor whenever a cheaper route to a node already on OPEN appears. Greedy best-first removes the smallest h and ignores g. Both stop only when G is removed from OPEN.

steps.title: A*: expand S
steps.text: S generates A (g=4) and B (g=1). Compute both f values.

check.prompt: What is f(B) after expanding S?
check.retry: f(B) = g(B) + h(B) with g(B)=1.

steps.title: A*: expand B and update A
steps.text: B has the smaller f. It reaches A with cost 2 and G with cost 8. Compare the new g(A) with the stored 4.

check.prompt: What is A's new g via S→B→A?
check.why: 1+2=3 < 4, so A is updated to g=3, f=5 with predecessor B.
check.retry: Add g(B)=1 to the cost of B→A.

steps.worked: A: g=3, f=3+2=5, predecessor B. G added with g=1+8=9, f=9. OPEN: A (f=5), G (f=9).

steps.title: A*: expand A and update G
steps.text: A (f=5) is removed next. Its edge A→G gives another route to G; compare it with G's stored g=9.

check.prompt: Expanding A finds a new route to G. Should G’s stored entry change?
options: Yes, the route via A is cheaper than the stored g=9, so g, f and parent are updated
No, G was already generated via B so its first path is kept
No, A* stops as soon as G first appears on OPEN
check.why: g via A is 3+3=6 < 9, and A* always keeps the best g with its predecessor.
check.retry: Compute g(A)+c(A,G) and compare with 9.

steps.worked: G: g=6, f=6, parent A (replacing B). G is now the smallest f on OPEN and is removed.

steps.title: Greedy best-first trace
steps.text: From S, OPEN holds A (h=2) and B (h=4). Greedy uses h only.

check.prompt: Which node does greedy expand after S?
check.why: Greedy compares h values only; f is the A* rule.
check.retry: Ignore g; compare the remaining estimates.

steps.worked: Greedy expands A, which generates G (h=0). G has the smallest h and is removed, giving S→A→G.

steps.title: Greedy path cost
steps.text: Add the edge costs on the route greedy returns.

check.prompt: What is the cost of the first edge S→A that greedy ignored when it chose A?
check.why: c(S,A)=4, while A* reached A for only 3 via B.
check.retry: Read the S→A edge cost.

steps.worked: S→A→G costs 4+3=7, more than A*'s route, because greedy never counted the expensive first edge S→A (g=4).

steps.title: Check consistency
steps.text: Test h(n) ≤ c(n,n')+h(n') on every arc: S→A, S→B, B→A, A→G, B→G.

check.prompt: Is the heuristic consistent on all five listed arcs?
options: Yes, every arc satisfies the inequality
check.why: 5≤4+2, 5≤1+4, 4≤2+2, 2≤3+0, 4≤8+0; remember to add h at the arc's end.
check.retry: Include h(n') on the right-hand side, not just the arc cost.

steps.worked: S→A: 5≤6; S→B: 5≤5; B→A: 4≤4; A→G: 2≤3; B→G: 4≤8. All hold, so no closed node needs reopening.

steps.title: Write both traces
steps.text: Present the A* trace with every f value and both frontier improvements (A via B, then G via A), follow predecessors from G to state the A* route and cost, then give greedy's choices, its route and cost, and explain the difference by greedy ignoring g. Mention the consistency check.

solution: A*: expand S (f=5): B g=1,f=5; A g=4,f=6.
Expand B (f=5): A improves to g=1+2=3, f=5, predecessor B; G added with g=1+8=9, f=9.
Expand A (f=5): G improves to g=3+3=6, f=6, predecessor A (replacing B).
Remove G at f=6: A* returns S→B→A→G with cost 6.
Greedy: from S, h(A)=2 < h(B)=4, so expand A; it generates G with h=0, which is removed next. Greedy returns S→A→G with cost 4+3=7.
Greedy costs more because it ignores the paid cost g; the first edge S→A (4) is expensive.
Consistency: 5≤4+2, 5≤1+4, 4≤2+2, 2≤3+0, 4≤8+0, so h is consistent on every listed arc.
Answer: A* finds S→B→A→G (cost 6); greedy finds S→A→G (cost 7).

steps.title: Item counts and order
steps.text: Count each item across the six baskets {A,B,C}, {A,B}, {A,C}, {B,C}, {A,B,C}, {B}. All items with count ≥ 3 are kept. Order by descending count, breaking ties alphabetically.

check.prompt: What is the support count of B?
check.why: B is in baskets 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6.
check.retry: Only basket {A,C} lacks B.

steps.worked: Header: B:5, A:4, C:4 (A before C on the tie). All are frequent.

steps.title: Insert the ordered baskets
steps.text: Rewrite each basket in the order B, A, C and insert it from the root, sharing prefixes and adding 1 to each node passed.

check.prompt: Where does the basket {A,C} go?
options: A new branch root→A:1→C:1, because it has no B
check.why: Its ordered form is A,C; it does not start with B, so it cannot share the B prefix.
check.retry: An ordered path can only share a prefix that it actually begins with.

steps.worked: Ordered: BAC, BA, AC, BC, BAC, B. Tree: root→B:5 with children A:3→C:2 and C:1; root→A:1→C:1. Header links: C nodes are B-A-C:2, B-C:1, A-C:1.

steps.title: C's conditional pattern base
steps.text: Follow C's header links and take each prefix path weighted by the C node's count: (B,A):2, (B):1, (A):1. Sum the weights per item.

check.prompt: Conditional count of B given C?
check.why: B appears in (B,A):2 and (B):1, so 2 + 1 = 3.
check.retry: Add the weights of the prefix paths that contain B.

steps.worked: B|C = 2 + 1 = 3; A|C = 2 + 1 = 3. Both meet the minimum count 3.

steps.title: Frequent itemsets containing C
steps.text: Each surviving conditional item gives a pair with C. Check the triple {A,B,C} using only the paths that contain both A and B, and include {C} if its global count is ≥ 3.

check.prompt: Support count of {A,B,C}?
check.why: Only the (B,A) path with weight 2 contains both, so {A,B,C} has count 2 < 3.
check.retry: Which C prefix paths contain both A and B?

steps.title: Measures of A→B
steps.text: n(A∪B) is the number of baskets with both A and B. Then support = n(A∪B)/6, confidence = n(A∪B)/n(A), lift = confidence/(n(B)/6).

check.prompt: Confidence of A→B?
check.why: A and B appear together in baskets 1, 2 and 5, so 3/n(A) = 3/4.
check.retry: Count baskets with both A and B, then divide by n(A) = 4.

steps.title: Interpret the lift
steps.text: Compare the rule with both thresholds, then read the lift relative to 1.

check.prompt: What does a lift of 0.9 mean here?
options: B is slightly less common in A baskets (75%) than overall (83%)
A causes B in 90% of baskets
The rule fails the confidence threshold
check.why: Lift < 1 means negative association; confidence 0.75 still meets the inclusive 0.75 threshold.
check.retry: Lift compares conf(A→B) with supp(B); is 0.75 above or below 5/6?

steps.title: Write the three parts
steps.text: Present (1) the header table and the counted FP-tree with its branches, (2) C's conditional base, the frequent itemsets containing C with counts and the rejected triple, (3) support, confidence and lift of A→B with the threshold check and a non-causal reading of lift.

solution: Item counts: B:5, A:4, C:4; all ≥ 3. Order B, A, C (tie broken alphabetically).
Ordered baskets: BAC, BA, AC, BC, BAC, B.
FP-tree: root→B:5 with children A:3→C:2 and C:1; root→A:1→C:1. Header links connect the three C nodes and the two A nodes.
C's conditional pattern base: (B,A):2, (B):1, (A):1, giving B:3 and A:3.
Frequent itemsets containing C: {C}:4, {B,C}:3, {A,C}:3. {A,B,C} has count 2 < 3, so it is not frequent.
A→B: n(A∪B) = 3, support = 3/6 = 0.5, confidence = 3/4 = 0.75, which meets both thresholds.
Lift = 0.75/(5/6) = 0.9 < 1: B is slightly less common in A baskets than overall, so the rule passes the thresholds but shows a mild negative association, not a causal link.

steps.title: Max margin from convex hulls
steps.text: For separable data, the hard-margin boundary is the perpendicular bisector of the shortest segment between the two classes' convex hulls, and the full margin equals that hull distance.

steps.title: The two hulls
steps.text: Negatives (0,0),(0,4) form a segment on x = 0 with y from 0 to 4. Positives (4,1),(4,3) form a segment on x = 4 with y from 1 to 3.

check.prompt: What is the shortest distance between the two hulls?
check.why: The y-ranges [0,4] and [1,3] overlap, so a horizontal segment (e.g. (0,2) to (4,2)) of length 4 connects them.
check.retry: The segments are parallel and vertical; do their y-ranges overlap?

steps.worked: Hulls are vertical segments at x = 0 and x = 4 with overlapping y-ranges, so the shortest hull distance is 4, horizontally.

steps.title: The boundary
steps.text: The boundary is perpendicular to the shortest connecting segment and passes through its midpoint.

check.prompt: What is the maximum-margin boundary?
check.why: The connecting segment is horizontal from x = 0 to x = 4, so the bisector is x = 2.
check.retry: Take the midpoint of (0,2)–(4,2) and draw the perpendicular.

steps.worked: Boundary: x = 2, with each class 2 units away.

steps.title: Canonical parameters
steps.text: Write w = (w₁, 0). Require w₁·0 + b = −1 for the negatives and w₁·4 + b = +1 for the positives.

check.prompt: What is w₁?
check.why: b = −1 from the negatives; 4w₁ − 1 = 1 gives w₁ = 0.5.
check.retry: Solve for b first using a point with x = 0.

steps.worked: w = (0.5, 0), b = −1. Scores: (0,0),(0,4) → −1; (4,1),(4,3) → +1. All four are support vectors.

steps.title: Check the width
steps.text: Confirm the canonical parameters reproduce the hull gap via 2/‖w‖.

check.prompt: What is 2/‖w‖?
check.why: ‖w‖ = 0.5, so 2/0.5 = 4, equal to the hull distance.

steps.worked: Full width = 2/0.5 = 4, matching the hull gap.

steps.title: Scaling to (3w, 3b)
steps.text: Compute the new scores 3(w·x + b) and think about what changes and what does not.

check.prompt: After using (3w, 3b) = ((1.5,0), −3), what happens?
options: Same boundary and predictions; support points now score ±3, so it is no longer canonical
check.why: The zero set and signs are unchanged; geometric distances are unchanged; only functional scores scale by 3.
check.retry: Multiply the old scores −1 and +1 by 3, and ask where 3(w·x+b) = 0.

steps.worked: 3(0.5x − 1) = 1.5x − 3 is zero at x = 2 still; support points score ±3. Geometry is identical, but the ±1 canonical normalization is lost (2/‖3w‖ = 4/3 no longer equals the width).

steps.title: Write the three parts
steps.text: Structure the answer as: (1) hull argument giving the shortest gap and boundary x = 2; (2) canonical w, b, the ±1 check for all four points as support vectors, and full width 2/‖w‖; (3) the (3w, 3b) effect: same boundary, predictions and geometry, support levels become ±3. Each part is worth 3 marks.

solution: Negative hull: segment x = 0, y ∈ [0,4]. Positive hull: segment x = 4, y ∈ [1,3]. The y-ranges overlap, so the shortest hull distance is horizontal and equals 4.
The maximum-margin boundary is the perpendicular bisector of that gap: x = 2.
Canonical parameters: w = (0.5, 0), b = −1. Negatives score 0.5·0 − 1 = −1 and positives score 0.5·4 − 1 = +1, so all four points are support vectors.
Full width = 2/‖w‖ = 2/0.5 = 4, equal to the hull distance.

Replacing (w,b) by (3w,3b) multiplies every score by 3: the boundary 1.5x − 3 = 0 is still x = 2, all predictions and geometric distances are unchanged, but the support points now have functional levels ±3, so the pair is no longer canonical.

steps.title: Plan the passes
steps.text: Forward: net₁ = 0.4x + 0.1, net₂ = −x + 0.3, h_i = ReLU(net_i), o = 0.6h₁ − 0.5h₂ + 0.2 (linear). Backward: δ_o = t − o, δ_hi = ReLU'(net_i)·v_i·δ_o with v₁ = 0.6 and v₂ = −0.5. Bias update: b_i ← b_i + η δ_hi.

steps.title: Hidden activations
steps.text: Substitute x = 2 into both pre-activations and apply ReLU. Keep net₂: its sign determines ReLU' later.

check.prompt: What is net₂ = −2 + 0.3?
check.why: net₂ = −1.7 < 0, so h₂ = 0. Meanwhile net₁ = 0.8 + 0.1 = 0.9, so h₁ = 0.9.
check.retry: −x with x = 2 is −2. Add the bias 0.3.

check.prompt: What is o?
check.retry: 0.6 × 0.9 = 0.54. h₂ = 0 contributes nothing. Add the 0.2 bias.

steps.title: Loss and output delta
steps.text: The residual is t − o = 1 − 0.74. E = ½(residual)², and δ_o = residual × 1 (linear output).

check.prompt: What is the loss E?
check.retry: Square 0.26, then halve it.

steps.title: Hidden deltas
steps.text: δ_h1 = ReLU'(0.9) × 0.6 × δ_o. For δ_h2, check ReLU'(net₂) first.

check.prompt: What is δ_h1?
check.why: 1 × 0.6 × 0.26 = 0.156. δ_h2 = 0, because net₂ = −1.7 < 0 makes ReLU' = 0, even though v₂ = −0.5.
check.retry: Unit 1 is active (ReLU' = 1). Multiply its original outgoing weight 0.6 by δ_o = 0.26.

steps.title: Bias changes
steps.text: Δb_i = η δ_hi with η = 0.5.

check.prompt: What is Δb₁?
check.retry: Multiply η = 0.5 by δ_h1 = 0.156.

steps.title: Report everything
steps.text: List h₁, h₂, o and E; then δ_o, δ_h1 and δ_h2 (say why δ_h2 is zero); then add each Δb to its original bias (0.1 and 0.3) and report both new hidden biases. The rubric gives 3 marks to each of the three groups.

solution: δ_h1 = ReLU'(0.9) × 0.6 × 0.26 = 0.156, using the original outgoing weight.
δ_h2 = ReLU'(−1.7) × (−0.5) × 0.26 = 0, because the unit is inactive.
Answer: h₁ = 0.9, h₂ = 0, o = 0.74, E = 0.0338; δ_o = 0.26, δ_h1 = 0.156, δ_h2 = 0; new hidden biases 0.178 and 0.3.

steps.title: The projection pipeline
steps.text: Center: x − μ. Score: z = u₁ᵀ(x − μ). Reconstruct: x̂ = μ + z·u₁. Error: ||x − x̂||². Retained fraction: λ₁ / (λ₁ + λ₂).

steps.title: Center the point
steps.text: Subtract μ = (1,2) from x = (4,3).

check.prompt: What is the first coordinate of x − μ?
check.retry: Subtract the mean coordinate by coordinate.

check.prompt: What is z? (decimal)
check.retry: Add the centered coordinates and divide by √2.

steps.title: Reconstruct in original coordinates
steps.text: Centered reconstruction z·u₁ = (4/√2)(1,1)/√2, then add μ.

check.prompt: What is the second coordinate of x̂?
check.retry: (4/√2)·(1/√2) = 2; then add the mean back.

steps.title: Squared reconstruction error
steps.text: Residual x − x̂ = (4,3) − (3,4). Square its entries and add.

check.prompt: What is ||x − x̂||²?
check.retry: Use the reconstruction in original coordinates, not the centered one, against x.

steps.title: Retained variance
steps.text: R₁ = λ₁ / (λ₁ + λ₂) with λ₁ = 8, λ₂ = 2.

check.prompt: What fraction of variance does PC1 retain?
check.retry: Divide the kept eigenvalue by the sum of all eigenvalues.

steps.title: Present the four results
steps.text: Write in order: centered vector and score (3 marks), reconstruction in original coordinates with residual and squared error (4 marks), and the retained variance fraction (2 marks). You may note that flipping the sign of u₁ flips z but leaves x̂ unchanged.

solution: Centered point: x − μ = (4,3) − (1,2) = (3,1).
Centered reconstruction z·u₁ = (4/√2)(1,1)/√2 = (2,2); adding the mean gives x̂ = (3,4).
Residual x − x̂ = (1, −1), so the squared reconstruction error is 1 + 1 = 2.
Fraction of variance retained = λ₁/(λ₁ + λ₂) = 8/10 = 0.8.
A sign flip of u₁ flips z to −2√2 but gives the same reconstruction.

steps.title: OLS from centered sums
steps.text: m = Sxy/Sxx and b = ȳ − m·x̄, then ŷ(4) = 4m + b. Data: x = 0, 1, 2, 3 and y = 1, 2, 2, 5.

steps.title: Means
steps.text: Compute x̄ and ȳ.

check.prompt: What is ȳ?
check.retry: Sum the y values and divide by 4.

check.prompt: What is Sxy?
check.retry: Watch the sign of (0.5)(−0.5) = −0.25.

steps.title: Slope and intercept
steps.text: Compute m = Sxy/Sxx, then b = ȳ − m·x̄.

check.prompt: What is b?
check.retry: Find m first, then subtract m·x̄ from ȳ.

steps.title: Prediction at x = 4
steps.text: Substitute x = 4 into the fitted line.

check.prompt: What is ŷ(4)?
check.retry: Multiply 4 by the slope and add the intercept.

steps.title: Why PCA's slope can differ
steps.text: Compare what each method minimizes for the same four points.

check.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts the two fits?
options: OLS minimizes squared vertical residuals in y; PC1 maximizes variance, i.e. minimizes squared perpendicular distances, treating x and y symmetrically
Both minimize squared vertical residuals, so they always agree
PCA minimizes squared horizontal residuals in x
check.why: The different error directions generally give different optimal lines.
check.retry: Which distance does PCA's reconstruction error use?

steps.worked: OLS: vertical errors, y is the target. PCA: orthogonal errors / maximal variance, no target. Because the error directions differ, the two lines generally differ (they can coincide, e.g. for collinear or symmetric data).

steps.title: Write the full answer
steps.text: Show the means and centered sums, derive m and b (4 marks), state the prediction at x = 4 (2 marks), and contrast the OLS and PCA objectives, noting when they can coincide (3 marks).

solution: OLS treats y as the response and minimizes squared vertical residuals. The first principal direction maximizes projected variance, equivalently minimizing squared perpendicular (orthogonal) reconstruction error, and treats x and y symmetrically.
Because the objectives measure error in different directions, the PC1 slope need not equal 1.2 unless the points are exactly collinear.

steps.title: Tuple, start and goal
steps.text: Let a be the litres in the 4-litre jug and b the litres in the 3-litre jug. The state (a,b) is all the operators and the goal test need.

check.prompt: Which pair gives the initial state and the goal test?
options: Start (4,3); goal a = 2 and b = 0 only
check.why: Both jugs start empty, and the task only requires 2 litres in the 4-litre jug.
check.retry: Re-read which jug must hold 2 litres and how the jugs start.

steps.worked: State (a,b) with 0 ≤ a ≤ 4, 0 ≤ b ≤ 3 (integers). Start (0,0). Goal: a = 2.

steps.title: Fill and empty rules
steps.text: Write the four simple operators with their preconditions: fill or empty either jug.

steps.title: Capped pour rule
steps.text: When pouring, only as much moves as fits in the destination or is available in the source.

check.prompt: Pouring the 3-litre jug into the 4-litre jug from (a,b) gives…
check.why: The transfer is min(b, 4−a): the 4-litre jug cannot exceed 4 and b cannot go negative.
check.retry: What happens when a+b is larger than 4, and when it is smaller?

steps.title: Start of the path
steps.text: Fill the 3-litre jug, pour it into the 4-litre jug, then fill the 3-litre jug again.

check.prompt: From (0,0): Fill3, Pour3→4, Fill3. What is a now?
check.retry: After pouring 3 litres into the empty 4-litre jug, all 3 litres fit.

steps.title: The capped pour
steps.text: From (3,3), pour the 3-litre jug into the 4-litre jug. Only 4 − 3 litres fit.

check.prompt: From (3,3), Pour3→4. How many litres remain in the 3-litre jug?
check.why: Transfer min(3, 4−3) = 1, so b = 3 − 1 = 2 and the state is (4,2).
check.retry: Use max(a+b−4, 0) with a = 3, b = 3.

steps.title: Move the 2 litres across
steps.text: The 2 litres are in the wrong jug. Empty the 4-litre jug, then pour the 3-litre jug into it, and apply the goal test.
steps.worked: (4,2) → Empty4 → (0,2) → Pour3→4 → (2,0). Now a = 2, so the goal holds.

steps.title: Write the full answer
steps.text: Give (i) the tuple meaning, bounds, start and goal (3 marks), (ii) all six operators with preconditions and the capped pour updates (3 marks), and (iii) the full path from (0,0) with the operator for each move, ending in a goal state (3 marks).

solution: State (a,b): a = litres in the 4-litre jug, b = litres in the 3-litre jug, integers with 0 ≤ a ≤ 4, 0 ≤ b ≤ 3. Initial state (0,0). Goal: a = 2 (any b).
Pour3→4 (b > 0, a < 4): (min(a+b,4), max(a+b−4,0)). Pour4→3 (a > 0, b < 3): (max(a+b−3,0), min(a+b,3)); each pour transfers min(source volume, remaining destination capacity).

steps.title: Weighted Gini
steps.text: G = 1 − Σ p_c². For each split, weight each child's Gini by its share of the 16 samples, then subtract from the parent Gini to get the reduction.

steps.title: Parent Gini
steps.text: The parent has 8+ and 8− out of 16.

check.prompt: What is the parent Gini?
check.retry: Both class fractions are 1/2.

steps.title: Split A children
steps.text: Split A gives (6+,2−) and (2+,6−), each of size 8. Fractions are 0.75/0.25 in both children.

check.prompt: What is the Gini of each Split A child?

steps.worked: Both children: G = 0.375. Weights 8/16 each, so weighted Gini = 0.375 and reduction = 0.5 − 0.375 = 0.125.

steps.title: Split B right child
steps.text: Split B gives (4+,0−), which is pure, and (4+,8−) with p₊ = 1/3 and p₋ = 2/3.

check.prompt: What is the Gini of B's right child (4+,8−)?
check.retry: Square 4/12 and 8/12, add, and subtract from 1.

steps.title: Split B weighted Gini
steps.text: B's left child holds 4/16 of the samples and the right child 12/16.

check.prompt: What is Split B's weighted Gini?
check.retry: Multiply 4/9 by 12/16.

steps.title: Choose the split
steps.text: Compare the reductions 0.125 (A) and 1/6 (B), or equivalently the weighted impurities 0.375 and 1/3.

check.prompt: Which split does CART prefer?
options: Split B, lower weighted Gini (1/3 vs 0.375)
Split A, because its children are balanced in size
Split A, because it has a larger reduction
check.why: B's reduction 1/6 ≈ 0.167 exceeds A's 0.125; child balance is not the criterion.
check.retry: Which split leaves less weighted impurity?

steps.worked: B reduces impurity by 1/6 ≈ 0.167 > 0.125, so choose B.

steps.title: Checking generalization
steps.text: A lower training impurity does not guarantee the split helps on new data. Decide what data the check must use.

check.prompt: How should you check that the chosen split generalizes?
options: Evaluate on a validation set or by cross-validation, keeping a final test set untouched
Recompute the Gini on the same training data
Use the test set repeatedly to tune which split to keep
check.why: Only data not used to choose the split gives an honest estimate; reusing the test set for tuning leaks information.
check.retry: The check must use data the split never saw.

steps.worked: Compare tree performance with and without the split on validation data or by k-fold cross-validation; report final performance once on a reserved test set.

steps.title: Write the comparison
steps.text: Present: the parent Gini; for each split, child Gini values, weights and weighted Gini; both reductions side by side and the chosen split; then one or two sentences on validation/cross-validation with a reserved test set. Marks: 4 for both weighted Ginis, 3 for the comparison and choice, 2 for the held-out check.

solution: Split A: both children (6+,2−) and (2+,6−) have G = 1 − (0.75² + 0.25²) = 0.375; weights 8/16 each give weighted G = 0.375, reduction 0.125.
Since 1/6 > 0.125 (equivalently 1/3 < 0.375), choose Split B.
To check generalization, evaluate the tree with this split on held-out validation data or by cross-validation, and reserve a separate test set for the final estimate.

steps.title: What justifies the product
steps.text: Naïve Bayes replaces P(x_1,…,x_n∣c) with ∏ P(x_j∣c). A joint probability factorises into a product only when its factors are independent, and here every factor is conditioned on the class c.

check.prompt: Which statement would let you write P(x_1, x_2∣c) = P(x_1∣c)·P(x_2∣c)?
options: x_1 and x_2 are independent once the class c is known
x_1 and x_2 are independent in the whole population
every class has the same prior
check.why: The factorisation is inside a conditional on c, so it needs independence given c. Marginal independence is a different property, and the priors play no part.
check.retry: Every term in the product carries '∣c'. What does that tell you about the independence needed?

steps.title: Choose the assumption
steps.text: Equal class frequencies affect only the prior. Pooled independence is not needed, and features may be correlated overall. Pick the option stating independence given the class.

solution: Naïve Bayes writes P(x∣c) = ∏_j P(x_j∣c).
This is valid when the features are conditionally independent given the class. Equal priors and pooled independence are not required.
Answer: Features are modeled as independent conditional on the class.

steps.title: Read the denominator of Bayes' rule
steps.text: Bayes' rule is a fraction: the prior-weighted likelihood of one hypothesis on top, divided by the sum of prior-weighted likelihoods over all hypotheses. The normaliser is whatever sits underneath.

check.prompt: The denominator Σ_j P(E∣H_j)P(H_j) is equal to…
options: P(E), the total probability of the evidence
P(H_i), the prior of the chosen hypothesis
check.why: By the law of total probability, summing P(E∣H_j)P(H_j) over a partition gives P(E).
check.retry: Sum the joint probabilities P(E, H_j) over every hypothesis. What event is left?

steps.title: Pick the normaliser
steps.text: The normaliser is the same for every class and makes the posteriors add to 1. A class prior or one class's likelihood cannot do that. Pick the option that names the quantity in the denominator.

solution: Bayes' rule: P(H_i∣E) = P(E∣H_i)P(H_i) / Σ_j P(E∣H_j)P(H_j).
The denominator equals P(E) by total probability. It is shared by all classes and makes the posteriors sum to 1.
Answer: The marginal probability of the evidence.

steps.title: The four metric axioms
steps.text: A metric must satisfy nonnegativity, identity, symmetry and the triangle inequality d(a,c) ≤ d(a,b) + d(b,c). All three options are nonnegative and symmetric, so test the triangle inequality on simple 1D points such as 0, 1 and 2.

check.prompt: With points 0, 1 and 2, what is the squared Euclidean distance from 0 to 2?
check.why: Correct: (2 − 0)² = 4.
check.retry: Square the difference of the two coordinates.

steps.worked: Squared: d²(0,2) = 4 but d²(0,1) + d²(1,2) = 1 + 1 = 2. Euclidean and Manhattan give 2 ≤ 1 + 1, which holds.

steps.title: Pick the one that breaks an axiom
steps.text: Euclidean and Manhattan distances satisfy all four axioms. Choose the option for which the direct distance can exceed the sum of the two hops.

solution: Euclidean and Manhattan distances satisfy nonnegativity, identity, symmetry and the triangle inequality.
For points 0, 1, 2 the squared Euclidean distance gives d²(0,2) = 4 > d²(0,1) + d²(1,2) = 2, so the triangle inequality fails.
Answer: Squared Euclidean distance.

steps.title: What each linkage looks at
steps.text: Chaining happens when two large clusters merge just because one point in each is close to one point in the other. Ask which linkage lets a single close cross-pair decide the cluster distance.

check.prompt: Complete linkage between two clusters is determined by…
check.why: Complete linkage uses the maximum cross-pair distance, so one close pair cannot make clusters look close.
check.retry: Complete linkage requires every pair to be close; which pair does that depend on?

steps.title: Choose the chaining-prone linkage
steps.text: A fixed class label is not a linkage at all, and complete linkage resists chaining. Choose the linkage that uses the minimum cross-cluster distance.

solution: Single linkage uses the minimum cross-cluster distance, so one close pair is enough to merge two clusters.
Repeated merges through such close pairs produce long chains; complete linkage uses the maximum and resists this.
Answer: Single linkage.

steps.title: The K-means update rule
steps.text: After assigning points to their nearest centers, each center is moved to the point that minimizes the within-cluster sum of squared distances. Recall what μ_k = (1/|C_k|) Σ x_i computes.

check.prompt: A cluster holds the 1D points 1 and 3. What is its updated center?
check.why: The mean (1 + 3)/2 = 2 minimizes (1 − c)² + (3 − c)².
check.retry: Add the assigned points and divide by how many there are.

steps.title: Match the rule to an option
steps.text: Keeping the old center ignores the new assignment, and the furthest point does not minimize squared error. Choose the option that describes the formula you just used.

solution: K-means minimizes J = Σ_k Σ_{x∈C_k} ||x − μ_k||².
For a fixed nonempty cluster, J is minimized by μ_k = (1/|C_k|) Σ x_i, the arithmetic mean.
Answer: Take the arithmetic mean of its assigned vectors.

steps.title: One filter, one map
steps.text: Each standard filter slides over the input and produces one 2D feature map. The output volume is those maps stacked together. Spatial settings (stride, padding, window count) control only height and width.

check.prompt: Padding P and stride S appear in which part of the output shape?
check.why: O=⌊(I+2P−F)/S⌋+1 is applied per spatial axis. The depth is C_out=K and has nothing to do with P or S.
check.retry: Look at which variables appear in C_out=K.

steps.title: Choose the depth setting
steps.text: Padding and the number of horizontal windows only affect the spatial size. Pick the option that counts how many 2D maps get stacked.

solution: Each standard filter produces one 2D feature map.
The maps are stacked along depth, so C_out=K. Padding and stride change only the spatial size, O=⌊(I+2P−F)/S⌋+1.
Answer: The number of filters.

steps.title: A filter has the input's depth
steps.text: A standard convolution filter on an RGB input is not a flat 2D grid. It has one slice of weights for each of the three channels, so its shape is F×F×3, and it sits over the same spatial patch in all three channels at once.

check.prompt: At one spatial position, how are the red, green and blue contributions combined?
options: They are added together, along with one bias, to give a single number
They are kept as three separate outputs
Only the channel with the largest response is kept
check.why: The filter multiplies every aligned value in all channels and sums them all, so each position gives one scalar.
check.retry: Think about the dot product between a 3D patch and a 3D filter. How many numbers come out?

steps.title: From one number per position to the output
steps.text: Each position gives one scalar, and sliding the filter over every position fills one 2D grid. Pick the option that describes one grid built from contributions summed over all channels. Rule out the options that keep channels apart or give one output per kernel element.

solution: A standard filter on an RGB input has shape F×F×3, so it covers all three channels.
At each position it multiplies the aligned values in every channel, adds them all up and adds one bias, which gives one scalar.
Sliding it over all positions fills one 2D grid.
Answer: One feature map after summing contributions across all three channels.

steps.title: What average pooling computes
steps.text: Average pooling takes each window of a channel and returns the mean of its values. The rule is fixed (sum, then divide by the window size). Ask whether anything in that rule gets updated by gradient descent.

check.prompt: For a 2×2 average pool, the value used for each input in the window is…
options: a fixed 1/4 that is never learned
a learned weight, different for each position
a learned scale, one per channel
check.why: The mean always gives each element the same fixed weight of 1/(window size). Nothing is trained.
check.retry: Is the 1/4 in a mean ever changed by backpropagation?

steps.title: Count the learned values
steps.text: The averaging coefficients are fixed and standard average pooling has no bias. Choose the option that counts how many trainable weights that leaves.

solution: Standard average pooling replaces each window with the plain mean of its values, separately for each channel.
The weight 1/(window size) is fixed, and there is no bias, so backpropagation has nothing to update.
Answer: Zero.

steps.title: Four ways to judge an AI
steps.text: AI systems can be judged on two axes: thinking vs acting, and human-like vs rational. Each option here matches one of those criteria. Ask which one a conversation with a hidden judge can actually observe.

check.prompt: In the Turing test, what does the judge observe?
options: The optimality of the program's plans
check.why: The judge sees only conversational behaviour, never the internal process or plan quality.
check.retry: The judge is separated from the machine and only exchanges messages with it.

steps.title: Match the test to the criterion
steps.text: A test that only sees conversation can only measure whether behaviour looks human. Shortest routes are about rational action, and valid inference is about rational thinking. Pick the option that is about human-like behaviour.

solution: The Turing test lets a judge exchange messages with a hidden machine and a hidden person.
The judge only observes conversational behaviour, so the test measures acting humanly.
Shortest routes (acting rationally) and valid proofs (thinking rationally) are different criteria.
Answer: human-like conversational behaviour.

steps.title: MIN's backup rule
steps.text: Utilities are measured from MAX's point of view. MIN is the opponent, so at a MIN node it picks the child that is worst for MAX.

check.prompt: Which operation does a MIN node apply to its children's values?
check.why: MIN chooses the lowest value for MAX; averaging is for chance nodes.
check.retry: MIN wants MAX's utility to be as small as possible.

steps.title: Apply it
steps.text: Take the minimum of the child values 7, 2 and 4 and select that option.

solution: A MIN node backs up the smallest child value.
Answer: 2.

steps.title: What α and β mean
steps.text: α is the value MAX can already guarantee somewhere on the current path; β is the value MIN can already hold MAX to. Values worth exploring lie strictly between them.

check.prompt: If β (MIN's cap) has fallen to or below α (MAX's guarantee), what can the remaining siblings change?
options: They can still raise the root value
They must all be searched to get an exact value
check.why: MAX will never let play reach this node, because it already has α elsewhere and this node is worth at most β ≤ α.
check.retry: Would MAX ever choose a move worth at most what it already has?

steps.title: Pick the cutoff test
steps.text: The initial window α=−∞, β=+∞ never cuts, and α<β means the window is still open. Choose the relationship that means the window has closed.

solution: α is MAX's guaranteed lower bound and β is MIN's upper bound along the current path.
When α ≥ β no value at the current node can affect the choice above, so remaining siblings are skipped.
Answer: α≥β.

steps.title: Overfitting is a gap
steps.text: An overfit model has learned quirks of its own training sample. It does very well on the data it saw and much worse on new data from the same distribution. So look at both error levels and the gap between them.

check.prompt: Train error 2% and validation error 2%. What does that pattern suggest?
options: A model that fits and generalises well
check.why: Both errors are low with no gap, which is the healthy case. Overfitting needs held-out error to be much higher than training error.
check.retry: Overfitting means the model does worse on unseen data than on its training data. Is that happening here?

steps.title: Pick the overfitting signature
steps.text: Rule out the healthy case (both low) and the noise-floor statement, which says nothing about held-out error. Choose the option where training error is low but validation error is much higher.

solution: Overfitting means fitting quirks of the training sample that do not carry over to new data.
So training error is low while validation error is much higher, a large generalisation gap.
Answer: Low training error with much higher validation error.

steps.title: Augmentation must keep the label correct
steps.text: Augmentation creates new training inputs from existing ones and keeps the original label. That only helps if the label is still correct for the transformed input.

check.prompt: For digit classification, which augmentation is risky?
check.why: A 180° rotation can turn a 6 into a 9, so the copied label becomes wrong.
check.retry: Which change could make a person read a different digit?

steps.title: State the condition
steps.text: Augmentation is a training-time method, and how much it changes the input is not the test. Choose the option that states the condition you just used: the transformed example must still have the correct target.

solution: Augmentation adds transformed copies of training inputs with their original labels.
If the transformation changes the true class, for example rotating a 6 into a 9, it adds wrong labels.
Answer: When the transformation preserves the target label for the task.

steps.title: Roles of the three splits
steps.text: Training data fits the weights. Validation data is for choices such as hyperparameters and which epoch to keep. Test data is touched once, after every choice is fixed, to report performance.

check.prompt: If you used the test set to choose the checkpoint, its reported score would be…
options: optimistically biased, because the test set helped make the choice
unbiased, because the weights never trained on it
check.why: Choosing the best of many checkpoints on the test set fits the choice to that set, so the score is no longer a fair estimate.
check.retry: Does a dataset stay 'unseen' once you have used it to pick between models?

steps.title: Pick the split
steps.text: Checkpoint selection is a model choice. Choose the held-out split that exists for making choices, not the one kept back for the final report.

solution: Weights are fitted on training data, choices are made on validation data, and the test set is kept for one final evaluation.
Picking a checkpoint is a choice, and using the test set for it would make the test score biased.
Answer: Validation set.

steps.title: Paid plus remaining
steps.text: A* estimates the total cost of the cheapest solution that passes through n. That total is made of the part already travelled and the estimated part still to travel.

check.prompt: Which quantity is the cost already travelled from the start to n?
check.why: g(n) is the known path cost so far; h(n) is the estimate of what remains.
check.retry: Which letter is the known, already-incurred part?

steps.title: Combine the two costs
steps.text: Costs along a path add, they do not multiply, and using h alone would be greedy best-first. Pick the option that combines the paid cost and the remaining estimate correctly.

solution: A* ranks nodes by f(n), its estimate of the total cost of a solution through n.
That total is the cost already paid, g(n), plus the estimated remaining cost, h(n).
Answer: g(n)+h(n).

steps.title: Two heuristic bounds
steps.text: One property compares h(n) with the true remaining cost h*(n), which depends on whole optimal paths. The other compares h(n) with c(n,n′) + h(n′) for a single arc n→n′.

check.prompt: Which condition can be checked using only one arc's cost and the h values at its two ends?
check.why: c(n,n')+h(n') uses only the arc and its endpoint; h*(n) needs the whole optimal remaining path.
check.retry: Which inequality mentions an arc cost c?

steps.title: Name the property
steps.text: Goal depth and being 'goal-directed' are not edge-by-edge tests. Choose the property whose definition is the per-arc inequality above.

solution: Consistency requires h(n) ≤ c(n,n')+h(n') on every directed arc n→n'.
This inequality involves only one arc at a time, so it is checked locally; admissibility needs the true cost-to-go h*(n).
Answer: Consistency.

steps.title: g versus h
steps.text: Search algorithms rank frontier nodes using g(n), the cost already paid to reach n, and h(n), an estimate of the cost still to go. Greedy best-first only looks ahead: it wants the node that seems closest to the goal.

check.prompt: What does the heuristic h(n) estimate?
options: The cost from n to the nearest goal
The cost already paid from the start to n
The number of children n has
check.why: h(n) is a forecast of the remaining cost; g(n) is the cost already incurred.
check.retry: Is h about the path behind n or the path ahead of n?

steps.title: Pick greedy's priority
steps.text: Greedy best-first ignores how much was already paid and does not count children. Choose the option that matches 'how close does this node look to the goal'.

solution: Greedy best-first removes from OPEN the node with the smallest heuristic value.
h(n) estimates the remaining cost from n to a goal; the accumulated cost g(n) is ignored.
Answer: Estimated remaining cost h(n).

steps.title: Antimonotone support
steps.text: If X ⊆ Y then n(Y) ≤ n(X): adding items can only keep or reduce the number of transactions that contain the set. Apply this with X = {A,B}.

check.prompt: {A,B,C} contains {A,B}. Compared with n({A,B}), n({A,B,C}) is…
check.why: Every basket containing A, B and C also contains A and B, so the larger set's count cannot exceed the pair's.
check.retry: Can a basket contain {A,B,C} without containing {A,B}?

steps.title: Which direction the property runs
steps.text: Infrequency propagates upward to supersets, not downward to subsets: a subset like {A} can still be frequent. No counting is needed for supersets because the bound already rules them out. Pick the option that states the upward consequence.

solution: Antimonotonicity: X ⊆ Y implies n(Y) ≤ n(X).
Any superset of {A,B} therefore has count ≤ n({A,B}), which is below minsup.
Subsets such as {A} can still be frequent, and supersets need not be counted.
Answer: Every superset containing both A and B is infrequent.

steps.title: What a prefix path represents
steps.text: In an FP-tree, the path from the root to a suffix node stands for the transactions that end at that node. The suffix node's count says how many transactions contain both that prefix and the suffix item. Prefix nodes higher up may carry larger counts because other transactions also pass through them.

check.prompt: Path root→B:5→A:3→C:2. How many transactions contain B, A and C together along this path?
check.why: Only the C node's count (2) counts transactions that reach C; B:5 and A:3 include transactions that stop earlier.
check.retry: Which node's count only includes transactions that actually contain the suffix item?

steps.title: Choose the weight
steps.text: When collecting the conditional pattern base, each prefix path must be weighted by how many transactions it shares with the suffix. Pick the option that names the node whose count gives that number.

solution: A prefix path is collected for each occurrence of the suffix item in the tree.
Prefix nodes can have larger counts because transactions that do not contain the suffix also pass through them.
Only the suffix node's count measures co-occurrence of the prefix with the suffix.
Answer: The count at the suffix node.

steps.title: Labelled vs unlabelled tasks
steps.text: Data mining tasks differ in what they start from. Classification learns from records that already carry a class label. A primary-key retrieval just fetches a known record. The question describes records with no labels that must be grouped by how similar they are.

check.prompt: What does classification need that this task does not have?
options: A known class label on the training records
check.why: Classification is supervised: it learns a mapping from features to given labels. Here the records are unlabelled.
check.retry: Classification predicts a label. Where do the labels it learns from come from?

steps.title: Name the discovery task
