steps.text: Retrieval by key is a query, not discovery, and classification needs labels. Pick the task that discovers groups of similar unlabelled records.

solution: Classification is supervised: it predicts labels learned from labelled records.
Retrieval by primary key is a database query; it discovers nothing.
Grouping unlabelled records by similarity is unsupervised discovery of groups.
Answer: Clustering.

steps.title: The three rule measures
steps.text: Write each measure's numerator and denominator. Support uses n(X∪Y)/N, confidence uses n(X∪Y)/n(X), and lift divides confidence by supp(Y). A measure is directional if swapping X and Y can change its value.

check.prompt: Which of these is symmetric in X and Y (unchanged if you swap them)?
check.why: n(X∪Y) and N do not depend on which item is the antecedent, so support is symmetric.
check.retry: Which expression has no term that belongs to only one side of the rule?

steps.title: Match the measure to P(Y|X)
steps.text: P(Y|X) = n(X∪Y)/n(X): the denominator is the antecedent's count, which changes when the rule is reversed. Lift equals P(X∪Y)/(P(X)P(Y)), which is symmetric. Pick the measure whose formula is n(X∪Y)/n(X).

solution: Support n(X∪Y)/N is symmetric in X and Y.
Lift = conf/supp(Y) = P(X∪Y)/(P(X)P(Y)) is also symmetric.
Confidence n(X∪Y)/n(X) = P(Y|X) divides by the antecedent count, so it is directional.
Answer: Confidence of X→Y.

steps.title: Minkowski family
steps.text: d_r = (Σ|x_j − z_j|^r)^(1/r). r = 1 is Manhattan (sum of absolute differences), r = 2 is Euclidean, and as r → ∞ the largest difference dominates the sum.

check.prompt: For differences (1, 5), what does d_r approach as r grows very large?
check.why: Raising to a huge power makes the largest term dominate, so the r-th root tends to max(1, 5) = 5.
check.retry: Compare 1^r and 5^r when r is large.

steps.title: Match the name
steps.text: Manhattan adds all differences and squared Euclidean adds squared differences. Pick the option that names the r → ∞ (maximum-difference) case.

solution: Manhattan sums |x_j − z_j|; squared Euclidean sums (x_j − z_j)².
The Minkowski limit r → ∞ gives max_j |x_j − z_j|, the supremum (Chebyshev, L∞) distance.
Answer: supremum distance.

steps.title: Canonical constraints
steps.text: A hard-margin SVM requires y_i(w·x_i + b) ≥ 1 for every point. The margin planes are w·x + b = +1 and w·x + b = −1.

check.prompt: A positive point lies exactly on the plane w·x + b = +1. What is y_i(w·x_i + b)?
check.why: y_i = +1 and w·x_i + b = 1, so the product is 1.
check.retry: Multiply the label +1 by the score on that plane.

steps.title: Identify the points
steps.text: Points on a margin plane make the constraint tight. Points far from the boundary have y_i(w·x_i+b) > 1 and are not on the planes. Pick the option stating the tight constraint.

solution: The canonical margin planes are w·x + b = ±1.
A training point lies on its class's plane exactly when y_i(w·x_i + b) = 1; these are the support vectors.
Answer: points for which y_i(w·x_i + b) = 1.

steps.title: Slack and the signed score
steps.text: ξ_i = max(0, 1 − y_i f(x_i)). So y_i f(x_i) = 1 − ξ_i whenever ξ_i > 0.

check.prompt: If ξ_i = 0.4, what is the signed score y_i f(x_i)?
check.retry: Rearrange ξ = 1 − y f(x).

steps.title: Interpret 0 < ξ < 1
steps.text: With 0 < ξ < 1 the signed score lies strictly between 0 and 1: positive means the sign is correct, below 1 means it is closer than the margin plane. Pick the option matching that.

solution: With 0 < ξ_i < 1, y_i f(x_i) = 1 − ξ_i lies strictly between 0 and 1.
A positive signed score means correct classification; a score below 1 means the point is inside the margin.
Answer: correct sign inside the margin.

steps.title: Hidden-delta formula
steps.text: δ_j = G'(net_j) Σ_k w_kj δ_k. The sum runs over the downstream units k that receive unit j's output. Their deltas must already be known.

check.prompt: In the weight w_kj, unit k is…
options: a downstream unit that unit j feeds into
an upstream unit that feeds into j
the same unit j at the next iteration
check.why: w_kj connects j to k. Error flows back from k to j along that outgoing edge.
check.retry: The notation w_ji means 'from i to j'. Apply that to w_kj.

steps.title: Pick the weights in the sum
steps.text: The sum uses the edges leaving j toward units with known deltas, at their forward-pass values (not yet updated). Pick the option that matches.

solution: Hidden delta: δ_j = G'(net_j) Σ_k w_kj δ_k, where k ranges over the units that j feeds into.
The weights are j's outgoing weights, at the same values used in the forward pass, not values already updated in this iteration.
Answer: Outgoing weights to units with known deltas.

steps.title: Two quantities at each unit
steps.text: Each unit first computes net_j = Σ w_ji o_i + b_j and then applies its activation, o_j = G(net_j). The next layer's formula uses the upstream outputs o_i.

check.prompt: In net_j = Σ w_ji o_i + b_j, what is o_i?
options: The activation output of upstream unit i
The target value for unit i
check.why: o_i = G(net_i) is what unit i emits. Targets are used only in the loss, and each bias stays inside its own unit.
check.retry: o_j = G(net_j) is defined at every unit. Which quantity is that?

steps.title: Choose what flows forward
steps.text: Targets appear only in the loss, and a bias is added inside its own unit. Pick the option naming the value G(net) that each unit sends downstream.

solution: A unit computes net = Σ w·(inputs) + b, then outputs G(net).
The next layer uses these outputs as its inputs. Targets enter only the loss, and a bias is not passed on by itself.
Answer: The activation output.

steps.title: Gradients multiply along a path
steps.text: By the chain rule, the gradient for an early layer is a product of local derivatives along every later layer. A sigmoid's derivative o(1−o) is at most 0.25.

check.prompt: If four sigmoid derivative factors along a path are each 0.2 (weights 1), what is their product?
check.why: 0.2⁴ = 0.0016, so the signal reaching the early layer is tiny.
check.retry: Multiply 0.2 by itself four times.

steps.title: Choose the cause
steps.text: Early-layer weights are neither frozen nor reset. They receive a tiny gradient because many small factors are multiplied together. Pick the option describing that effect.

solution: Backprop multiplies local derivatives along the path from the loss to an early layer.
The sigmoid's derivative is at most 0.25, so many such factors shrink the gradient (for example 0.2⁴ = 0.0016). This is the vanishing-gradient problem.
Answer: Several small local derivatives multiply along a path.

steps.title: Eigenvalues are variances
steps.text: For a unit eigenvector u of the covariance S, the variance of the data projected on u is uᵀSu = λ. The first principal direction is the one along which the projected variance is largest.

check.prompt: Covariance diag(9, 1) has eigenvectors (1,0) and (0,1). Which one is the first principal direction?
check.why: The direction with eigenvalue 9 carries the most variance.
check.retry: Which eigenvalue is larger, and what does an eigenvalue measure here?

steps.title: Match the definition
steps.text: The mean vector is not computed from the covariance, and the smallest-variance eigenvector is the last component. Choose the option describing the eigenvector you picked in the example.

solution: Projected variance along a unit eigenvector u_j of the covariance equals its eigenvalue λ_j.
PCA orders directions by descending variance, so PC1 is the unit eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue.
Answer: A unit eigenvector of covariance for its largest eigenvalue.

steps.title: Encode and decode
steps.text: Encoding subtracts the mean first: z = Uᵀ(x − μ). Decoding Uz therefore only gives the centered point; you must undo the centering to return to the original coordinates.

check.prompt: With μ = (2,2), u = (1,0) and score z = 3, what is the first coordinate of x̂ = μ + uz?
check.why: x̂ = (2,2) + 3(1,0) = (5,2), so the first coordinate is 5.
check.retry: Compute uz = (3,0), then add μ.

steps.title: Name what was added
steps.text: In that example, the vector added to Uz was the same one subtracted before encoding. Choose the option that names it.

solution: PCA encodes z = Uᵀ(x − μ), working on mean-centered data.
Decoding gives x̂ = μ + Uz, so the centering mean is added back.
Answer: The mean used to center the original data.

steps.title: Supervised vs unsupervised
steps.text: A supervised method is trained to predict a designated target (response) variable. Unsupervised methods only describe structure among the inputs.

check.prompt: Which kind of method needs a designated target variable?
check.why: Supervised learning fits a mapping from inputs to a known target.
check.retry: Which kind is trained with labels or responses?

steps.title: Classify the options
steps.text: PCA and clustering both work on inputs alone. Choose the one supervised method in the list.

solution: PCA and clustering are unsupervised: they use only the feature values.
Ordinary linear regression is supervised: it predicts a response y from x.
Answer: Ordinary linear regression.

steps.title: Which direction is the error?
steps.text: In y-on-x regression the residual for point i is eᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ: the gap measured along the response axis at the same x. OLS adds up eᵢ² over all points.

check.prompt: For a point (2, 7) and fitted line ŷ = 2x + 1, what is the residual?
check.why: ŷ(2) = 5, so e = 7 − 5 = 2, a vertical gap at x = 2.
check.retry: Evaluate the line at x = 2 and subtract from the observed y.

steps.title: Pick the objective
steps.text: Perpendicular distances are what PCA uses, and a single largest error is a minimax criterion. Choose the option matching the squared gaps you just computed.

solution: OLS residuals are eᵢ = yᵢ − (mxᵢ + b), measured vertically along y.
OLS chooses m, b to minimize Σ eᵢ².
Answer: Squared vertical response residuals.

steps.title: What backtracking does at a failure
steps.text: When the current state CS is a dead end, it is added to DE and removed from the current path SL. The search returns to the nearest ancestor that still has an untried child in NSL and continues from there.

check.prompt: A tries B before C. B is a leaf dead end. Where does the search continue?
options: At C, the untried child of A
Back at the start with a fresh search
At B again, since it was just visited
check.why: B is removed from SL and put in DE; A still has the untried alternative C.
check.retry: Which ancestor of B still has a child that has not been tried?

steps.title: Match the behaviour
steps.text: A dead end never joins the solution path, and backtracking only retreats as far as needed, not to depth zero. Pick the option that describes retreating to an untried alternative.

solution: A dead-end leaf is recorded in DE and removed from the current path SL.
The search retreats to the nearest ancestor with an untried child and tries that child next.
Answer: The path retreats and an untried alternative is selected.

steps.title: Queue vs stack
steps.text: BFS keeps OPEN as a FIFO queue so a whole level is finished before the next one starts. DFS keeps OPEN as a LIFO stack so the most recently generated branch is followed first.

check.prompt: A has children B, C. After expanding A, BFS expands B, which has child D. Where does D go in OPEN = [C]?
check.why: FIFO appends new children at the back, so C (depth 1) is removed before D (depth 2).
check.retry: In a queue, are new arrivals served before or after those already waiting?

steps.title: Pick the FIFO rule
steps.text: Removing the deepest node is DFS behaviour, and removing the lowest estimated cost is a heuristic (best-first) search. Choose the option that describes the FIFO queue.

solution: BFS uses a FIFO queue: remove the node at the front and append its unseen children at the back.
Highest-depth-first is DFS; lowest estimated cost is best-first/heuristic search.
Answer: Remove from the front and append unseen children at the back.

steps.title: Forward vs backward
steps.text: Data-driven (forward) reasoning starts from known facts and fires applicable rules. Goal-driven (backward) reasoning starts from the target you want to establish and looks for rules whose conclusion matches it, turning their premises into subgoals.

check.prompt: To check 'eligible' using the rule age≥18 AND enrolled → eligible, goal-driven reasoning next tries to establish…
options: every fact in the database, one by one
the rule with the shortest distance to the goal
check.why: Backward reasoning turns the premises of a rule that concludes the goal into new subgoals.
check.retry: Which part of the rule must be true for 'eligible' to follow?

steps.title: Choose the matching description
steps.text: Expanding every fact equally describes forward reasoning, and Euclidean distance is a heuristic for geometric search, not a reasoning direction. Pick the option that starts from the goal.

solution: Goal-driven reasoning begins with the target hypothesis and finds rules that conclude it.
The premises of those rules become subgoals, which are established recursively.
Answer: A specified goal and its premises.

steps.title: How iterative deepening runs
steps.text: Iterative deepening runs a depth-limited DFS with bound 0, then 1, then 2, and so on. Each new bound begins a fresh search from the start state; nothing is resumed from the previous pass.

check.prompt: When the bound goes from 1 to 2, which node is expanded first in the new pass?
options: The last leaf reached at bound 1
The first node in a BFS queue carried over
check.why: Each pass restarts from the root and repeats the shallow levels before going one level deeper.
check.retry: Does iterative deepening keep a frontier between passes?

steps.title: Name what is restarted
steps.text: The restart is from the start state, and the search that restarts is depth-first with a depth limit, not a BFS queue. Pick that option.

solution: Iterative deepening repeats depth-limited DFS with bounds 0, 1, 2, ….
Each time the bound increases, a new depth-limited DFS starts from the start state.
Answer: A depth-limited DFS from the start.

steps.title: What a state is for
steps.text: A state is used for two jobs: deciding which operators are legal from it and what successor each produces, and testing whether the goal has been reached. Anything those two jobs depend on must be stored; anything else is extra.

check.prompt: For two jugs, why is the pair (a,b) of current volumes enough as a state?
options: Every legal fill, empty or pour and the goal test depend only on the current volumes
It records the order in which jugs were filled
It counts how many moves have been made so far
check.why: Preconditions, successor updates and the goal test all read only a and b, so nothing else is needed.
check.retry: What does a pour rule or the goal test actually need to look at?

steps.title: Test each option against both jobs
steps.text: The expansion order is a property of the search, not of the situation. A move count alone cannot tell you which actions are legal or whether the goal holds. Pick the option that covers both legal transitions and the goal test.

solution: A state must let you decide which operators apply (and what they produce) and whether the goal is satisfied.
The expansion order belongs to the search algorithm, and a move count alone cannot decide legality or the goal test.
Answer: Everything needed for legal transitions and the goal test.

steps.title: Recall's formula
steps.text: Recall (TPR, sensitivity) = TP/(TP+FN). Look at which population the two terms in the denominator belong to.

check.prompt: TP and FN have what in common?
check.why: TP is a positive predicted positive; FN is a positive predicted negative. Both are actual positives.
check.retry: A false negative was predicted negative, so what must its true label be?

steps.title: Name the denominator
steps.text: Recall asks: of the cases that really are positive, how many were found? Predicted positives is precision's denominator and all predictions is accuracy's. Pick the population TP+FN describes.

solution: Recall = TP/(TP+FN).
TP + FN counts every actually positive case, whether it was caught or missed.
Answer: all actual positives.

steps.title: Pre- vs post-pruning
steps.text: Pre-pruning stops growing a branch before a weak split is made. Post-pruning first grows the tree, then goes back and simplifies parts that do not help on validation data.

check.prompt: When does post-pruning act?
options: After the tree has been grown
Only while bootstrap samples are drawn
check.why: The 'post' means it operates on an already built tree.
check.retry: What does the prefix 'post' tell you about timing?

steps.title: What the simplification looks like
steps.text: Post-pruning collapses a subtree into something simpler, typically a leaf predicting the majority class. It does not add data or train one tree per feature. Choose the option that describes collapsing an existing subtree.

solution: Post-pruning is applied after the full tree has been grown.
It replaces a subtree that does not improve held-out performance with a simpler prediction, such as a leaf with the majority class.
Answer: replaces an existing subtree with a simpler prediction.

steps.title: Children can differ in size
steps.text: After a split, one child may receive most of the parent's samples and the other only a few. The combined impurity should reflect how many samples actually end up in each impure or pure child.

check.prompt: A split sends 9 samples to a pure child and 1 sample to a mixed child. Which child should influence the split score more?
options: The pure child, because it holds 9 of the 10 samples
Both equally, because there are two children
The mixed child, because it has the higher impurity
check.why: Each child's impurity counts in proportion to the share of parent samples it receives, here 9/10 vs 1/10.
check.retry: Think about how many of the parent's samples each child is responsible for.

steps.title: Pick the combination rule
steps.text: The formula sums |D_j|/|D| · impurity(D_j) over the children. A plain mean ignores child sizes and a maximum class count is not an impurity at all. Choose the option that matches the |D_j|/|D| weights.

solution: Child impurities are combined as Σ_j (|D_j|/|D|)·I(D_j), where |D_j|/|D| is the fraction of parent samples reaching child j.
An arithmetic mean would let a tiny child count as much as a large one, and a maximum class count is not an impurity measure.
Answer: weighted by the fractions of parent samples entering each child.

steps.title: Unsmoothed estimates and zero factors
steps.text: Without smoothing, P(x_j = v∣c) is estimated as count(v in class c) / count(class c). If the value v never appears in that class's training rows, the estimate is 0. The class score is a product of all the factors.

check.prompt: If one factor in s_c = P(c)·∏P(x_j∣c) is 0, the score is…
options: unchanged, because the other factors dominate
undefined, because you divide by zero
check.why: Any product that contains a zero factor is zero.
check.retry: What happens to a product when one term is 0?

steps.title: Judge the claim
steps.text: Join the two facts: an unseen value gives a zero estimate, and a zero factor makes the product zero. Decide whether the statement is True or False. This is the problem that Laplace smoothing fixes.

solution: Unsmoothed, P(x_j = v∣c) = 0 when v never occurs in class c's training rows.
The class score is a product, so a single zero factor makes s_c = 0, however strong the other evidence is.
Answer: True.

steps.title: Definition of conditional probability
steps.text: Conditional probability is defined as P(E∣A) = P(A,E)/P(A) when P(A) > 0. Rearrange the definition to see what P(A,E) equals.

check.prompt: Multiplying both sides of P(E∣A) = P(A,E)/P(A) by P(A) gives…
check.why: This is the product (chain) rule: joint = conditional × the probability of what is conditioned on.
check.retry: Keep the conditional term exactly as P(E∣A) and multiply it by P(A).

steps.title: Compare with the claim
steps.text: The claim calls P(E∣A) the likelihood and P(A) the prior. Check whether their product matches the rearranged identity, then answer True or False.

solution: By definition, P(E∣A) = P(A,E)/P(A).
Rearranging gives P(A,E) = P(E∣A)P(A), which is likelihood × prior (the chain rule).
Answer: True.

steps.title: Cosine depends on direction only
steps.text: cos(u, v) = u·v / (||u|| ||v||). Replace v by cv with c > 0 and see what happens to the numerator and the denominator.

check.prompt: If v is replaced by 3v, the dot product u·v is multiplied by…
check.retry: The dot product is linear in each argument.

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: The numerator and the norm in the denominator are both multiplied by the same positive c. Decide whether the ratio therefore changes.

solution: cos(u, cv) = c(u·v) / (||u|| · c||v||) for c > 0.
The factor c cancels, so the cosine similarity is unchanged.
Answer: True.

steps.title: How a cut works
steps.text: A horizontal cut at height h keeps only merges below h. Every merge above the cut is undone, and each merge undone adds one cluster.

check.prompt: Five points are merged at heights 1, 2, 4, 7. A cut at height 3 gives how many clusters?
check.why: Only the merges at 1 and 2 are kept: 5 − 2 = 3 clusters.
check.retry: Start with 5 singletons and subtract one for each merge below the cut.

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: Compare with a cut at height 5 in the same example. Decide whether the number of clusters depends on the cut height.

solution: Cutting at height h keeps merges below h; the number of clusters is N minus the number of merges kept.
E.g. merges at 1, 2, 4, 7 on 5 points: cut at 3 gives 3 clusters, cut at 5 gives 2.
Answer: True.

steps.title: Local, not global, optimization
steps.text: Each Lloyd step never increases J, and the algorithm stops once assignments stop changing. Ask whether that stopping point must be the global minimum of J.

check.prompt: When K-means stops, its solution is guaranteed to be…
options: a fixed point (local optimum) of the assign–update steps
check.why: Lloyd's algorithm only guarantees no further improvement from its own steps.
check.retry: Does each step look at all possible clusterings, or just improve the current one?

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: Different starting centers can lead to different fixed points. Decide whether the statement is true or false.

solution: Lloyd's algorithm decreases J monotonically but only converges to a local optimum (fixed point).
Different initial centers can reach different fixed points with different clusters.
Answer: True.

steps.title: Where stride appears
steps.text: With I, P and F fixed, the number of positions is O=⌊(I+2P−F)/S⌋+1. The top of the fraction is fixed, and only the divisor S changes.

check.prompt: With I+2P−F = 12, how many positions are there for S=2 and for S=3?
check.why: ⌊12/2⌋+1 = 7 and ⌊12/3⌋+1 = 5. The larger stride gives fewer positions.
check.retry: Work out ⌊12/S⌋ + 1 for each S.

steps.title: Generalise
steps.text: Dividing a fixed non-negative number by a larger S cannot give a bigger result, and taking the floor keeps that order. Decide whether a larger stride can ever increase the count.

solution: The number of positions is ⌊(I+2P−F)/S⌋+1, and the top of the fraction stays fixed.
A larger S makes the fraction no bigger, and the floor keeps the order. For example, 12 gives 7 positions at S=2 and 5 at S=3.
Answer: True.

steps.title: Shape of a multi-channel filter
steps.text: A standard filter on a C-channel input has F_h×F_w×C weights. Each channel slice has its own weights, and the result is summed over channels.

check.prompt: A 3×3 filter on a 3-channel input has how many weights, not counting the bias?
check.why: 3·3·3 = 27. That is one separate 3×3 slice for each channel.
check.retry: Multiply the spatial size by the number of channels.

steps.title: Judge the claim
steps.text: Each channel has its own slice of free weights, and nothing forces those slices to be equal. Decide whether the different channel slices can therefore hold different weights.

solution: A standard filter on C channels has F_h×F_w×C weights, one slice per channel, and the channel contributions are summed.
Each slice is learned on its own, so the weights can differ between channels.
Answer: True.

steps.title: Pooling works within one channel
steps.text: Standard max pooling takes a small spatial window in one feature map and keeps its largest value, then does the same for every other channel separately.

check.prompt: A 16×16×8 map goes through 2×2 max pooling with stride 2. What is the output depth?
check.why: Each of the 8 channels is pooled on its own, so the depth stays 8 and only the spatial size halves.
check.retry: Does pooling merge channels, or treat each one separately?

steps.title: Judge the claim
steps.text: The claim says pooling compares values across channels and reduces depth. Compare that with the per-channel behaviour and the unchanged depth you just found, then decide True or False.

solution: Standard max pooling looks at a spatial window inside each channel separately.
It shrinks height and width but leaves the number of channels as it was.
Answer: False.

steps.title: What 'acting rationally' is judged on
steps.text: Acting rationally means choosing the action that best achieves the objective given the information available. The definition is about the outcome of the decision, not about how the decision was computed.

check.prompt: A route planner is judged rational when…
options: its chosen route best serves the objective given what it knows
its search process resembles how a person plans
it can explain its route in natural language
check.why: Rationality is measured against the objective and the available information.
check.retry: Which option measures the quality of the decision itself?

steps.title: Apply the criterion to the claim
steps.text: Since rationality does not mention how the decision is reached, a system whose internal process differs from human reasoning can still make the best decision. Decide whether the statement is therefore true or false.

solution: Acting rationally is judged by whether the action best achieves the objective given the available information.
That criterion says nothing about the internal process, so a graph-search planner that thinks nothing like a person can still pick the optimal route.
Answer: True.

steps.title: One utility scale
steps.text: Standard minimax uses a single number per leaf: MAX maximises it and MIN minimises it. MIN's preference is represented by the min operation, not by a separate score.

check.prompt: If leaves were scored from each mover's own perspective, what would go wrong?
options: max and min would compare numbers on different scales
The tree would need more depth
check.why: Backing up with max/min only makes sense when larger always means better for the same player.
check.retry: What does 'larger is better' refer to at a MIN node?

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: Given that MIN's opposing preference is already captured by minimising, decide whether all leaves must use one player's perspective. Choose True or False.

solution: Minimax backs up max at MAX nodes and min at MIN nodes over one utility scale (MAX's perspective).
The min operation already represents the opponent's preference, so every leaf must be scored on that single scale.
Answer: True.

steps.title: Order affects bounds
steps.text: Alpha–beta cuts once α ≥ β. How quickly the bounds tighten depends on which children are seen first: a strong first move gives a high α early.

check.prompt: Which ordering tends to give the most cutoffs?
check.why: Good moves first tighten α and β early, so later siblings are pruned sooner.
check.retry: When is α large earliest at a MAX node?

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: The root value is the same under any ordering, but the question is about the number of leaves examined. Decide True or False.

solution: Cutoffs occur when α ≥ β, and how early that happens depends on the order children are visited.
Examining strong moves first tightens the bounds sooner and prunes more leaves; poor ordering prunes fewer. The root value is unchanged.
Answer: True.

steps.title: Levels versus gap
steps.text: The gap shows variance: how much worse the model does on new data. The level of training error shows bias: whether the model can fit the data at all. A model can have a small gap and still have high errors on both splits.

check.prompt: Train error 30% and validation error 31%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
check.why: The gap is small, but both errors are high, so the model is too rigid or under-trained.
check.retry: A small gap is only good news when the errors themselves are low.

steps.title: Judge the claim
steps.text: The claim describes exactly that situation: high errors on both splits with a small gap. Decide whether high bias is a possible explanation.

solution: The gap measures how much worse the model does on new data, while the error levels show whether it can fit the data at all.
High training and validation error with a small gap means the model underfits, which is a sign of high bias.
Answer: True.

steps.title: How dropout masks work
steps.text: In standard dropout, each unit is kept with probability p independently, and a fresh random mask is drawn for every training example or mini-batch. At test time no mask is applied (the activations are scaled instead).

check.prompt: If the same mask were used for every update, dropout would be the same as…
check.why: A fixed mask just deletes some units permanently. The regularising effect comes from changing the mask.
check.retry: What would a mask that never changes do to the network's structure?

steps.title: Judge the claim
steps.text: Dropout regularises because the set of active units keeps changing. Decide whether standard dropout redraws its masks during training.

solution: Standard dropout draws a new random mask for each training example or mini-batch.
Because the active units keep changing, no unit can rely on a fixed set of others. A fixed mask would just be a smaller network.
Answer: True.

steps.title: Preprocessing is learned too
steps.text: Scalers, PCA and imputers estimate statistics such as means, variances and components from data. If they are fitted on the full dataset, the held-out folds help determine those statistics.

check.prompt: Standardising with the mean and standard deviation of all samples before CV means the validation fold…
options: influenced the scaling applied to its training fold
is unaffected, because no labels were used
check.why: The held-out samples helped set the mean and standard deviation, so information crosses the split even without labels.
check.retry: Which samples were used to work out the mean and standard deviation?

steps.title: Judge the claim
steps.text: Held-out data has shaped the features the model is trained and scored on. Decide whether that counts as leakage into cross-validation.

solution: Learned preprocessing (scaling, PCA, imputation) estimates statistics from the data it is fitted on.
When it is fitted on the full dataset, each held-out fold affects those statistics and therefore the features of its training fold. That is leakage, and it inflates CV scores.
Answer: True.

steps.title: Substitute h = 0
steps.text: A* ranks by f(n)=g(n)+h(n). Set h(n)=0 for every node and simplify f.

check.prompt: With h(n)=0 everywhere, f(n) equals…
check.retry: Only the h term vanishes.

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: g(n) is the accumulated path cost, so compare that with what the statement says A* ranks by. Decide True or False.

solution: A* priority is f(n)=g(n)+h(n).
With h=0, f(n)=g(n), the accumulated cost, so A* behaves like uniform-cost search.
Answer: True.

steps.title: Admissibility bound
steps.text: Admissibility requires 0 ≤ h(n) ≤ h*(n), where h*(n) is the true cheapest remaining cost.

check.prompt: If h(n) overestimates, how does h(n) compare with h*(n)?
check.why: Overestimating means the estimate is larger than the true cost.
check.retry: 'Over' means the estimate is above the true value.

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: Check whether h(n) > h*(n) is compatible with the required h(n) ≤ h*(n). Decide True or False.

solution: An admissible heuristic must never exceed the true remaining cost: h(n) ≤ h*(n).
Overestimating means h(n) > h*(n) for some n, which violates that bound.
Answer: False.

steps.title: Frontier versus single path
steps.text: Hill climbing keeps only its current state and moves to a neighbour. Greedy best-first keeps every generated but unexpanded node on OPEN and each time picks the smallest h from the whole list.

check.prompt: After greedy best-first expands a node, what happens to its unexpanded siblings?
options: They stay on OPEN and can be chosen later
They are discarded like in hill climbing
They are moved to CLOSED without expansion
check.why: Greedy best-first is a frontier search; generated nodes remain on OPEN until expanded.
check.retry: Does greedy keep a frontier or only the current state?

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: If siblings stay on OPEN, consider whether a later selection with the smallest h could be one of those older alternatives. Decide True or False.

solution: Greedy best-first keeps all generated, unexpanded nodes on OPEN.
Each step selects the smallest h from the whole frontier, so if the current branch looks worse, an older alternative can be chosen.
Answer: True.

steps.title: Antimonotone support
steps.text: Each pair of a triple is a subset of it, so n(pair) ≥ n(triple). Use this with the same minsup threshold.

check.prompt: If n({A,B,C}) = 4, what is the smallest possible n({A,B})?
check.why: Every basket containing A, B and C contains A and B, so n({A,B}) ≥ 4.
check.retry: Count the baskets containing {A,B,C}; do they all contain {A,B}?

steps.title: Judge the claim
steps.text: If the triple's count is at least minsup and each pair's count is at least the triple's, decide whether every pair must also meet minsup.

solution: Each pair of a triple is a subset, so n(pair) ≥ n(triple).
The triple is frequent: n(triple) ≥ minsup, hence n(pair) ≥ minsup for every pair.
Answer: True.

steps.title: How FP-growth avoids candidates
steps.text: FP-growth compresses the database into an FP-tree, then for each suffix item builds a conditional pattern base and a conditional FP-tree and recurses. Patterns grow from these conditional trees.

check.prompt: Which algorithm relies on generate-and-test of candidate itemsets C_k?
check.why: Apriori generates C_k by join and prune, then counts; FP-growth grows patterns from conditional trees.
check.retry: Which algorithm has explicit join and prune steps?

steps.title: Judge the claim
steps.text: The claim says FP-growth must first enumerate Apriori-style candidates. Compare that with how FP-growth mines and decide true or false.

solution: FP-growth builds one FP-tree, then recursively mines suffix-specific conditional pattern bases and conditional FP-trees.
It never enumerates Apriori candidate sets C_k; avoiding candidate generation is its main advantage.
Answer: False.

steps.title: Shapes of data
steps.text: Record data has a fixed set of attributes per row. Transaction data instead lists what each basket contains, with a variable number of items. Association analysis counts how many baskets contain a given set.

check.prompt: What does support count in association analysis?
options: Baskets that contain every item of a set
Total units sold of each product
check.why: Support counts transactions containing the itemset, so each transaction must be a set of items.
check.retry: Support is a fraction of what unit?

steps.title: Judge the claim
steps.text: If support is counted per basket as 'contains the set or not', each basket must be represented as a set of items. Decide whether the statement matches this.

solution: Transaction data records, for each basket, the set of items it contains.
Association analysis counts how many such sets contain an itemset (support).
Answer: True.

steps.title: Denominators of the two rules
steps.text: conf(X→Y) = n(X∪Y)/n(X) and conf(Y→X) = n(X∪Y)/n(Y). The numerators are equal; compare the denominators.

check.prompt: With n(X)=8, n(Y)=10, n(X∪Y)=6, what is conf(Y→X)?
check.retry: The antecedent of Y→X is Y, so divide by n(Y).

steps.title: Judge 'always'
steps.text: The two confidences match only when n(X) = n(Y). One counterexample is enough to refute 'always'. Decide true or false.

solution: conf(X→Y) = n(X∪Y)/n(X) and conf(Y→X) = n(X∪Y)/n(Y).
They are equal only when n(X) = n(Y). Example: 6/8 = 0.75 versus 6/10 = 0.6.
Answer: False.

steps.title: Scaling one feature
steps.text: Euclidean distance adds squared differences across coordinates. Multiplying one coordinate by s multiplies its contribution by s², but leaves the others unchanged.

check.prompt: From query (0,0): a = (1,0), b = (0,2). If x₁ is multiplied by 10, what is the new distance to a?
check.why: a becomes (10,0), distance 10, while b stays at distance 2, so b is now nearer.
check.retry: Scale a's first coordinate by 10, then take its distance.

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: Before scaling a was nearer (1 < 2); after scaling b is nearer. Decide whether a positive rescaling of one coordinate can change the neighbour order.

solution: Rescaling one coordinate changes its weight in the Euclidean sum but not the others'.
Example: with query (0,0), a = (1,0) is nearer than b = (0,2); after multiplying x₁ by 10, a is at distance 10 and b is nearer.
Answer: True.

steps.title: Zero set under scaling
steps.text: The boundary is the set of x with w·x + b = 0. Replacing (w,b) by (cw, cb) with c > 0 multiplies the left side by c.

check.prompt: If w·x + b = 0, what is (3w)·x + 3b?
check.why: 3(w·x + b) = 3·0 = 0, so x is still on the boundary.
check.retry: Factor out the 3.

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: Every point on the old boundary stays on it, and every sign of w·x + b is preserved for c > 0. Decide whether the boundary moves.

solution: c(w·x + b) = 0 exactly when w·x + b = 0 for c > 0.
So the boundary and all predicted signs are unchanged; only the functional score scale changes.
Answer: False.

steps.title: Correct sign vs unit margin
steps.text: Correct classification needs y_i f(x_i) > 0. The unit margin constraint needs y_i f(x_i) ≥ 1. These are different thresholds.

check.prompt: A point has y_i f(x_i) = 0.5. What is its minimum slack?
check.why: max(0, 1 − 0.5) = 0.5 > 0, so it violates the margin while its sign is correct.
check.retry: Use ξ = max(0, 1 − y f(x)).

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: A point with signed score between 0 and 1 is classified correctly yet needs positive slack. Decide whether a correctly classified sample can violate the unit margin.

solution: If 0 < y_i f(x_i) < 1 the sign is correct but y_i f(x_i) < 1.
For example y_i f(x_i) = 0.5 needs ξ = 0.5, a margin violation.
Answer: True.

steps.title: Differentiate the logistic function
steps.text: σ(z) = 1/(1 + e^(−z)). Differentiating gives σ'(z) = e^(−z)/(1 + e^(−z))². Try writing this using σ(z) itself.

check.prompt: At z = 0, σ(0) = 0.5. What is σ'(0)?
check.retry: Substitute z = 0 into e^(−z)/(1 + e^(−z))².

steps.title: Judge the claim
steps.text: Note that e^(−z)/(1 + e^(−z)) = 1 − σ(z), so σ'(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)). With o = σ(net), compare this with the claim and answer True or False.

solution: With o = σ(net), the derivative is o(1 − o) (e.g. 0.25 at o = 0.5).
Answer: True.

steps.title: Compose two affine maps
steps.text: Take layer 1 as h = W₁x + b₁ and layer 2 as y = W₂h + b₂. Substitute the first into the second and simplify.

check.prompt: Substituting gives y = …
options: W₂x + W₁x, with the biases cancelling
check.why: y = W₂(W₁x + b₁) + b₂ = (W₂W₁)x + (W₂b₁ + b₂): a single matrix times x plus a constant.
check.retry: Distribute W₂ over (W₁x + b₁).

steps.title: Judge the claim
steps.text: The result has the form Wx + b, which is again affine, and the same argument repeats for any number of layers. Decide True or False.

solution: y = W₂(W₁x + b₁) + b₂ = (W₂W₁)x + (W₂b₁ + b₂), which is affine.
By induction any stack of affine layers without nonlinear activations is affine, so depth adds no expressive power.
Answer: True.

steps.title: Examples per update
steps.text: A full-batch update computes the gradient over all N training examples. An SGD update with one example computes it from that single example.

check.prompt: With N = 1000 training examples, how many examples does one full-batch update evaluate?
check.why: Full batch uses every example per update. SGD uses 1.
check.retry: 'Full batch' means the whole training set.

steps.title: Judge the claim
steps.text: Compare 1 example with N examples per update for any training set larger than one. Decide True or False, and remember the trade-off: cheaper updates, noisier gradient.

solution: Full-batch gradient descent evaluates all N examples for each update. Single-example SGD evaluates 1.
For N > 1, an SGD step is cheaper but its gradient estimate is noisier.
Answer: True.

steps.title: Units change the covariance
steps.text: If a variable is rescaled by c (e.g. metres to centimetres, c = 100), its variance is multiplied by c² and its covariances by c. The eigenvectors of the new matrix can point elsewhere.

check.prompt: A variable with variance 2 is converted from metres to centimetres. What is its new variance?
check.why: Variance scales by c² = 100² = 10000, so 2 × 10000 = 20000.
check.retry: Variance scales with the square of the unit factor.

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: A variable whose variance grows that much will tend to dominate PC1. Decide whether covariance PCA can therefore change with units.

solution: Rescaling a variable by c multiplies its variance by c² and its covariances by c.
The covariance matrix and its eigenvectors change, so the principal directions can change (which is why standardization is sometimes used).
Answer: True.

steps.title: Full orthonormal basis
steps.text: If U contains all d orthonormal directions, it is a square orthogonal matrix, so UUᵀ = I. Reconstruction of a centered point is UUᵀ(x − μ).

check.prompt: With U = I (2×2), what is the reconstruction of the centered point (3,−1)? Give its second coordinate.
check.why: UUᵀ = I, so the point is returned unchanged: (3,−1).
check.retry: Multiply by the identity twice.

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: Nothing is discarded when every component is kept. Decide whether the reconstruction is exact.

solution: With a complete orthonormal basis U, UUᵀ = I.
The reconstruction UUᵀ(x − μ) equals x − μ exactly; no residual remains.
Answer: True.

steps.title: What PCA is given
steps.text: Standard PCA takes a set of feature vectors, computes their covariance and returns its eigenvectors. Ask whether a target variable or prediction loss appears anywhere in that recipe.

check.prompt: PCA chooses directions by maximizing…
check.why: PCA is unsupervised: its objective is projected variance (equivalently reconstruction error).
check.retry: Recall Su = λu: which quantity does λ measure?

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: Since the objective never refers to a dependent variable, decide whether the statement is true or false.

solution: PCA maximizes projected variance of the features, using only the feature covariance.
No dependent variable or prediction loss is used, so PCA is unsupervised.
Answer: False.

steps.title: The intercept equation
steps.text: With an intercept, b = ȳ − m·x̄. Evaluate the fitted line ŷ = mx + b at x = x̄.

check.prompt: With m = 2, x̄ = 3, ȳ = 10, what is ŷ(x̄)?
check.retry: Find b first, then evaluate the line at x = 3.

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: In general ŷ(x̄) = m·x̄ + ȳ − m·x̄. Simplify and decide whether the line passes through (x̄, ȳ).

solution: OLS with an intercept gives b = ȳ − m·x̄.
Then ŷ(x̄) = m·x̄ + ȳ − m·x̄ = ȳ, so the line passes through (x̄, ȳ).
Answer: True.

steps.title: How far a retreat goes
steps.text: After a dead end, backtracking returns to the parent. If the parent has no untried children, it too is a dead end and is removed, and so on up the path until an ancestor with an untried alternative is found.

check.prompt: Path A→B→D, where D is a dead end, B has no other children and A has untried child C. How many nodes leave the path before C is tried?
check.why: D fails, then B has nothing left, so both D and B are removed; the retreat stops at A.
check.retry: Check whether B still has a child to try once D fails.

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: The example removed more than one level of the path. Decide whether a dead end can cause multiple levels to be removed.

solution: Backtracking pops the current path until it reaches an ancestor that still has an untried alternative.
E.g. A→B→D with D a dead end and B exhausted removes both D and B before trying A's child C.
Answer: True.

steps.title: What BFS minimises
steps.text: BFS expands nodes level by level, so it finds a goal with the fewest edges. With unequal edge costs, the fewest edges need not mean the lowest total cost.

check.prompt: Route 1: one edge of cost 10. Route 2: two edges of cost 1 each. What is the total cost of route 2?
check.why: 1 + 1 = 2, which is cheaper than 10, yet BFS reaches the one-edge route first.
check.retry: Add the two edge costs.

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: In the example BFS returns the one-edge route of cost 10, not the cost-2 route. Decide whether BFS necessarily finds the cheapest route when edge costs differ.

solution: BFS orders by depth (number of edges), not by accumulated path cost.
E.g. a one-edge route of cost 10 is found before a two-edge route of cost 2.
Cheapest routes with unequal costs need a cost-based search such as uniform-cost search.
Answer: False.

steps.title: Where each direction starts
steps.text: Forward (data-driven) reasoning starts from the facts and fires every applicable rule. Backward (goal-driven) reasoning starts from a goal and selects only rules whose conclusion matches it.

check.prompt: Starting from all facts and firing every applicable rule describes…
check.why: That is the definition of data-driven reasoning.
check.retry: Which direction moves from facts towards conclusions?

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: The statement attributes the forward behaviour to backward reasoning. Decide whether it is true or false.

solution: Starting from all facts and firing every applicable rule is forward (data-driven) reasoning.
Backward reasoning starts from a goal and selects rules that can establish it.
Answer: False.

steps.title: Passes in iterative deepening
steps.text: Tree iterative deepening keeps no frontier between passes. Each bound runs a new depth-limited DFS from the root, so the shallow levels are revisited every time.

check.prompt: In a unary chain A→B→C searched at bounds 0, 1, 2, how many times is A visited?
check.why: A is the root, so each of the three passes visits it again.
check.retry: Count one visit of the root per pass.

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: The root being revisited in every pass shows what happens at each new bound. Decide whether the statement is true or false.

solution: Each new depth bound starts a fresh depth-limited DFS from the start state.
The shallow levels are repeated, trading extra time for O(bd) storage.
Answer: True.

steps.title: Graph vs search tree
steps.text: The state space is a graph: each state appears once. A search tree has one node per path from the start, so if two different paths reach the same state, that state appears as two tree nodes.

check.prompt: In two jugs, (0,0)→(4,0)→(4,3) and (0,0)→(0,3)→(4,3) both reach (4,3). How many tree nodes labelled (4,3) do these paths create?
check.why: Each distinct path gives its own tree node, even though the graph state is the same.
check.retry: A tree node corresponds to a path, not to a state.

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: Since different legal move sequences can reach the same graph state, decide whether that state can occur more than once in the search tree.

solution: A search tree has a node for each path from the start, while the graph has each state once.
Different move sequences can reach the same state, e.g. (4,3) via filling either jug first.
Answer: True.

steps.title: Specificity's formula
steps.text: Specificity = TN/(TN+FP). The denominator TN+FP is every actual negative.

check.prompt: Specificity measures the fraction of which group that is classified correctly?
check.why: TN+FP are all the truly negative cases; TN of them are correct.
check.retry: Which true label do TN and FP share?

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: A 'true-negative rate' is TN divided by all actual negatives. Compare with the specificity formula and decide true or false.

solution: Specificity = TN/(TN+FP), computed over actual negatives.
That is exactly the true-negative rate (TNR = 1 − FPR).
Answer: True.

steps.title: Training vs held-out error
steps.text: A deep subtree may fit noise in the training data. Removing it can make a few training points wrong again, but the simpler tree may predict new data better.

check.prompt: Collapsing a subtree into a leaf usually does what to training error?
options: Keeps it the same or increases it
check.why: The subtree was grown to fit training data, so removing it cannot improve the training fit.
check.retry: The subtree was chosen because it helped on training data.

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: Post-pruning keeps a simplification when it helps validation performance, even if training error rises. Decide whether the statement is true or false.

solution: Subtrees fitted to chance variations reduce training error but hurt generalization.
Pruning them can raise training error slightly while improving held-out accuracy.
Answer: True.

steps.title: Entropy of one class
steps.text: H = −Σ p_c log₂ p_c. In a pure node one class has p = 1 and all others have p = 0 (with 0·log 0 taken as 0).

check.prompt: What is −1·log₂(1)?
check.why: log₂(1) = 0, so the term is 0.
check.retry: What power of 2 equals 1?

steps.title: Decide the claim
steps.text: Every term in the entropy sum is zero for a pure node. Decide whether the statement that a pure node has entropy zero is true or false.

solution: In a pure node one class has p = 1 and the rest have p = 0.
H = −1·log₂1 − 0 = 0, using 0·log 0 = 0.
Answer: True.

steps.title: Aligned dot product
steps.text: With cross-correlation there is no flip. Multiply 2·1, 5·(−1), 1·1 and 4·(−1), then add the four products.

check.prompt: What is the dot product before the bias?
check.retry: The products are 2, −5, 1 and −4. Add them carefully with their signs.

steps.title: Add the bias
steps.text: Add the bias of 1 once to the dot product. No activation is applied. Submit the resulting pre-activation.

solution: Line up the filter with the patch without flipping: products 2·1, 5·(−1), 1·1, 4·(−1).
The sum is 2 − 5 + 1 − 4 = −6.
Add the bias: −6 + 1 = −5.

steps.title: Positions in 1D
steps.text: With no padding and dilation 1, the number of full positions is ⌊(I−F)/S⌋+1. Here I=20, F=5, S=2 and P=0.

steps.title: Divide before the floor
steps.text: Work out (20−5)/2, then take the floor. The floor drops any start position whose filter would run past the end.

check.why: 15/2 = 7.5, and the floor is 7.
check.retry: Work out 15/2, then round down.

steps.worked: ⌊15/2⌋ = ⌊7.5⌋ = 7. The last start index is 14, covering positions 14–18.

steps.title: Count the starts
steps.text: The floor gives the number of stride steps after the first position. Add 1 for the first position at index 0 and submit that count.

solution: Use O = ⌊(I − F)/S⌋ + 1 with I = 20, F = 5, S = 2.
(20 − 5)/2 = 7.5, and the floor is 7.
O = 7 + 1 = 8 full filter positions.

steps.title: Count each layer on its own
steps.text: For each layer, parameters = K(F_h·F_w·C_in + 1). C_in is the depth of that layer's own input: 3 for the first layer and 12 for the 1×1 layer.

steps.title: What a 1×1 filter spans
steps.text: A 1×1 convolution still spans every input channel. Decide how many weights one filter of the second layer has.

check.prompt: How many weights (not counting the bias) does one filter of the 1×1 layer have?
check.why: Its shape is 1×1×12. It mixes all 12 incoming channels.
check.retry: A standard filter spans all input channels. How many channels go into the second layer?

steps.worked: One 1×1 filter is 1×1×12 = 12 weights plus 1 bias.

steps.title: First layer
steps.text: There are 12 filters, each 3×3×3, each with one bias.

check.prompt: How many parameters does the 3×3 layer have?
check.retry: Work out 3·3·3 + 1 first, then multiply by 12.

steps.title: Second layer
steps.text: There are 5 filters, each 1×1×12, each with one bias.

check.prompt: How many parameters does the 1×1 layer have?
check.retry: Each filter has 12 weights and 1 bias. Multiply by 5.

steps.title: Total
steps.text: The layers have separate parameters, so add the two layer counts and submit that single number.

solution: Layer 1: 12 filters of 3×3×3 plus bias, 12(27 + 1) = 336.
Layer 2: 5 filters of 1×1×12 plus bias, 5(12 + 1) = 65.

steps.title: Euclidean distance
steps.text: d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). Work out each coordinate difference between (1,3) and (5,6) first.

steps.title: Squared differences
steps.text: Differences are 5 − 1 and 6 − 3. Square and add them.

check.prompt: What is (5 − 1)² + (6 − 3)²?
check.retry: Square 4 and 3, then add.

steps.title: Take the root
steps.text: Euclidean distance is the square root of the sum of squares you found. Submit that number.

solution: Sum of squares = 16 + 9 = 25.
Distance = √25 = 5.

steps.title: Effect of one switch
steps.text: Each vote moved from A to B lowers A by 1 and raises B by 1 at the same time. C stays at 2.

check.prompt: After one A→B switch, what are the votes for A and B?
check.why: 5 − 1 = 4 for A and 4 + 1 = 5 for B.
check.retry: A switch changes both counts, not just one.

steps.title: Check the plurality
steps.text: Find the smallest number of switches after which B is strictly ahead of both A and C. Check whether zero switches already works, then whether the counts after the first switch give B a unique lead, and submit that number.

solution: Initially A = 5, B = 4, so B is not the leader.
One switch gives A = 4, B = 5, C = 2, so B is the unique plurality.
Answer: 1.

steps.title: Single-path shortcut
steps.text: If a conditional FP-tree is a single path, every combination of its nodes is a frequent pattern with the suffix, and its support is the smallest count among the chosen nodes. So only combinations whose minimum count is at least 4 qualify.

steps.title: Check the counts
steps.text: The path is A:8 → B:6 → C:4 and the minimum count is 4.

check.prompt: Which nodes can appear in a frequent combination?
options: A, B and C, since every count is ≥ 4
Only A and B, since C is not above 4
check.why: Thresholds are inclusive: C:4 meets the minimum count 4, so every subset's minimum count is ≥ 4.
check.retry: Is a count of 4 enough when the minimum support count is 4?

steps.title: Count the combinations
steps.text: Count the nonempty subsets of {A,B,C}; each one is combined with X.

check.prompt: How many nonempty subsets does {A,B,C} have?
check.why: 2³ − 1 = 7: A, B, C, AB, AC, BC, ABC.
check.retry: Use 2³ and remove the empty subset.

steps.worked: AX:8, BX:6, CX:4, ABX:6, ACX:4, BCX:4, ABCX:4 — 7 itemsets.

steps.title: Add the suffix itself
steps.text: X is frequent, so {X} on its own also counts. Add it to the itemsets from the path and submit the total.

solution: The conditional tree is a single path, and all counts (8, 6, 4) are ≥ 4.
Every nonempty subset of {A,B,C} combined with X is frequent: 2³ − 1 = 7 itemsets (AX:8, BX:6, CX:4, ABX:6, ACX:4, BCX:4, ABCX:4).
{X} itself is frequent and also counts.
Answer: 7 + 1 = 8.

steps.title: Three layers to back up
steps.text: Work bottom-up: the bottom MAX nodes take the max of each leaf pair, the two MIN nodes take the min of their MAX children, and the root takes the max.

steps.title: Left MIN subtree
steps.text: Bottom MAX values for (2,9) and (3,5), then MIN over them.

check.prompt: What does the left MIN node back up?
check.why: max(2,9)=9 and max(3,5)=5, then min(9,5)=5.
check.retry: Take max within each pair first, then the min of the two results.

steps.title: Right MIN subtree
steps.text: Bottom MAX values for (6,1) and (4,8), then MIN over them.

check.prompt: What does the bottom MAX node with leaves (4,8) back up?
check.why: max(4,8)=8; the other MAX node gives max(6,1)=6.
check.retry: A MAX node keeps the larger leaf.

steps.title: Root decision
steps.text: The root is a MAX node: take the larger of the two MIN values and submit that number.

solution: Bottom MAX nodes: max(2,9)=9, max(3,5)=5, max(6,1)=6, max(4,8)=8.
MIN nodes: left min(9,5)=5, right min(6,8)=6.
Root MAX: max(5,6)=6.
Answer: 6.

steps.title: Cutoff at MIN children
steps.text: Left to right: the first MIN child sets α at the root. Each later MIN child lowers β leaf by leaf; when β ≤ α, its remaining leaves are skipped. A cutoff on the last leaf skips nothing.

steps.title: First child sets α
steps.text: Evaluate [7,6] completely (with α=−∞ nothing can be pruned).

check.prompt: What is the root's α after the first child?
check.retry: The MIN child returns its smaller leaf.

steps.title: Second child [2,8,9]
steps.text: The first leaf is 2, so β=2. Compare with α=6.

check.prompt: Which leaves of the second child are skipped?
options: None, every leaf must be read
check.why: β=2 ≤ α=6 immediately after the first leaf, so 8 and 9 are never read.
check.retry: Compare the first leaf 2 with α=6.

steps.title: Third child [9,7,4]
steps.text: Track β as each leaf is read, with α=6.

check.prompt: When does the third child reach β ≤ α?
options: Only at its last leaf 4, so nothing is skipped
At its first leaf 9, skipping 7 and 4
check.why: β goes 9, then 7 (both > 6), then 4 ≤ 6, but no leaves remain.
check.retry: A cutoff needs β ≤ 6; check 9 and 7 against 6.

steps.worked: β = 9 → 7 → 4; the cutoff condition only holds after the last leaf, so 0 leaves are skipped.

steps.title: Count the skips
steps.text: Add the skipped leaves from the three children (the first child skips none) and submit the total.

solution: First child [7,6] returns 6; root α=6.
Second child: leaf 2 gives β=2 ≤ 6, so 8 and 9 are skipped.
Third child: β becomes 9, 7, then 4; it only drops to ≤6 at the last leaf, so nothing is skipped. Root value is 6.
Total skipped: 0+2+0 = 2.
Answer: 2.

steps.title: Order and scale
steps.text: The gap is validation error minus training error. Both are already percentages, so subtracting them gives percentage points. Do not compute a relative change.

check.prompt: Which expression gives the gap in percentage points?
check.why: Points means a simple difference on the same percentage scale, taken as validation minus training.
check.retry: The question asks for validation minus training, as a difference rather than a ratio.

steps.title: Compute and submit
steps.text: Work out the difference and submit it as a plain number of percentage points.

solution: Both rates are on the same percentage scale, so take a simple difference.
Gap = validation − training = 19 − 7 = 12 percentage points.

steps.title: Gini drop
steps.text: Drop = G(parent) − Σ (|D_j|/|D|)·G(D_j), with G = 1 − Σ p_c². Work in fractions so the final answer is exact.

steps.title: Parent Gini
steps.text: The parent has 6+ and 4− out of 10, so p₊ = 0.6 and p₋ = 0.4.

check.prompt: What is the parent Gini?
check.retry: Compute 1 − (0.6² + 0.4²).

steps.title: Child Gini values
steps.text: The left child (4+,0−) is pure. The right child (2+,4−) has p₊ = 1/3 and p₋ = 2/3.

check.prompt: What is the right child's Gini (fraction allowed)?
check.retry: Square 1/3 and 2/3, add, and subtract from 1.

steps.title: Weighted child impurity
steps.text: The left child holds 4/10 of the samples and the right child 6/10.

check.prompt: What is the weighted child Gini?
check.retry: Multiply 4/9 by the right child's weight 6/10.

steps.title: Subtract
steps.text: Subtract the weighted child impurity 4/15 from the parent Gini 12/25 using a common denominator of 75. Submit the exact fraction.

solution: Answer: 16/75.

steps.title: Full batches
steps.text: Each mini-batch of 16 examples gives one update. First count how many complete batches fit into 70.

check.prompt: How many complete batches of 16 fit into 70 examples?
check.retry: Find floor(70 / 16).

steps.title: Count the partial batch
steps.text: The 6 leftover examples form an incomplete final batch, which is kept and gives one more update. Add it to the full batches and submit the number of updates per epoch (that is, ⌈70/16⌉).

solution: 70 / 16 = 4.375, so there are 4 full batches (64 examples).
The remaining 6 examples form a kept, incomplete fifth batch.
Updates per epoch = ⌈70/16⌉.
Answer: 5.

steps.title: Average linkage
steps.text: d_avg(A,B) = Σ d(a,b) / (|A||B|), summing over every cross pair. Here |A| = 3 and |B| = 2.

steps.title: Count and list the pairs
steps.text: Compute |a − b| for a ∈ {0, 2, 4} and b ∈ {6, 10}.

check.prompt: How many cross pairs are there?
check.why: 3 × 2 = 6 pairs.
check.retry: Multiply the two cluster sizes.

steps.title: Sum the distances
steps.text: Add the six cross-pair distances.

check.prompt: What is the sum of the six cross distances?
check.retry: Recheck each |a − b|, e.g. |4 − 10| = 6.

steps.title: Divide by the pair count
steps.text: Divide the sum by the number of cross pairs (not by the number of clusters) and submit the result.

solution: Sum = 36 over 3 × 2 = 6 pairs.
Average linkage = 36/6 = 6.

steps.title: Each pass starts fresh
steps.text: Iterative deepening restarts at the root for every bound, so a node at depth k is visited once in every pass whose limit is at least k. Repeated visits must be counted every time.

steps.title: Nodes within a limit
steps.text: A perfect binary tree has 2^k nodes at depth k, so a pass with limit L visits 1 + 2 + … + 2^L = 2^(L+1) − 1 nodes.

check.prompt: How many nodes does the pass with limit 2 visit?
check.retry: Add the counts at depths 0, 1 and 2.

check.prompt: How many nodes does the pass with limit 3 visit?
check.retry: Use 2^(L+1) − 1 with L = 3.

steps.text: Add the four pass counts, keeping repeated visits, and submit the total.

solution: Each pass restarts at the root, so repeated visits count again.
A pass with limit L visits 2^(L+1) − 1 nodes: 1, 3, 7, 15 for L = 0, 1, 2, 3.
Answer: 26.

steps.title: Midpoint boundary and mean update
steps.text: In 1D, a point goes to the closer of two centers; the boundary is their midpoint. A point exactly on the boundary is tied, and the question says ties go to the smaller center.

steps.title: Find the boundary
steps.text: Compute the midpoint of centers 0 and 8.

check.prompt: What is the midpoint between centers 0 and 8?
check.retry: Average the two centers.

steps.title: Resolve the tie
steps.text: Point 4 is at distance 4 from both centers. Apply the stated tie rule.

check.prompt: Which cluster does point 4 join?
options: Neither; it is dropped this round
check.why: |4 − 0| = |4 − 8| = 4, and ties go to the smaller center.
check.retry: Re-read the tie-breaking rule in the question.

steps.title: Average the higher cluster
steps.text: The larger center is updated to the mean of the points assigned to center 8. Average those points and submit the result.

solution: Boundary between centers 0 and 8 is 4.
0 and 3 go to center 0; 4 is tied and goes to the smaller center 0; 7 and 11 go to center 8.
Updated larger center = (7 + 11)/2 = 9.

steps.title: Coordinate differences
steps.text: Squared Euclidean distance = Σ(x_j − z_j)², without a square root. Subtract the sample (−1,3) from the query (2,−1) coordinate by coordinate.

check.prompt: What is the second-coordinate difference −1 − 3?
check.why: −1 − 3 = −4; the first difference is 2 − (−1) = 3.
check.retry: Subtract 3 from −1.

steps.title: Square and add
steps.text: Square both differences (signs disappear) and add them. Do not take a square root, since the question asks for squared distance.

solution: Differences: 2 − (−1) = 3 and −1 − 3 = −4.
Squared distance = 3² + (−4)² = 9 + 16 = 25.
Answer: 25.

steps.title: Inverse-distance weights
steps.text: Each neighbour votes with weight 1/d, so closer neighbours count more. A class's share is its summed weight divided by the total weight of all three neighbours.

check.prompt: Which neighbour gets the largest weight?
check.why: 1/1 = 1 is larger than 1/2 and 1/3.
check.retry: Smaller distance means larger 1/d.

steps.title: B's total weight
steps.text: B's neighbours are at distances 2 and 3.

check.prompt: What is B's total weight (fraction allowed)?
check.retry: Add 1/2 and 1/3 using denominator 6.

steps.title: Total weight
steps.text: Add A's weight and B's weight.

check.prompt: What is the total weight?
check.retry: Write 1 as 6/6 and add 5/6.

steps.title: Form the fraction
steps.text: Divide B's weight 5/6 by the total 11/6 and simplify. Submit the exact fraction. (Notice what this says about who wins despite B having two neighbours.)

solution: Weights 1/d: A gets 1/1 = 1; B gets 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6.
Total weight = 1 + 5/6 = 11/6.
B's fraction = (5/6)/(11/6) = 5/11 ≈ 0.4545, so A wins the weighted vote despite B's majority count.
Answer: 5/11.

steps.title: Observed vs unobserved features
steps.text: An observed value, even 0, is evidence and contributes the factor P(X=0∣c). An unobserved feature is marginalised. In Naïve Bayes this means simply leaving it out of the product, not pretending it was recorded as 0.

check.prompt: How should the unobserved binary feature be handled?
options: Leave it out of the product (marginalise it)
Set the class score to zero
check.why: Summing P(f∣c) over both values gives 1, so a missing feature drops out. Treating it as 0 invents evidence.
check.retry: What is P(f=0∣c) + P(f=1∣c)?

steps.title: From scores to a posterior
steps.text: Once each class has its score, decide what turns the scores into posteriors.

check.prompt: Which operation turns the class scores into posteriors?
options: Divide each score by the sum of all class scores
Replace each likelihood with the pooled marginal P(x_j)
Take the largest score as the posterior directly
check.why: The sum of the scores is P(evidence), the Bayes denominator. Pooled marginals ignore the class, and a raw score is not a probability.
check.retry: Bayes' rule divides by the evidence. How do you get that from the scores?

steps.title: Select the two operations
steps.text: Select the option that includes the observed X=0 as a factor and the option that normalises. Reject treating the missing feature as a recorded zero, and reject class-free pooled marginals.

solution: The observed X=0 is evidence, so each class score includes the factor P(X=0∣c).
The unobserved feature is marginalised (left out). Recording it as 0 would add false evidence.
Pooled marginals P(x_j) carry no class information, so they cannot replace P(x_j∣c).
The posterior is each score divided by the sum of the class scores.
Answer: 'Multiply by the conditional probability of observing x=0.' and 'Normalize class scores by their sum.'

steps.title: Score each class
steps.text: s_c = P(c)·P(x₁∣c)·P(x₂∣c)·P(x₃∣c). The given triples already refer to the observed values (1,0,1), and the classes are equally likely, so P(S) = P(T) = 0.5.

check.prompt: What is s_S?
check.retry: Multiply the three S probabilities, then multiply by the prior 0.5.

check.prompt: What is s_T?
check.retry: Use T's triple (0.4, 0.5, 0.2) and the prior 0.5.

steps.title: Normalise
steps.text: P(S∣x) = s_S / (s_S + s_T). Divide and submit the decimal. With equal priors you could drop the 0.5s, but you must still normalise.

solution: Equal priors: P(S) = P(T) = 0.5.
Answer: 0.6.

steps.title: Hidden unit
steps.text: Compute net = 0.5 × 3 − 1 and apply ReLU.

steps.title: Linear output with the skip term
steps.text: Substitute h and x = 3 into o = 2h + 0.2x − 0.4. Include the direct 0.2x term and submit o (no activation on the output).

steps.title: Half sum of squared errors
steps.text: E = ½ Σ_k (t_k − o_k)². Pair each target with its own output: (0.4, 0.1) and (0.3, 0.7).

steps.title: Squared residuals
steps.text: Residuals are 0.4 − 0.1 and 0.3 − 0.7. Square each one and add.

check.retry: Squares are always positive: (−0.4)² = 0.16.

solution: Squares: 0.09 and 0.16, sum 0.25.
Answer: 0.125.

steps.title: Bias update via the hidden delta
steps.text: The hidden bias changes by Δb = η δ_h, where δ_h = ReLU'(net_h) × 0.5 × δ_o and δ_o = (t − o)·1 for the linear output.

steps.title: Forward pass
steps.text: net_h = 0.6 × 2 + 0.1. Apply ReLU, then o = 0.5h + 0.1.

check.prompt: What is o?
check.retry: 0.6 × 2 = 1.2, plus b = 0.1, gives net_h. Then o = 0.5h + 0.1.

steps.title: Output delta
steps.text: δ_o = (t − o) × 1 with t = 0.25.

check.prompt: What is δ_o?
check.retry: Target minus output, with the linear derivative = 1.

steps.title: Hidden delta
steps.text: δ_h = ReLU'(1.3) × (outgoing weight 0.5) × δ_o.

check.prompt: What is δ_h?
check.retry: ReLU' = 1 because net_h > 0. Multiply by 0.5 and δ_o.

steps.title: Update the bias
steps.text: b_new = b + η δ_h with b = 0.1 and η = 0.2 (equivalently b − η ∂E/∂b). Submit the new hidden bias.

solution: Answer: 0.05.

steps.title: Line through the means
steps.text: An OLS line with intercept passes through (x̄, ȳ), so b = ȳ − m·x̄. Here m = 1.4 and (x̄, ȳ) = (5, 8).

check.retry: Multiply the slope by x̄ = 5.

steps.text: Subtract that product from ȳ = 8 and submit the intercept.

steps.title: Centered slope formula
steps.text: m = Sxy / Sxx with Sxy = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) and Sxx = Σ(x − x̄)². Data: x = 1, 2, 3, 4 and y = 3, 4, 8, 9.

check.retry: Multiply each pair of deviations, e.g. (−1.5)(−3) = 4.5, then add.

steps.title: Pythagoras for projections
steps.text: For a unit vector u, ||x||² = z² + ||residual||², where z = uᵀx. So the squared reconstruction error is ||x||² − z². Check that u = (3/5, 4/5) has length 1.

check.prompt: What is the score z?
check.retry: Multiply matching entries and add.

steps.title: Total squared length
steps.text: Compute ||(2,1)||².

check.prompt: What is 2² + 1²?
check.retry: Square each centered coordinate and add.

steps.title: Subtract the kept part
steps.text: The squared error is the total squared length minus the squared score. Compute it and submit. (You can check it by forming x − z·u directly.)

solution: u = (3/5, 4/5) has length 1.
Score z = (3/5)(2) + (4/5)(1) = 2; reconstruction z·u = (6/5, 8/5).
||x||² = 5, so squared error = 5 − 2² = 1 (equivalently residual (4/5, −3/5) has squared norm 16/25 + 9/25 = 1).
Answer: 1.

steps.title: Trace equals eigenvalue sum
steps.text: For any square matrix, the sum of its eigenvalues equals its trace (the sum of diagonal entries). Off-diagonal covariances change the individual eigenvalues but not their sum.

check.prompt: Does the off-diagonal covariance affect the sum of the eigenvalues?
options: No, the sum equals the trace
Yes, it must be added to the sum
Yes, it must be subtracted twice
check.why: The characteristic polynomial's λ coefficient is the trace, independent of off-diagonals.
check.retry: Check with [[3,1],[1,3]]: eigenvalues 4 and 2.

steps.title: Add the diagonal
steps.text: Add the two given diagonal entries (the variances 5 and 3) and submit that number.

solution: The sum of a matrix's eigenvalues equals its trace.
Trace = 5 + 3 = 8, regardless of the off-diagonal entries.
Answer: 8.

steps.title: Sum the window
steps.text: Average pooling returns the window's sum divided by the number of values. First add 1, 7, 5 and 3.

check.prompt: What is the sum of the window values?
check.retry: Add the four values.

steps.title: Divide by the count
steps.text: Divide the sum by the number of activations in the window, which is 4, and submit the mean. Do not confuse it with max pooling, which would return 7.

solution: Sum of the window: 1 + 7 + 5 + 3 = 16.
There are 4 activations, so the mean is 16/4 = 4.
Answer: 4.

steps.title: F1 definition
steps.text: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall: F1 = 2PR/(P+R), equivalently 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN). TN is not used.

steps.title: Precision
steps.text: Predicted positives = TP + FP = 24 + 16 = 40.

check.prompt: What is precision?
check.retry: Divide TP by TP + FP.

steps.title: Recall
steps.text: Actual positives = TP + FN = 24 + 6 = 30.

check.prompt: What is recall?
check.retry: Divide TP by TP + FN.

steps.title: Harmonic-mean pieces
steps.text: Compute the numerator 2PR and the denominator P + R separately.

check.prompt: What is 2·P·R?
check.retry: Multiply 0.6 by 0.8, then double it.

steps.title: Simplify to a proportion
steps.text: Divide 0.96 by 1.4 (or 48 by 70) and reduce to lowest terms. Submit the exact fraction.

solution: Check: 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN) = 48/70.
Both reduce to 24/35 ≈ 0.6857.
Answer: 24/35.

steps.title: What confidence needs
steps.text: conf(A→B) = n(A∩B)/n(A), where n(A∩B) counts baskets containing both A and B. You are given n(A) = 70 and n(B) = 60 but not the joint count, so it must be derived.

steps.title: Use the 'at least one' fact
steps.text: Every one of the 120 baskets contains A or B, so the number of baskets with A or B equals 120. Inclusion–exclusion links that union to the joint count.

check.prompt: Which identity gives the joint count?
options: n(A or B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A and B)
n(A and B) = n(A) · n(B) / N
check.why: Adding n(A) and n(B) counts the overlap twice; subtracting it once gives the union. The product form assumes independence, which is not given.
check.retry: When you add the A baskets and the B baskets, which baskets are counted twice?
Rearrange: n(A∩B) = n(A) + n(B) − 120.

steps.title: Form the confidence
steps.text: Divide the joint count by the antecedent's count n(A) (not by n(B) or by 120). Submit as a simplified fraction or decimal.

solution: All 120 baskets contain A or B, so the number of baskets with A or B is 120.
Inclusion–exclusion: 120 = 70 + 60 − n(A∩B), so n(A∩B) = 10.

steps.title: Lift formula
steps.text: lift(X→Y) = conf(X→Y)/supp(Y), with conf = n(X∪Y)/n(X) and supp(Y) = n(Y)/N. Here N = 50, n(X) = 20, n(Y) = 25, n(X∪Y) = 15.

steps.text: Compute the confidence of X→Y and the overall rate of Y.

check.prompt: conf(X→Y) as a decimal?
check.retry: Divide the joint count by n(X) = 20.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Divide the confidence by the baseline rate of Y and submit the result as a number.

solution: Answer: 1.5.

steps.text: One-vs-one trains a separate binary SVM for every unordered pair of classes, so the count is K(K−1)/2. One-vs-rest would train only K.
